>> In Asia, there are a few companies building prediction markets, and they frame it as "the information market." >> I agree with that. I think we should think of them as information markets, not prediction markets. I agree. >> Could you explain why?

>> Because — to your point — polling was a good science when we didn't have the ability to gauge actual sentiment. When we didn't have people's opinions in digitized form. When we didn't have the ability — meaning Twitter, meaning X, right? — when we didn't have the ability to get the X firehose engaged sentiment of very large groups of people. Calling up a thousand people and getting a statistically relevant sample set was the best we had.

So information — trading is always about having, using, the best information available. No one has perfect — if you have perfect information, you're insider trading, right? By definition. So unless you have inside information, you're trading on imperfect information. And so it's all about just having slightly better information than my competitor. That's all I need.

And knowing the views and beliefs — the behind-the-scenes views and beliefs from 10 million people — is better than interrupting a thousand people at dinner and getting their non-unbiased belief. Anonymity has value. Understanding how people act versus what they say — what they do versus what they say they do. All of that is valuable information, and it can be used by professional traders to make better-informed decisions.

十五、散户 vs Citadel：绵羊与狮子

>> How are the world's best algorithmic trading companies and funds — the Citadels of the world — going to compete in a world where the average 15-year-old with OpenAI or Claude is going to build a bot that does pretty much the same thing?

>> I'm a seller on that. I think good luck competing with Citadel for a long time. I don't care if you have Claude. I don't care how good you are — Claude. >> Until everything is run by agents? >> Yeah. And even then, not all agents will be created equal. And I guarantee you, Citadel will have the best agents. Jane Street will have the best agents.

So that's why I always tell you: be careful about day trading. You're a sheep amongst lions. It's very, very challenging. Buy and hold, invest in ETFs. I don't think you can compete. Whatever you have in your home, they have on steroids, and they've had it for longer than you.

>> Yeah. Okay, fair enough. >> There is this index that shows retail investor does not outperform the NASDAQ. >> Right? We know, by the way, 75% of hedge funds don't outperform the S&P's. That's not just — >> Well, what are people trying to do then?

>> I try not to judge. I think it's hope. I think they want to believe that they have the ability to outperform. It's ego. Why do people buy lottery tickets? Because somebody won, right?

So I think there's an element — I believe in an element of freedom that everyone should be allowed to take that chance. I think that with a reasonable amount of your wealth, it's probably smart to do so, because we should all have hope. We should all swing for the fences with something in our lives.

But in general, the average investor who doesn't have the ability to monitor markets at least 5 hours a day at minimum would do better off investing in pooled vehicles — Bitcoin, ETFs, things like that. But I don't want laws that tell people what to do with their money. That's why I shy away from restrictive laws about things like prediction markets.

十六、给孩子的金融教育与"未来价值电子表格"

>> My last question to you: you've got two kids, like you said. Would you encourage them to study finance?

>> So my 12-year-old daughter has a show on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange — >> You're kidding. Wow. >> — Children's Financial Network — where she interviews big investors and she asks them how they teach their kids about money.

So it is a constant source of conversation in our home. And I think the schools do a horrible job of teaching children financial literacy. And so I think it's incumbent upon all of us — not just in crypto, but in TradFi — to strongly encourage our children to find joy in this particular topic.

>> What is one rule you teach at home?

冲动消费的未来价值 App

>> It's kind of near you. I have a little — I moved it to Claude — I used to have a little spreadsheet on my phone that computed future value.

Money should be for joy. So I don't want to be that "look at everything on the net present value basis" person. But if we walk into a store and want to buy X, and they say "oh, X was great, I also saw Y" — impulse purchase — I make them put the present value of that impulse purchase into this little app (now spreadsheet), and it pops out at a 6% annualized return what that would be in 20 years.

>> Wow. >> And I ask them: "Are you sure you want this? Because this is what you're giving up."

So — opportunity cost and future value calculations. They're super simple to understand. And it forces you to make smart decisions. So: "Sweetheart, would you like this or would you like $120 in 20 years?" And we do it. We have it on my phone. We do it all the time. And their kids are smart. I'd say 80% of the time they go "yeah, I want the 120 bucks." Sometimes they go "I want the toy." But that's okay — they're making an informed decision at that point.

>> I'd be curious to see how their decisions progress as they age. Maybe you can do it every year and track that. >> My 12-year-old does it all the time. She has the math in her head now, and she rounds it up, and she says "you know what, this isn't worth it, Daddy." But now she tracks it, so I have to give her that when she's older.

But I think just basic lessons in opportunity costs. What does it mean to take on risk? When is risk a good risk versus a bad risk? Kids are really smart. They understand this stuff.

>> Excellent. Do you do that when you buy things too? >> All the time. All the time. I think about when I'm 80. We all value different things. I value safety and security. I'd rather have the security of knowing the money's there than the shiny thing. That's my personality. I don't judge other people for how they think about it.

But I think you just have to teach — that's a non-intuitive thing. That math is non-intuitive. And so I think you have to be taught that. I was lucky enough to be taught that at business school. And I think these are not hard concepts. We put jargon around things to make it seem more complicated than it is. Future value versus present value is not a difficult concept.

关于那个"未来自己敲窗"的表情包

You know, there's a meme going on that my daughter has showed me about — like — your future self screaming because you're not studying. All the kids are doing this meme, and it's like — it's funny to them, but it's sad to me. It's like a grown person seeing their teenage self not studying for the test, and like, banging on the window. It's horrifying as an adult. The kids think it's funny.

And I'm trying to help her understand why that's so popular — because it's speaking to a universe of people who wish they could go back in time and make those smart decisions, but they weren't given the ammunition to do so. It was unfair of them. It was unfair to expect them to do that.

So that's what I try to teach — not just my kids. I teach at schools, and I do as much as I can. And my daughter and I are working on a little YouTube video channel that we hope to push out just for that reason. Children's Financial Network. We try to teach kids in fun ways using games we make on Claude — things like opportunity cost and all that stuff.

十七、地位游戏与父亲的第二份工

>> My last question for you: you live in New York. >> New York City. Yes. >> Yes. And people — that was a very obnoxious thing, that was — when you ask somebody, say, "New York" and they go "I live in Staten Island." >> Which I grew up in. I grew up in Staten Island. New York City. I'm very snobbish there. Yes.

>> What — do you ever play the status game? You have to up your car, your houses.

>> I grew up — my mom worked three jobs. My mom cleaned toilets. My dad worked two jobs. I remember when he used to come home from his first job. I used to be waiting for him with my baseball mitt to play catch.

And I remember waiting for the street lights to go on and being very sad and anxious — because I knew they were about to come on, because when the street lights went on, my dad had to get into his car and go to his second job.

And so — no. But I don't want to virtue signal here. I don't begrudge people who want to work hard and have toys. I'm just not — I just didn't grow up like that. So it's just not important to me.

But you know, I have a status of like wanting my daughter to get straight A's. That's my status. So I pay for tutors and things like that. We all splurge on things.

Don't judge. Find out what's important to you. Try to give back a little bit. It's the best you can hope for.

>> That was a beautiful ending. >> Yeah. Well, thank you very much.

尾声

>> I encourage everyone to check out John's daughter's channel. >> Oh, thank you. >> What is it called again? >> The Children's Financial Network. >> Children's Financial Network. And also, you were featured in the book Rigged: The True Story of an Ivy League Kid Who Changed the World of Oil. We don't have time to go over that book, but — >> This one. >> Yeah. What was your — ? >> I was lucky enough to be in a place where I was tasked by the New York Mercantile Exchange to build the first ever oil exchange in the Middle East. >> Yeah. Okay. Check out that book. Check out his channel. Check out our channel. Subscribe.

Thank you very much for watching. Thank you, John.

item.description:
## 一、隐藏的心理钩子：他童年"路灯焦虑"与今日"稳定币福音"是同一件事
John 反复讲的两个故事看似无关——小时候等待路灯亮起时的心痛（因为爸爸要去做第二份工作），以及现在痛斥"银行把 4.5% 利息吞掉、只给客户 10 个基点"——**其实是同一段创伤在两个时空的回响**。他不是在做商业布道，他是在**为童年那个无力的男孩追讨迟到几十年的利息**。这解释了一个悖论：为什么一个华尔街老将会主动放弃 Coinbase 的短期利润去做"复利返还"？因为对他而言，10 basis points vs 3% 复利 20 年 = "一年学费" = **他父亲不必打第二份工的那个平行宇宙**。华尔街最坚定的稳定币收益派，动机是心理学的，不是金融的。
## 二、最反直觉的观察：泡沫是"文明的孵化器"，理性投资才是创新的敌人
他引用与 Nouriel Roubini 合作的研究抛出了一个几乎没人敢说的结论——**资产泡沫期，相关技术专利申请量增长 4 倍**。这意味着：如果所有人都变成"冷静的价值投资者"，人类的技术进步会立即减速。这是一个跨领域的连接——它与**古生物学的"寒武纪大爆发"

item.title: [Mercatus Center] Why Americans Still Argue About the Founding with Thomas Merrill
item.dc:creator: Mercatus Center
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、当"美德的梦"成为自我欺骗的引擎

Merrill 对杰斐逊最锋利的诊断藏在一个看似矛盾的观察里：让杰斐逊背叛《独立宣言》的，不是他的利益，而恰恰是他对"自己是有德之人"的信念。传统的道德叙事总把私利视作原罪——利益扭曲原则、金钱腐蚀灵魂。但杰斐逊的悲剧走得更深：他之所以能在 1790 年后逐渐沉默、在密苏里危机中站到日后卡尔霍恩阵营的一边，不是因为他放弃了自然权利，而是因为他太确信自己"手里握着正确的观念"。"我脑子里有对的东西"这一自信，反而成了他不必真的去做什么的许可证。

这里有一个几乎令人不寒而栗的结构性发现：杰斐逊在《独立宣言》被删除的那段关于奴隶制的文字里，把责任全推给英王——"是他把奴隶制强加给我们"。Merrill 称之为"无辜的暴君"（the innocent tyrant）叙事。这不是虚伪，虚伪太表层了；这是一种更精致的道德结构——把自己塑造为受制于外力的正义者，就无需真的承担改变现状的代价。这个模式在今天几乎无处不在：AI 公司一边警告"超级智能会毁灭人类"，一边加速训练前沿模型并游说限制开源竞争者；ESG 部门的存在本身就成了继续原有商业模式的免罪符。杰斐逊是第一个"表演型自由主义者"，而我们仍活在他开创的这种修辞政治里。

二、一个被忽视的结构陷阱：农业共和主义与奴隶制的物质捆绑

大多数关于建国的讨论把杰斐逊的"自相矛盾"看作观念层面的张力：洛克式的自然权利 vs 古典共和主义的公民美德。但 Merrill 让人看到一个更硬的东西——杰斐逊心中的"美德公民"（自耕农、有土地、能对抗僭主的独立人格），在美国南方的物质条件下，几乎必然要靠奴隶制来维持。他崇拜的那种"上帝的选民"式的农民，其经济基础就是奴隶劳动。于是他的政治联盟——那些能对抗汉密尔顿式金融权力的"农业利益"——恰好就是最深陷奴隶制、日后会孕育出卡尔霍恩派的那批人。

这是一个跨领域的深刻教训：一种理念的道德纯洁性，可能被它所依赖的物质基础悄悄取消。这正是当代技术批评里最难谈的部分——"清洁能源"依赖刚果的钴矿童工，"数字自由"跑在被剥削的东南亚内容审核员之上，"开放科学"由能源密集的算力堆出来。杰斐逊不是没看到矛盾，而是他的整个政治想象力被物质基础反向殖民了：为了保护他心中的"美德共和国"，他必须保护那个让美德得以存在的、不义的生产关系。这是任何一场以"高尚理想"为名的政治都要面对的镜子。

三、一个反直觉的历史因果重排：真正塑造 20 世纪美国的不是 1776，也不是 1619，而是重建时代

这是全场对话里我认为最反常识、也最有政治后果的观察：南方在战场上输掉了内战，但在思想战场上赢了重建。Merrill 提醒我们，1619 和 1776 之争其实都过度聚焦于"起源"——仿佛美国的原罪或荣光在最初一刻就已铸就，此后只是展开。但决定 20 世纪美国种族秩序的关键决策，发生在 1865 到 1900 之间：谁被允许投票、谁的暴力被合法化、哪种历史叙事进入教科书。起源叙事的过度加权，恰恰是逃避近代责任的一种方式——把问题推到"建国父亲"身上，就不用面对我们自己的祖父辈做过什么。

这个因果重排揭示了一个更普遍的模式：当一个共同体反复争论"我们从哪里来"，往往是为了不谈"我们最近做了什么"。这一点惊人地适用于当代科技史。硅谷不断讲述"两个年轻人在车库里"的创世神话，是为了掩盖 2010 年后的一系列关键决策——广告驱动的注意力商业模式、算法推荐的规模化部署、并购竞争者以垄断数据。起源崇拜与近期责任的规避，在结构上是同一件事的两面。

四、一个令人不安的对称性：进步派与保守派共享同一套元结构

Merrill 顺口说出的一个观察值得单独放大："进步"（progressive）和"保守"（conservative）这两个词本身就是相互定义的，它们都是关于"你对变化的态度"的立场，而不是关于"我们要走向什么样的政体"的立场。古代政治学问的是"什么是好的政体"（regime），现代政治问的是"变还是不变"。这意味着——当代美国左右两派，在深层结构上共享着同一个哲学框架，只是分居在时间轴的两端。

这个观察让人后背发凉，因为它解释了为什么政治辩论会陷入某种"结构性同构的对骂"：双方都缺乏对"好生活"本身的实质性描述，只能不断攻击对方对"变化速度"的判断。这也是为什么"后自由主义"（post-liberalism）的兴起并不是复古，而是一次真正的哲学位移——它试图把政治重新拉回到"共同善"的实质讨论。跨到技术领域看，"AI 加速派"（e/acc）与"AI 安全派"其实也是这套时间性立场的翻版：都不问"我们究竟想要什么样的人-机共存秩序"，只争"该跑多快"。真正稀缺的，永远是关于"好"本身的实质想象。

五、"对话的内在无政府主义"作为文明的免疫机制

最后一个让人意外的连接：Merrill 用来描述好的经典阅读研讨课的那个短语——"the inner anarchism of a genuine conversation"（真正对话的内在无政府主义）——其实是一个可以推广到整个自由社会的免疫学原理。经典之所以不会变成教条，恰恰是因为经典之间彼此矛盾：读阿里斯托芬的《云》时苏格拉底否定宙斯，读奥古斯丁《忏悔录》时又满纸上帝。学生被迫在矛盾中自己拼装意义。

这与算法推荐系统的问题形成刺眼的对照。推荐系统把"对话"优化成了"共识"，把"矛盾的经典"替换成了"相似的内容"，于是文明的免疫系统就被抽走了。杰斐逊说宪法应该每 19 年重写一次——他真正抓住的是同一个直觉：任何秩序的正当性都必须由每一代人重新自我立法，否则就会退化为祖先崇拜。而每一代人要能重新立法，就必须先能真正地不同意彼此。这或许是这场关于 250 年前的对话，留给 2026 年的我们最锋利的一份遗产。

📝 转录文本

Why Americans Still Argue About the Founding — with Thomas Merrill

主持人开场

Welcome to Virtual Sentiments. I'm your host, Kristen Collins.

On today's episode, I talk to Dr. Thomas Merrill. Tom is an associate professor in the School of Public Affairs at American University, where he directs the Lincoln Scholars Program, a core techs program for first and second year students. He is the author of Hume and the Politics of Enlightenment, published in 2015 by Cambridge University Press, and he has edited a number of volumes, including The Political Thought of the Civil War, and is a co-editor of the journal American Political Thought.

We discuss Tom's work on early American political thought, especially the writings of Thomas Jefferson, author of the Declaration of Independence. This episode concludes a set of episodes on the 250th anniversary of the American founding, with earlier conversations with Laura Field and Osita Nwanebu. This episode focuses more directly on the historical context of the founding.

We talk about how the tensions and self-contradictions within Thomas Jefferson's long career make him, in Tom's words, "a tragic figure." We talk about how, even as we celebrate the principles of liberty and equality set down in the Declaration, we must also acknowledge the dark side of the founding and the dark sides of our founding fathers, especially as they relate to the legacy of slavery.

Thomas Jefferson was a complicated figure, and by studying him, warts and all, we learn not only about the intellectual strengths of the Declaration's defense of equal rights — which subsequent Americans drew on to overturn slavery and other inherited hierarchies and forms of domination — but also the dangers of self-righteousness, which can blind us to the political implications of our ideas and of the coalitions that we build. Sometimes, even with the best intentions, our actions might lead us down paths contrary to our values and hopes.

And we also talk about the value of higher education, and great books programs in particular, for helping us have difficult conversations about the past while also providing a space to learn from each other, to disagree, and to see how disagreement helps us learn and grow. These are spaces governed by equal respect that provide opportunities for students and teachers alike to reflect on ourselves and our own beliefs.

This episode concludes our regular episodes of this fourth season, although we'll have another crossover episode with my colleague Pete Becky at the Hayek Program podcast next month. If you enjoyed this episode, feel free to check out the rest of this season and our past three seasons. And if you've been an avid listener of Virtual Sentiments, then please share a positive review on your favorite podcasting platform and subscribe or follow so that you don't miss a new episode, especially when our next season premieres. You can also subscribe to my free Substack where I post about each episode and more at Theory of Virtual Sentiments.

Before we get to my conversation with Tom, I also want to thank my fantastic producer, Jacob Ngo, who has made this season such a stellar set of conversations. Thank you for all your hard work.

Without further ado, I hope you all enjoy this conversation with Tom as much as I did.

对话开始：为什么建国仍在被争论

On today's episode of Virtual Sentiments, I talk to Dr. Thomas Merrill. Tom is an associate professor in the School of Public Affairs at American University, where he is also the director of the Lincoln Scholars Program, as well as the associate director at the Political Theory Institute. He is also the editor of the academic journal American Political Thought, and he is the author of Hume and the Politics of Enlightenment from Cambridge University Press, and has edited a number of volumes, including The Political Thought of the Civil War.

Tom, thank you so much for joining me today.

Thanks for having me. It's great to be here.

I'm so excited because this year is a really big anniversary for America. It's the 250th anniversary of the American founding. We are recording this in August, but just last month we had a lot of big celebrations here in D.C. across the country. And this conversation I really see as a part of a small series of episodes that we're doing here. We have an episode with Laura Field on her work and how some people draw on the founding today to critique liberalism or modern liberalism as they see it. And we have an episode with Osita Nwanevu on his work on reflecting on the founding for developing a future vision of America.

And so I kind of thought this episode would really help us get — give a lot of historical context, right? And so I think always when we look back on the founding, we look back at it from our present perspective, but your expertise will really help us kind of give ourselves a deep historical perspective from which we engage with the founding. I think theorists, we often talk about the idea of like the past being like a foreign country in a lot of ways and sort of acknowledging that difference from our time, while we inevitably are going to be kind of looking back through our own lenses and in our own state of things.

Yeah. So I think that's really true. And I think that — I mean, it's a sign of the greatness, but also of the weirdness of the American founding that we're still arguing about it. It's still very present to us that it's a reference point that we're always appealing to in our political debates and our cultural conversations. So it's on the one hand feels very familiar. And on the other hand, I think that it's hard for us to do justice to just how different it is from where we are right now. And so I just — I mean, if I could say anything on this conversation, I just think studying these things for their own sake is really important and life affirming and helps give us perspective on our own time and place and our own political positions.

洛克、革命与新的政治想象

Yes, you've said it so well. Thank you so much. And so why don't [we start] kind of just getting us into that moment almost a little bit over 250 years ago today. So what were some of the conflicts, the disagreements, everything that was leading up to the big anniversary that we have, which is the signing of the Declaration of Independence?

Well, I mean, the big context is that many human beings at this time are rethinking the fundamental premises of political thought as it came down through the tradition. They were coming out of a tradition that still saw various kinds of hierarchies as natural and necessary. And there was a lot of people coming, especially coming out of the thought of John Locke, the English philosopher, who thought, well, that's all wrong. What we really believe in is human equality and natural rights. That all human beings have a right to govern themselves. They have a right to consent to the government that rules them.

And so it's a really different way of seeing political life that is tremendously powerful — that we probably have not yet sort of gotten to the bottom of. But it's a new idea. It's revolutionary. It's revolutionary both in the sense that the Americans are going to have a revolution against Great Britain, but it's also revolutionary in a philosophical or political theory kind of way. It's a new way of thinking about the world.

Great, great. And so — but were the founding fathers, should we see them as kind of being in total agreement with each other when they thought about these ideas, or were there kind of different strands within their debates?

So definitely different strands. There's a moment in which I think the founders are all together in terms of having a revolution against Great Britain. Differences developed very quickly, especially in the 1790s. But I would say even within founders, and I think the thing that still agitates us today is how do we think about the place of slavery and racism in the American tradition — that the meaning of the ideas of the Declaration of Independence were problematic and conflictual within the tradition itself. I guess it would be one way to say it. So I don't think that the founding represents a single thing. I think it represents a complex of things that are in tension with each other and that are perhaps so productive because they're in tension with each other.

1619 vs 1776：两种美国叙事的对峙

Great. Yeah. No. So I wonder if you could kind of outline for us a little bit more on that about this kind of the ways in which — there's sort of two different ways of getting at this. And how would we get at it in terms of the ideas that were in tension with each other, especially around and related to slavery, or the different interests that individuals had? I mean, do we — should we understand the disagreements because of anything in their differences of approach, their own — like what they relied on for their own wealth, their own kind of politics in that sense — versus the kind of ideas that they had?

Yeah, probably the best way to talk about this is something that is very close to contemporary political discussion is to talk about the slavery issue. And I think that it helps — it might help your listeners to situate this within our contemporary political debates.

The structure of the Declaration as we have it is often described as a syllogism. That there's an initial part that has what's called a major premise that's like a theoretical or universal claim. And that's the part that we all know — that all men are created equal, that people have natural rights, that people that governed have the right to consent to the government that is over them. That's the part that everybody knows.

Then there's a long part that is called the minor premise part where they're meant to be facts — that say, if the major premise says if a government is tyrannizing you, you have a right to rebel, the minor premise part explains what the facts are. They're sort of the predicates to say, yes, the first part of that is true. And so it's providing the evidence for the claim.

And then it concludes with the conclusion, right, which is if you've got a right to rebel under these circumstances, these circumstances exist. Therefore, you know, we are going to rebel. That's the punchline of the declaration.

The passage about slavery occurs in that middle part in the passage — in the part where they're discussing "let these facts be submitted to a candid world," in which they're trying to make the case for why they're justified in rebelling. And that part of the text has an interesting structure in that it starts from what you might think of as the least grievous crimes of the King of England. And it moves slowly through a whole list, but sort of getting more and more heavy. And so it's really interesting that the passage on slavery actually occurs at the very end — that this is sort of the peak of things that the king has done.

And, you know, it says that slavery is a cruel war against human nature. I think that it is very clear that Jefferson understands slavery to be contradictory to the idea of natural rights of all human beings.

Now, what's important is, number one, it was taken out, right? So there's controversy, and we could talk about why somebody might want to take it out. Jefferson himself, in his autobiography, says that the southern states who still were invested in slavery did not want to have this thing criticizing the basis of their economy. And so he says that was the source.

But there might be other reasons to take it out. I mean, it is sort of a weird thing to say. That paragraph does not say, you know, we had slavery is an injustice and therefore we're going to end it. It says that the king has put Americans — meaning the colonists, the white Americans — in an untenable situation in which their rights are in conflict with someone else's rights. And so it sort of leaves you with this unresolved tension, I would say. It doesn't have sort of a positive vision for: if you were to put this into effect, what would this mean for slavery and persons of African descent in the United States?

And it's not that they don't want to, it's that they kind of want to learn those skills and to be engaging in that. And in fact, and I would say like in our seminars, I definitely think like our fellowships, we really do create space for critique and disagreement and engagement and also in a way that I think is welcoming and I hope and it seems to be something that where people feel comfortable to do that. And I think especially kind of the more spaces we have like that the better for [it]. And it won't be, you know, I think as we've just been talking about the founding, we've been talking about politics, we've been talking about like major conflicts and interests and all sorts of parts of politics that have nothing to do with what happens in a classroom, and a classroom is not going to change that. But it is a key part, I think, though, of also this idea of also retaining this vision of, you know, rights matter and also civic skills matter and habits matter and the culture we create matters.

Yeah. Can I connect this back to the earlier part of our conversation that, you know, the sort of the core idea of the Declaration of Independence — [if you'd] leave aside all the complications — you know, all men are created equal, human beings are created equal — it's a vision of human dignity that — and I think liberal education, you know, within organizations, there's something to be said for aristocracy, for people making decisions. But liberal education is a space in which we come to the table as equals and it's meant to be a space for people to practice working out their own takes on things. And it's founded on a basic belief of human dignity. And so I just don't think that we should let go of that or lose sight of the fact that we might do it badly certainly as a country. We've messed up in, you know, many, many different ways. But there's something praiseworthy and noble about that that we need to hold on to.

Yeah. And that kind of — and having that shared commitment to having that equal respect is crucial. And I think, you know, from the point of — I mean, I think partly Jefferson, if you were around today, I'm sure there'd be a lot of complicated things but he'd be like, "guys, you're in charge of your own fates. You don't have to sit around waiting for those stupid founders to solve your problems."

Yeah. Do you know The Onion? One of my favorite Onion articles is if the founders were around today, they'd be too busy shoving things into a garbage disposal and it's sink-shrink.

Yeah, just seeing how it works. I think that's — you know, as a political theorist, as somebody who loves reading all these dead figures, I mean, it's always humbling to remember if they were alive today, they would not want to talk to us about all these ideas. They'd want to just see all this crazy junk that we have now.

Right, right, right, right, right. Okay. Well, I really love talking to you so much, Tom. This is really fantastic. I could keep going, but I think this is a nice bit of conversation to share with people. So thank you so much for joining us.

Thank you. I appreciate it. It's a great thing that you're doing. Oh, thank you. And, you know, look forward to hearing the episode and seeing the others.

Yeah. Thank you. Awesome. Awesome. Yay.

主持人结语：从杰斐逊到 AI —— 自义的危险

As usual, I want to wrap up with a few reflections on Tom's great insights.

Tom gave us a great overview of the historical context of the founding and of America's early years. And in doing so, he helped us avoid the pitfalls of either excessively glorifying the founding fathers, nor completely vilifying them either. Instead, we see how they were working within a particular political economic moment that inspired and constrained their actions and writings.

I loved Tom's points about how the tensions and contradictions of the founding become easier to comprehend if we think of the founding as a nascent civil war. Both Tom and Osita Nwanevu get at this in their works. Especially as the early Americans work towards the U.S. Constitution, they make a lot of compromises in accommodating slavery, which was in the interests of many of the participants in these political discussions. And they do this in order to keep the country acting as one whole and establish the modern American state. We cannot ignore how this political history continues to shape our culture, as well as Americans' sense of national identity and the meanings of these founding texts, like the Declaration and the Constitution, to our own politics today.

I love Tom's arguments about Jefferson being more than a hypocrite or hero, but a tragic figure. And you can read the essay where he discusses this in the show notes. For me, the appeal of this thesis has as much to do with Jefferson and understanding him in context as it does with the timelessness of the lessons that his story may hold for us today. Often we think that people fail to realize good moral values in our actual political reality because of things like the corrupting effect of self-interest. And I do think interest is important. We need to understand how interest motivates behaviors, both in private and public spheres, and how the pursuit of interest can be at odds with one's principles and values, as well as the good of society. But this does also distract from the fact that the risks of self-righteousness, a faith in one's own virtue or moral goodness, might end up being its own source of self-delusion. Confidence in my moral infallibility might make me turn a blind eye to the dangerous beliefs and actions of my political allies, or neglect that we actually do not share the same values at the end of the day, or it might mean that I end up acting in a manner that is ironically even more likely to create the suffering or bring about the dystopian world that I am trying to avoid in the first place.

We didn't talk about tech and AI much in this episode, but since Virtual Sentiments is all about using historical perspective to think deeply about digital technologies today, I will just be explicit that when I think about these aspects of Jefferson's legacy, I actually think a lot about the most pressing topics of discussion today, which is the rise of AI. What comes to mind for me are companies that are currently sounding alarms about the existential dangers of runaway, misaligned, super-intelligent AI while using these risks to justify, first, their race towards building it themselves, and secondly, towards pushing for, lobbying for, restricting open model competitors on the basis of these risks. At the same time, companies engage in ethics washing or championing their employment of philosophers and other thinkers as illustrating just how committed they are to being morally upstanding in their work. But the most important thing is that companies are well-structured and investing in and listening to privacy and security teams, as Catherine Jarmol discussed in our July episode. Otherwise, this is all a little bit like cheap talk rather than actually ensuring responsible innovation and business practices.

Finally, to get back to the topics of the episode, Tom and I also discussed the value of a great book's education. And I think that this can be applied more widely to all sorts of humanities classes that are rooted in a seminar setting. I love Tom's point about how the dangers of treating the books we read as grand authorities to which we must defer can and should be mitigated by the very nature of a well-organized discussion seminar. The books are always a part of a set of texts. And so ideally, these books are often in tension and direct contradiction with one another. The reading list then illustrates the value of disagreement and debate, the fact that history was not one uniform monoculture after another. It was defined by disagreement. And I love this turn of phrase from Tom: the inner anarchism of a genuine conversation is the necessary counterweight to the tendency to defer to the text. Students and instructors sit as equals with a goal of attaining self-knowledge, of clarifying, questioning, and refining our own commitments and ideas.

As I mentioned at the start of the episode, this is our last episode of our regular season. But next month, we'll be back with a crossover episode with my colleague Pete Becky at the Hayek Program podcast. So keep an eye out for that one. If you enjoyed this season of Virtual Sentiments, please review and subscribe so you don't miss when our next season comes out. And feel free to follow me at Substack at Theory of Virtual Sentiments.

Thank you so much for listening. It really means a lot. And I'm so grateful to be able to have these conversations with you. Till next time.

Oh —

## 一、当"美德的梦"成为自我欺骗的引擎
Merrill 对杰斐逊最锋利的诊断藏在一个看似矛盾的观察里：**让杰斐逊背叛《独立宣言》的，不是他的利益，而恰恰是他对"自己是有德之人"的信念**。传统的道德叙事总把私利视作原罪——利益扭曲原则、金钱腐蚀灵魂。但杰斐逊的悲剧走得更深：他之所以能在 1790 年后逐渐沉默、在密苏里危机中站到日后卡尔霍恩阵营的一边，不是因为他放弃了自然权利，而是因为他太确信自己"手里握着正确的观念"。**"我脑子里有对的东西"这一自信，反而成了他不必真的去做什么的许可证**。
这里有一个几乎令人不寒而栗的结构性发现：杰斐逊在《独立宣言》被删除的那段关于奴隶制的文字里，把责任全推给英王——"是他把奴隶制强加给我们"。Merrill 称之为"无辜的暴君"（the innocent tyrant）叙事。**这不是虚伪，虚伪太表层了；这是一种更精致的道德结构——把自己塑造为受制于外力的正义者，就无需真的承担改变现状的代价**。这个模式在今天几乎无处不在：AI 公司一边警告"超级智能会毁灭人类"，一边加速训练前沿模型并游说限制开源竞争者；ESG 部门的存在本身就成了

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一场加州"资源诅咒"的深层病理

Peter Thiel 那句"硅谷是加州的资源诅咒"（resource curse），在 Steve Hilton 的十分钟叙事里被反向验证了——这是全场最被低估、也最反直觉的洞察。

传统的"资源诅咒"讨论石油国家：委内瑞拉、尼日利亚、沙特。它们坐拥地下财富，反而不需要建立良治，因为税基从地下涌出而非从公民口袋。加州完成了这一诅咒模型的"知识经济版本"：硅谷替代了油井，代码替代了原油，资本利得税替代了石油特许权使用费。政府因此无需向公民负责——反正钱会来。这解释了为何"过去十年预算翻倍、人口净减 200 万"这个数学上的荒谬能长期稳定存在。加州不是一个失败的民主州，它是一个石油国家披着蓝色外衣。

"合法性"作为最深层的腐败载体

Spencer Pratt 在争辩到最激烈时说了一句极容易被忽视的话："我不是说他们作弊，问题在于——法律被设计成让他们做的事不叫作弊。"

这句话打开的问题远比选举本身要大。真正的系统性腐败从来不是违法，而是立法——把原本会被视为舞弊的行为写入法条，让批评者陷入"你连法律都不懂"的失语。街头摊贩合法化法案、非营利组织派发针管的资助结构、邮寄选票签名与信封的强制脱钩——这些都不是漏洞，是特性（feature, not bug）。

跨领域连接：这在金融领域有一个完美镜像——2008 年前的次贷证券化。没有一个环节是违法的：评级机构给 AAA 是合法的，投行打包 CDO 是合法的，贷款员发放无收入证明贷款是合法的。灾难恰恰产生于"每一步都合法"的合成物。加州的政治机制走上了同一条路：它不是被腐败入侵，它是被合法化了。

洛杉矶火灾与"倒置激励"的热力学

Spencer 讲述了整个访谈里最出人意料的因果链：加州州立公园法规保护一种叫"milk vetch"（紫云英）的植物，禁止清除枯枝——于是 6 十年枯燥可燃物在社区周围堆积，最终燃烧的不是植物而是他家、他父母家、他邻居的家。50 万美元的防火隔离带没有被划出，随后是数十亿美元的赔付黑洞。

这不是"环保过头"的老套故事。这里有个更深的系统性真相：当一个系统同时给两个不可兼容的目标写入了不可撤销的合规条款，它必然进入自燃状态。加州同时承诺（1）保护每一株濒危植物（2）在野火频发气候中维护住宅安全。这两条法规同时被立法且都不能违反——热力学上不可能，因此系统选择了让居民而非法规承受违规成本。

这与航空业有个残酷类比：波音的 MCAS 系统之所以失败，是因为它试图同时满足两个不兼容的合规要求——新发动机气动特性 + 沿用旧型号培训认证。当合规约束互相打架时，系统不会崩溃在监管上，而是崩溃在乘客身上。加州的合规约束打架时，崩溃在了 Palisades 居民身上。

一个更让人不安的观察

Steve Hilton 提到那对拉丁裔鞋店夫妇："做对的事被惩罚，做错的事被奖励。"如果你把这句话作为滤镜扫描整个转录，你会发现它不是加州的问题——它是任何一个把复杂性无限累积而不做定期垃圾回收的系统的最终状态。1,118 条年度法案的堆叠、42 万条现行法规、街头摊贩合法化叠加在鞋店 14 年的税单之上——这不是意识形态问题，这是软件工程里没有 refactor 的代码库的下场。

真正令人意外的推论是：这不能被"投票"解决。你可以换掉执行代码的 CPU（州长），但你无法通过投票让代码库重构。Steve Hilton 提出把法规从 42 万削减到 20 万——这在软件术语里就是一次 delete 50% of the codebase 的操作。历史上，任何组织自愿完成这种量级重构的案例，几乎为零。它们通常只在破产之后发生。这就是为什么 Spencer 那句半开玩笑的话可能才是真正的诊断："要等四年纯粹的毁灭后，人们才会打电话给我。"

📝 转录文本

开场：一位不寻常的加州州长候选人

A candidate for the governor of California who is extremely unique in a number of ways. First of all, he's a Republican. And second, he's a Brit. Welcome to the program, Steve Hilton.

It's a joke. I mean, what are these Democrats doing? We already have the highest taxes in the country. Your first 100 grand tax-free. Even Katie Porter agrees with that.

Prior to that, he was in Silicon Valley as a tech entrepreneur.

People are so sick of the nonsense. Is everything twice as good when they've doubled the budget? Of course not. California means to America what America means to the world.

Please welcome Steve Hilton. Wake up. Wake up, buddy. Let's go.

— Hi. — All right. Wake up, California. We have seven weeks to save our state. Are you ready? — Are we going to do it? We got seven weeks. That's all. But we can do it. — Seven weeks. Um, there's a lot of people here who aren't from California. — Well, actually, who's from California? Raise your hand. Some. Yeah.

加州为何重要

— But help explain why California is so important.

— California is not just the biggest state, the richest state and the richest most important country on earth. It's — as I said just then, and you saw — California means to America what America means to the world. I'm an immigrant, moved here in 2012, neighbors with Chamath. So how about that? I picked a good spot.

And I was inspired by this state. It represents for me and for so many people over the century-plus that this state has been growing and leading in so many ways — the absolute essence of what we love about America. Innovation and energy and ambition and hustle and that kind of rebel spirit — that's why we've created so many industries here that have completely transformed the world, starting right here in Los Angeles over a century ago: the entertainment industry, obviously tech that you're all so familiar with, but also our great agriculture — we have the leading agriculture industry in the world. In so many different fields we have led the world. That's why it's so important we don't let California go down any further.

州情诊断：全国最差的一系列指标

— What is the state of the state then?

— This state, I'm afraid, despite all our incredible advantages — and of course, we still have them: the things that the people in charge haven't managed yet to ruin, our incredible natural beauty and the weather and the energy that you see in our startup communities, the best innovation ecosystem anywhere in the world, great universities. But look at the facts. We've had 16 years of one party in control.

Today in California, we have the highest poverty rate in the country, the highest unemployment rate, the highest cost of living by far. Look at housing cost — the highest in the country. That's why people are leaving. They are leaving. Millions of people leaving California, this beautiful place.

— You got two right here.

— Exactly. Chief Executive Magazine has ranked California in its annual survey of business leaders for more than a decade 50th out of 50 for business climate. It's just incredible when you look at the range of issues where the policies that we've been subjected to have just created the worst outcomes. Not just bad in comparison to other states — the worst out of every state.

一党执政的根源分析

— So look, we know how you measure the outcome, but go back a few layers and think about the root causes. Democrats have run this state for a long time. Democrats used to be sort of peace and love and permissiveness and openness. So corral that for us — because I think this is a place that has become rules on top of rules on top of rules. How did a group of people who basically were just like peace and love and leave us alone become the rule police?

— It's exactly right. This is what happens with one-party rule, actually, and you see that in history — whether from the right or the left, it always ends up with a kind of insular, self-regarding elite that just forgets about their responsibility to everyone else and gets obsessed with their own ideology, their internal motivations, whoever their interest groups are that they represent.

And by the way, in Sacramento, we have one of the most corrupt systems anywhere in the country in terms of the power of the donors to the politicians who make the decisions — the unions, the trial lawyers. That's why we have the worst litigation risk anywhere in the country. You run a business in California, you start a business in California — 90% chance you're going to end up in litigation. So it's just a complete mess when you get one-party rule.

Now, 16 years, the Democrats have run everything. All eight statewide elected positions, the state legislature with a two-thirds majority, every big county, every big city, the state supreme court with a 6-1 Democrat-appointed majority. So this is what happens. The rules get piled up because every year they pass legislation that just adds to the burden and the bloat.

1,118 条法案的重量

Last year, the Sacramento legislature passed 1,118 bills. So we printed them out.

— Very productive.

— We'd very exact productivity going up there. We're going to be doing this year's in Sacramento on Thursday. We printed it all out. I mean, I'm not that tall, but it was twice my height. Okay. Nobody's reading this. You think Gavin Newsom is reading all this before signing it? No. It's written in the interests of the narrow groups that control that process and it benefits them but hurts everybody else.

That's why we have by far the highest regulatory blow. That's why one of the things I'm announcing today actually is that we're going to cut the number of regulations in California from where we are today — which is over 420,000 — by the end of my first term to under 200,000, which makes us competitive with the rest of the country.

打破"机器"：胜选路径

— If there's a narrow interest group that controls the legislature, is it not also the case that that narrow interest group controls the machinery that I would argue doesn't necessarily elect people, but appoints people, which makes it difficult for rational outsiders to have a shot at a true democratic campaign? That they own the ballot harvesting machines, that they own the campaigning machines, that they get everyone in the state behind them — all the unions, all the votes, everything is aligned under one controlled mechanism. And therefore, it has at this point gotten so far down the road that it is impenetrable and we cannot actually break in.

— Well, it's definitely the case that we have this very powerful and corruptly funded machine that's running everything. I agree with that. In fact, one of the ways that we're telling the story of this campaign is: the people versus the machine. That's what this is.

But there's a majority of Californians who want change. That's clear from every single poll. When we started the general election part of this campaign, if you look at the primary results on primary night in California in the governor's race — myself and the other Republican — that's 35%. I got 25%, the other Republican 10. You add up all the Democrats, 65%. That's a 30-point gap. The first poll came out, it was a 25-point gap. I know a lot of people were discouraged by that, but we were just beginning our campaign.

And look what's happened just in the last couple of months: from a 30-point gap on primary night to 25 points, 18 points, 14 points. The latest poll — an 8-point gap. We are showing that people want change in this state.

And I just don't accept that we have to put up with this — that your only choice is to put up with all this nonsense and bloat and tax and cost and all the hassles of living here, or trying to work here — your only choice is to put up with it or leave. That, if I may say so as a new American citizen, is a very un-American attitude — that it can't be done, that we can't make change happen. We've got to fight for it.

民主党选民的心理转变

— Steve, why do you think that people feel that it would be almost a betrayal, even if they want change, to not vote Democrat? There seems to be in California, at least as I've lived it, a lot of very rational people who feel sort of out of place. They're not quite sure whether they should be a Republican. They're made to feel guilty for not being completely a Democrat. So they either don't vote or they just go in and they find the D and check the box. And so all of the insanity sort of compounds. If that continues to happen, don't we need to hit rock bottom? Isn't there going to be some financial event or otherwise that needs to happen to reset?

— I got to tell you, I think it's pretty rock bottom now in terms of what it's actually like to live here. I've traveled this state. I've been to every one of our 58 counties. No candidate's done that in a very long time. We've done hundreds of events, town halls up and down the state. Every single day, I see the pain and the struggle in people's eyes to live here.

You try and own a home here. We used to have the highest rate of home ownership in the country in California and the most affordable housing. Now the median house price in California is nearly a million dollars. The median salary in California for an individual: 65,000. I mean it's just completely broken. People are broken by this and they are desperate for change.

The number one thing that people say to me when they come up to me at the airport or the street — wherever we are at my events — it's not "good luck, hope you do well." There's an intensity this year. It's almost word for word. This is what everyone says to me. I've heard it even here backstage: "You have to win." There's an intensity about it this year.

一个 911 纪念活动上的场景

I was at the 9/11 memorial event in Sacramento — not there participating, just there to show my respects. I took my seat in the back. People came up to take pictures. Just there randomly in a pretty small event. I had a number of people — must have been four or five people — just randomly all almost said the same word-for-word thing: "I'm a lifelong Democrat, but I'm voting for you this year."

I think we have reached that point. And that's why I'm saying we've got to wake up — because the other thing I hear all the time from business leaders or business owners every single day is: "If you don't make it in November, we're out." I'm serious about this. If we think it's bad now, I think the exodus of business we've seen from California in the last couple of years, if we don't show some change here and some balance in our system, it's going to turn into a stampede for the exits. I think this is a now-or-never election for California.

数据、辩论与政策纲领

— Let's talk about the metrics and the path to victory. Polymarket has you at 5% chance of winning. The actual polls have you as close as 8% to 20%. And it's incredibly polarized. You have 90% or 89% of Republican voters — okay, mission accomplished. You've only got 30% of independents — work to do. And then if you look at Democrats, you've got less than 10%. You've captured the Republicans, making some headway with independents, but you're not making, aside from the anecdotal stories you're telling us, massive headway with these Democrats yet. But you have one debate September 30th versus Becerra. What do you have to do in that debate to change the narrative and to shake this up? What's the plan?

— It's a great question. The question in many ways. I'll give you our metric and our numbers, which is — we wanted to see what is the pathway to victory for real. So this is not us cooking the numbers at all. This is a poll that we took right at the beginning of the campaign, when it was clear that it was myself and Javier Becerra:

  • 33% solidly with me
  • 41% solidly with Becerra
  • 26% up for grabs

Now most of that 26% have voted Democrat before, but they are not committed Democrats. They are open to persuasion. And when you ask who are those people and what are they focused on: overwhelmingly non-college-educated regular working people in California who are at breaking point financially. And their overwhelming interest is practical things to help with the cost of living.

竞选政策要点

That's what our campaign's been all about, and I can tell you what it is very simply:

（1）削减预算浪费。 They've doubled the budget of the state of California in the last 10 years with two million people having left the state. Everything's gotten worse. We're going to cancel high-speed rail. We're going to have a 10% headcount reduction in the government. 5% efficiency, many other things. Stop the funding of these nonprofits that are making homelessness worse.

（2）大幅减税。 That all adds up to enough money for us to cut state income tax — your first 150 grand tax-free, no state income tax. That puts thousands of dollars in the pockets of regular working people.

（3）合理能源政策。 Instead of shipping oil halfway around the world pretending that we're doing something about climate change — even though we're actually increasing emissions by doing that — we're going to use California energy resources. That means getting rid of the ridiculous outdated regulations and the hidden taxes on gas so we can deal with the number one thing that's hurting working people every day, which is gas prices. Instead of $6 gas, we can get towards $3 gas in California like you have in other states right now.

— By getting rid of the emissions premium, or getting rid of the cleaning of the gasoline?

— No, it's not that at all. It's the hidden taxes — the low-carbon fuel standard, the cap-and-invest program. That's about $1.50 on the gas price right there. Guess where that money goes? The cap-and-invest program — that's what's funding high-speed rail. You dig into all these things in California: they are gouging you on every single possible thing they can.

（4）废除 DMV，封顶车辆登记费。 The announcement we made last week — it's going to help regular working people. To register your car or truck in California: hundreds of dollars. Many people paying $8, $900, over $1,000. In most other states, it's under $100. It's another hidden tax. I've now had firefighter whistleblowers tell me that there was clearly smoldering coals on the side of this hill. And now in the depositions with the state park employees, we have their photos. They took photos of the hillside just smoking. And when asked, "Why didn't you do anything?" they say, "Oh, we're not firefighters."

So the state park is liable for allowing a dangerous condition to burn down the community. The LADWP is liable for leaving the reservoirs empty and having no water. And the city is liable.

参选的真正意义

— So basically you're just trying to set the record straight, hopefully get back some recompense for you and these other families — but is most of it this first part of just making the record public of all of this incompetence and the hope that people realize that it doesn't need to be this way?

— That was initially why I was out making my videos and doing the content to help my community. And then when I saw Mayor Bass was just automatically going to be the mayor again, I was like, "Oh, no way." And then I called Rick Caruso. I said, "Are you going to run or what?" He's like, "No." I was like, "Oh, it's on."

So then I ran with the intention to just try to stop her from becoming mayor. If that meant me being mayor — honestly, people are like, "Oh, you have no experience." Oh, to enforce the law. What LA needs is a mayor that enforces the law. Neither Mayor Bass nor Nithya Raman have any intention of enforcing the laws because it doesn't look good. It doesn't look good if you tell the illegal food vendors that they can't ruin a small business that's been paying taxes for 40 years. "Oh, you're messing with this community, this at-risk community." No, this is illegal — they're destroying this family's business.

So these simple things I would have been able to do as mayor. It's unfortunate that it's going to take four years of pure destruction for people to call me up in four years like, "Let's go" — and I'll be ready.

从洛杉矶到纽约：媒体、真相与愤怒

— Spencer, are you still doing content? What are you doing right now with your time?

— There's three opportunities in play. And yes — content. What I realized when I got out of this — and this sounds very pot-lies — is there's so many lies that I witnessed all day long firsthand in my city that I was like, "I need to be out here making content with the truth." It's not — it's in the center. I keep saying, people are like, "Oh, he's a Republican." No, the truth doesn't have a side. That's that simple. And these people across the country now are trying to destroy it. They truly are.

And when you start living this all day long like me, it's not for LA now. I'm like, "Damn, I got to fight for America. Like, I'm like Jason Bourne. This is crazy." So yeah, now I'm flying to New York and meeting with people in New York, trying to help them, because I don't want New York to go down even worse than —

— I have a suggestion for you. So what were the other two things? You said there was three things.

Skid Row 数据中心构想

— There there's three plays. I mean, I was going to be the big guy in AI as mayor because I was going to turn Skid Row into all just data centers.

— I mean, you're weaving. You're speaking our language.

— I actually had a call trying to get the information about data centers with a guy that knows data centers. He said — and he said — "Spencer, do you understand this is the time for a city like LA whose infrastructure is collapsing into the ground to take private business and billions of dollars, be like: 'Hey, yes, you can put this data center where we have naked drug-addict zombies and no actual human being can go for 50 blocks. We're going to put that here. But you need to redo our water pipes. You need to redo our —'"

— We can retrain the fentanyl addicts to be electricians. Meta's got a program for that.

— You know, as I drove over here, I — you know, I was going to solve a lot of problems.

为什么不做真人秀

— But Spencer, in all seriousness — you're incredibly quick-witted and entertaining on camera. You should consider doing reality TV.

— You know why I don't like reality TV? And it's the only thing worse than people in politics — is there's too much image crafting. And that's what makes bad reality shows. Now everyone is image crafting, trying to create a persona. "What's going to be in the comment section? What are people going to say on the blogs?" You cannot be… real. Like the last reality show I was on when they rebooted The Hills —

— You were on a reality show?

— A couple. A couple. You know, I am the reality candidate. That's a reality check.

But everybody was just faking their actual identity. And now what's so funny is if you watch any politician, they're just a bad TikTok influencer. You look at Abdul — say, he thinks he's Alix Earle. It's like — what are you doing?

— Honestly, I just got to tell you, I love you. And what a mistake — because not only would you have gotten some great done, this would have been the most entertaining mayorship in history.

— Well, he's got time.

— Yeah, you got to run again.

— This is — yeah, I know. What's funny is I actually am way more of a threat to these people now, because I have —

— You're dangerous.

— Two years to really get into these communities.

最后一刻：DSA 是谁？

— I suggest you torture them. Torture Karen Bass for the next two years.

— You know, Karen Bass is not our worst nightmare. And I will never say anything positive — Nithya Raman and the DSA people. People do not get — my Democrat friends do not understand what the DSA is. I keep telling them: go on their website. It's not a conspiracy. Read their website and you tell me — abolish the police. Yes.

I mean, the list goes on and on and this is what they stand by. And then I used to call them commies and everybody was like, "Oh, you can't call them commies." Now I'm like — that sounds nice.

— It's a compliment to them. They're anarchists. Like gassing them up like crazy.

— Ladies and gentlemen, Spencer Pratt. Wow. Thanks, bro. All right. Great stuff.

item.description:
## 一场加州"资源诅咒"的深层病理
Peter Thiel 那句"硅谷是加州的资源诅咒"（resource curse），在 Steve Hilton 的十分钟叙事里被反向验证了——这是全场最被低估、也最反直觉的洞察。
传统的"资源诅咒"讨论石油国家：委内瑞拉、尼日利亚、沙特。它们坐拥地下财富，反而不需要建立良治，因为税基从地下涌出而非从公民口袋。**加州完成了这一诅咒模型的"知识经济版本"**：硅谷替代了油井，代码替代了原油，资本利得税替代了石油特许权使用费。政府因此无需向公民负责——反正钱会来。这解释了为何"过去十年预算翻倍、人口净减 200 万"这个数学上的荒谬能长期稳定存在。加州不是一个失败的民主州，它是一个石油国家披着蓝色外衣。
## "合法性"作为最深层的腐败载体
Spencer Pratt 在争辩到最激烈时说了一句极容易被忽视的话："**我不是说他们作弊，问题在于——法律被设计成让他们做的事不叫作弊。**"
这句话打开的问题远比选举本身要大。真正的系统性腐败从来不是违法，而是**立法**——把原本会被视为舞弊的行为写入法条，让批评者陷入"你连法律都不懂"的失语

item.title: [Latent Space] 🔬 Google's AI Scientist Started as an Attempt to Automate Kaggle — John Platt, Google Fellow
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的核心颠覆：ERA 的真正起源，是"自动化 Kaggle"

大多数关于 AI 科学家的宣传都把它塑造成一场自上而下的"科学革命"，但 John 无意间揭示了一个更诡异的真相：Google 的 AI 科学家，起点是"打 Kaggle 比赛"。这不是浪漫的科学梦，而是一个极其功利的工程问题——如何让机器在排行榜上赢过人类。

这里有一个让人后脊发凉的观察：科学本身可能正在被"Kaggle 化"。当你能把一切科学问题映射为"可打分任务"时，你其实是在把科学的本体论从"寻找真理"悄悄替换为"最大化某个函数"。John 自己也警觉地指出——Goodhart 定律（任何指标一旦成为目标，就不再是好指标）如今应用于每一个排行榜。这意味着 AI for Science 面临的最大风险不是算法弱，而是整个科学范式正在滑向一种"高维过拟合的文明"——我们越擅长优化分数，就越可能失去对"世界真实结构"的把握。

二、跨领域连接：进化算法为何 50 年没用，却突然复活了？

这里藏着一个惊人的跨领域联系。John 提到进化式代码变异从 70 年代起就存在，但从未起飞——因为"在代码空间的随机突变几乎毫无价值，就像 DNA，大多数突变是有害的"。

真正的类比不是"AI 加速进化"，而是"AI 扮演了寒武纪大爆发中的发育调控基因（Hox genes）"。 生物学中的一个反直觉发现是：寒武纪之所以出现物种爆炸，不是因为突变率提高，而是因为发育调控网络（gene regulatory network）让突变变得"有方向"——一个 Hox 基因突变可以整体重塑一个身体分区。

Gemini 在 ERA 里扮演的正是这个角色：它不是让突变更快，而是让突变空间坍缩到"合理的梯度"上。这解释了为什么 Gemini 2.0 时代不行、2.5 时代突然可行——不是 LLM 变强了，而是它的"世界先验"密度终于足够高，能够作为一个"发育调控器"起作用。AI for Science 的关键不是计算力，而是先验知识密度的相变（phase transition）。

三、你没意识到的悖论：气候科学比生物学更"AI-抗性"

一个让人意外的洞察埋在对话深处：John 说气候比天气难做 AI，不是因为它复杂，而是因为它非平稳（non-stationary）——吸引子本身在移动。

但真正让人啊哈的是他随后的比喻："contrails（飞机凝结尾）的物理，其实和气候模型的深层不确定性直接耦合"。冰晶如何在云中沉降，取决于晶体形状；晶体形状取决于微观物理；而微观物理的近似误差，会在气候预测里放大成300 ppm 的 CO2 不确定性——几乎相当于现在整个大气浓度的 2/3。

这是一个鲜有人指出的系统性真相：气候科学的核心瓶颈，不在气候模型，而在你飞机窗外那道白线的形状。 这正是复杂系统的可怕之处——局部微观机制以非线性方式支配全局命运。

而这条线索还可以进一步跨界：这正好呼应了 John 对生物学的评价——"生物系统里全是例外和 hacks"。所以你可以推演出一个更大的假设：凡是"非平稳、多尺度耦合、数据稀疏"的系统，AI 都表现为"辅助工具"而非"颠覆者"。这解释了为什么蛋白质折叠被 AlphaFold 打穿了（数据丰富、准闭合），而气候、细胞、经济、意识这些"开放非平稳"系统，AI 至今只在边缘打转。

四、埋在角落的"啊哈"：品味 vs 严谨的隐藏对偶

John 说了一句几乎没人接住的话——"以前大家说 taste（品味）是未来的关键，但新时代的对偶是 rigor（严谨）。"

这是一个极其深刻的观察。当生成变得几乎免费时，价值不再来自创造，而来自"甄别"。 你可以让 AI 生成一千个假设，但只有极少数人能识别哪一个是真的。这某种意义上是回到了 17 世纪科学革命前夜的状态——不是缺乏观察，而是缺乏方法论。

跨界的意外映射：这与编辑（editor）在文学史上的角色惊人地相似。当印刷术让书写民主化后，真正稀缺的不再是作者，而是能筛选、结构化、批判的编辑。AI for Science 时代，最稀缺的职业可能不是"科学家"，而是"科学编辑"——那些能把 LLM 生成的假设洪流筛选成真知识的人。

而这条线最讽刺的地方在于：John 自己就是那种人。他谈自己命名小行星、拿 Oscar、听 Feynman 上课，看似炫耀，其实无意间给出了他对"未来科学家"的隐含定义——跨领域的品味 + 打不烂的严谨，二者缺一不可。

📝 转录文本

🔬 Google 的 AI 科学家源起于"自动化 Kaggle" —— John Platt, Google Fellow

引子：预测模型 vs 描述模型

问： Are you talking about introducing explicit priors that you know based upon some human intuition or maybe in this case LOM intuition?

John： When you talk about multiple hypothesis testing right there's predictive models and there's descriptive models. A predictive model is like let's say you just have a you have some inputs and you have some outputs and you just I just want to build a piece of code that tries to just have the lowest error rate on some data set — statistical model.

A descriptive model is actually what science is trying to get to, which is okay it should be able to extrapolate because it has sort of the physics or the actual some description of reality that's captured within it and then you can use it to extrapolate.

Yes, Newton thought of apples and gravity, but gravity isn't actually about apple, right? If you take the 17th century machine learning model like "oh apples will fall," but how about planets? You know, I don't know, I have no data about planets, so who knows what they do, right?

The distinction between those is a little bit blurry, right? Because when a physicist or scientist comes, they use their intuition — or maybe even more than intuition — like essentially there's maybe a solid pile of facts that they know about the world and then they make sure that whatever model they build is sort of consistent with what's known.

开场介绍

主持人： My co-host R.J. — uh, it's a pleasure to have John Platt with us today. John is a Google fellow and head of applied science at Google Research. He has really a fun background. He — I guess you described yourself when we were talking a few minutes ago as a mega nerd.

John： Oh, giga nerd.

主持人： Giga nerd. He's excited in absolutely everything, and it really shows.

You — correct me if I'm wrong about any of this stuff — but um, so you started college at 14 and started your PhD at 18 at Caltech. You were advised or co-advised by John Hopfield, right?

John： Oh, yeah. Yeah.

主持人： Who just won a Nobel Prize two or three years ago.

John： Yes.

主持人： So John created several textbook algorithms — one known as Platt scaling, another one sequential minimal optimization which is the textbook algorithm for training SVMs. Even today it's still in sklearn. John has discovered and named two asteroids, has an Oscar for technical developments from 2006 — so if you've ever watched a Pixar movie, you've seen John's algorithms and work. John has an Erdős–Bacon number of six, or three-and-three from either side.

I'm going to skip over like 20 years of your career, but then jumping to Google — working at Google Sciences, you worked on fusion, quantum computing, climate modeling and many other topics. Is that more or less right?

John： That's right, yeah.

主持人： Okay, cool. Did I miss anything important for today?

John： No, I mean I've also done lots of applied math and signal processing and all sorts of fun things.

主持人： Yeah. I think your Wikipedia has a fun story about patents and the iPhone too.

John： The iPod.

主持人： iPod, yeah.

John： Welcome. Thank you for having me.

什么是 ERA？—— AI for Science 的框架

主持人： Can you tell us about ERA — I think that's the way that the acronym is pronounced? And I know that there's a lot of different semi-related stuff out there both within and outside of Google. So what can you tell us a little bit about the details of ERA and what makes it special?

John： Well, we've been doing AI for Science in Google Research for more than 10 years now. Around 10 years ago it was very much using — I don't know what you call it now, maybe classical machine learning models — things like convolutional nets or whatever to solve specific science problems.

But about two years ago we got very excited about these more general LLMs that have popped up in the last few years, and we were wondering what can be done with them. Of course a lot of people have been playing and trying to figure out what the right thing to do is.

核心洞察：可打分任务（Scorable Tasks）

We kind of stumbled into this mapping. In other words, we found that many different scientific problems can be mapped into something we call scorable tasks. So you can often phrase a scientific problem as "gosh, I really would like to have a piece of code that maximizes some score." And it's surprising the number of different scientific problems you can make a lot of progress on by mapping into that framework.

A lot of scientists spend a lot of time building models — they might be statistical models or physically-based models. If it's a statistical model, like in machine learning, your scoring function is: "well I have some data set and I'd like to have the fit the model and the data set go up." We can talk about overfitting in a minute —

主持人： That was one of our questions.

一个非统计的例子：渐近展开

John： So machine learning is kind of a subset of this scorable task, right? But you could do other kinds of things. Especially Michael Brenner, who's the lead author on the ERA paper — he's very skilled, he likes to knock out a scientific paper in an evening now with a tool.

There's something in applied math called asymptotic expansions. You're asking: how does an ordinary or partial differential equation behave? There's some parameter — has an epsilon in it — and you're trying to say how does it behave as epsilon goes to zero. It turns out you can turn that into an empirical task by essentially asking that it proposes some solutions that are asymptotically correct, and you check to see if the asymptotic solution is correct for like epsilon equals 1e-4 or something, and then you check that fit.

But then you ask Gemini — which is the core AI underneath it — to do the mathematical reasoning, try to solve the problem while also maximizing the fit to the data. So there's a lot of tricks you can do because the underlying thing that's altering the code or making the decisions is not a random process. It's an AI itself that is smart and knows about things and knows a lot about the world.

You can solve a lot of interesting problems because that core inner loop is an AI that has huge amounts of prior knowledge. So that's the trick.

另一个例子：卫星超分辨率与 CO2 监测

主持人： So what are some of the more — the statistical one is what everyone listening will probably know about. What are some of the other interesting ones?

John： Let's see, ones that we just put a paper up on arXiv — or actually I think it might be on GitHub. You often run into this in remote sensing because there's always a trade-off. There are satellites flying above the Earth, and there's a trade-off between how frequently they can revisit a spot on Earth, what their spatial resolution is, how big the pixels are, and their spectral resolution — how many bands they have.

Ideally you'd like to have monitoring of the Earth that's constant — a frame every five minutes at hyperspectral resolution at 10 centimeters. You can't get that.

But for example, to monitor CO2 — the atmospheric concentration of CO2 — you can take data from one satellite, for example OCO-2 or OCO-3 (OCO-3 is actually attached to the International Space Station), so it gets you a little strip of CO2 measurements that are highly accurate and pretty high resolution.

You can actually try to do — because a lot of it is in the infrared — weather satellites like GOES have some infrared bands and it takes a picture every essentially 5 minutes, but the pixels are very large and it doesn't have such great spectral resolution in terms of — it wasn't designed to find CO2.

So you just ask one to estimate the other, and you shovel other data in like what's the current weather, what's sort of the long-term albedo. And so you came up with this very nice model that can do almost like super-resolution — an informed super-resolution of one satellite to another.

ERA 的工程细节：蒙特卡洛树搜索与 UCB

主持人： So any scientific problem that you can map into this framework. So the input to ERA is sort of this mapping and the output is code, is that —

John： Well, sort of. I mean the input is — the way we've got it set up in the product, you just start talking. Because a lot of times it's nonobvious how to do this mapping. Although experts like Michael Brenner know how to do it, we actually wrote an agent that helps you — it talks to you to try to help you define what your scorable task should be.

So there's already an instance of Gemini sitting there trying to help you write code. That's actually sort of almost like an intermediate result. You start talking to it about your problem and it tries to produce essentially a Python notebook underneath that has a scorable function — which essentially produces a score. And then it starts to mutate that notebook in a clever way because, again, it's Gemini, and it will try to keep proposing code that tries to maximize the score.

主持人： So what is different about this than just a generally agentic system that can optimize notebooks?

John： Right now it's — essentially it's its own — in modern 2026 parlance we actually worked on this in '24 and '25 — but in the modern parlance it's kind of a specialized harness that runs an algorithm which, for ERA, was Monte Carlo tree search.

So essentially it's keeping hundreds or thousands of possible instances of notebooks, and then it selects one — and I can explain how it selects one. It decides: well, what can I do? Gemini asks itself: what can I do to make that notebook be better? And then it will make a new one and test it and put it back into the candidate pool.

You can imagine the candidate pool is actually tree-structured because every candidate possibly has some children. What you do is you pick based on something called — it's actually a fairly standard algorithm in reinforcement learning called Upper Confidence Bound (UCB). It's an optimistic algorithm. It tries to estimate: what's the 95th percentile outcome of mutation? It tries to estimate that and picks the one with the highest optimistic bound.

So in other words, it doesn't always pick the best-performing notebook. It tries to predict "what's the current performance plus two sigma of its guess." So it always hunts around.

主持人： So high-recall basically.

John： High recall. It's trying to make its bet so that it most efficiently tries to make progress, which isn't always greedily doing the best candidate. Sometimes it's the fifth-best.

We've also played around where it recombines — it sort of takes ideas from two candidates and smashes them together and tries to make a third candidate out of that.

初始种子与并行数

主持人： How does it seed the initial candidate pool?

John： Well, that's the amazing thing — underneath, Gemini is actually good at writing code. You just ask it "write me a thing" because you have a textual description of the problem. It isn't just "oh here's your scoring function, start." You give it a textual description of the function, and you might give it — in fact we have under some things like "here are five papers that people tried to solve this problem with" — and it's kind of smart. It actually goes and reads the papers and takes a first stab at code.

It might not be great, or it might sometimes have bugs and it returns essentially minus infinity, but it will then try to mutate the code and make it better.

主持人： How many agents are you spinning up? I guess maybe not agents, or how many different tree branches at each iteration?

John： At every iteration — well, there's a trade-off. You'd like to do a lot of parallel work, but if you do too much parallel work, you can't learn from previous things. Right now the default is 10. So you try to grow 10 leaves at a time. That seems to be about the right trade-off.

主持人： When you say you can't learn from previous iterations, what does that mean?

John： Why you can't do too many things in parallel is: if you have 10 parallel searches at once, then number one can't actually see what numbers two through 10 are doing. So if you do a thousand at once, then you're using a huge amount of computation without a lot of cross-learning.

Whereas once you finish a little batch, you get the history. Obviously you have to prune it so it doesn't blow up the context, but you get the history of what it was thinking about as it was writing the code and the results of the code. So it can learn from its previous attempts.

主持人： You're really pushing Gemini's long-context abilities.

John： That's right. And you have to do the right management.

最难的部分：定义正确的评分函数

主持人： Going back to R.J.'s question — the key point being: the first key goal is to identify what specific score that you are trying to optimize, right? Sometimes that is kind of the hardest part of the problem. I find it interesting that I'm not sure I'd always trust my agent to do that part. That part seems like the more human task in the loop.

John： It is. And often you have to be careful. A lot of what you do — it's very meta. You have to make sure that — one common thing is you come up with a scoring function, or the agent does, or you do it together, and then the iteration finds a way to cheat, and you go: "oh no, I didn't mean that." So you have to go through and often have a loop around it where you iterate: "no, no, I didn't mean that," or you have to tell it in its instructions "don't do this."

So there's often iterations. Even with agent help, you don't necessarily get the right scoring function from day one.

And it's really neat because — in the old days, i.e. 2024 — a lot of grad students would spend a lot of time doing scientific software, and it's just so much effort to write code at all that you kind of try maybe a few things or a few things that are very related, and then you sort of stop because you have to write your paper, you have to do your next experiment.

This thing is kind of relentless underneath — it keeps trying and keeps trying. So the people who use it are now spending all their time almost at the right level, almost at the scientific creativity level. What does it mean to have a cost function? That's almost the essence of the scientific problem. You're not so much now in the details of "oh, I have to import this CSV file" or "I have to get this database to work." You're now thinking almost deeply philosophically about your actual scientific problem, not down in the grungy goop of worrying about databases.

One cool thing the agent can do is actually suggest data sets to you: "oh, have you thought about maybe pulling in this data set and doing a join?" So it'll make suggestions about data sets you can join with, which is kind of cool.

奖励劫持与"精灵故事"

主持人： Going back to what you said a second ago — in terms of agents love to hack things and the reward hack — do you have any fun stories about where things were comedically run off the rails?

John： Boy, I'm blanking. I know other folks have run into it. I don't know if I have enough details to sort of express the comedy of it, but you kind of get surprised. Sorry, I'm blanking.

预测模型 vs 描述模型（再展开）

John： I guess there's two questions embedded in your question, because when you talk about multiple hypothesis testing, there's predictive models and there's descriptive models — I've been doing machine learning for a long time in statistics.

主持人： That's actually a really good point — do you mind expanding that? I'm not sure that's something everyone in the audience would be familiar with. Especially in modern days I think people are trying to obscure the two. If you started with LLMs I'm not sure that distinction would be meaningful.

John： That's right. A predictive model is: let's say you have inputs and outputs, and I just want to build a piece of code that has the lowest error rate on some data set. That's just a statistical model.

A descriptive model is actually what science is trying to get to: it should be able to extrapolate because it has the physics or some description of reality captured within it. Then you can use it to extrapolate. Because — yes, Newton thought apples and gravity, but gravity isn't actually about apples. If he had just fit the 17th-century machine learning model: "oh apples will fall," but how about planets? I don't know, I have no data about planets, so who knows what they do.

主持人： So when you say "extrapolative" — there's different ways I could think about this. One is: you said a model of physics or model of the world. Are you talking about introducing explicit priors that you know based upon some human intuition — or maybe in this case LLM intuition — or are you talking about "the physics is actually learned by the model"?

John： The distinction between those is a little bit blurry, right? Because when a physicist or scientist comes, they use their intuition — or maybe even more than intuition. Essentially there's a solid pile of facts they know about the world, and they make sure whatever model they build is consistent with what's known.

Currently in ERA it is sort of LLM intuition — that's what I was trying to say about having a good gradient underneath. Especially if you point it at existing papers, it will try to build models that are kind of sane underneath. Especially if you give it guidance like "oh be sure to incorporate this" or "look at these papers," you get these things. So you can introduce a bias towards certain model choices, and it will have a bias because its own little world knowledge is accumulated inside itself in pre-training.

具体例子：物理先验

主持人： Can you give us examples of what that might look like? For example if you're doing something with partial differential equations, there's these formalisms people have — neural operators for example, or physics-informed neural networks — for fluid and PDE-type modeling systems. Or for molecular systems there's often this idea about equivariance. Is the model picking up on these tricks which have been developed in the literature, or are they adding some weights for some physical prior?

John： I don't know if I have enough data to say "oh, 73% of the time it does this." But especially when you point it at existing papers, it will do very well at adapting the methods described in the papers for the problem. In fact, we'll do an amazing job. Oh — we did this for the — we had this thing, it was actually kind of a hack, I suggested this to Michael. I believe Michael — we can ask him — I believe it actually just — I don't think he actually installed the simulator, I think the code just reproduced the code, because it has a coding agent inside of it. So it just reproduced the code from the paper and figured it all out.

That can get very hairy if you know about Clebsch-Gordan coefficients, it's pretty fun. So I don't know if it'll do the true equivariant stuff, but it actually knows a lot.

I remember when Gemini 2.5 came out — I know this is not exactly about ERA — but I remember thinking "oh, this is a new world." The day 2.5 came out, I said "hey Gemini 2.5, can you write me some boosted decision tree code?" And it did. And it worked. It just did. I said, "yeah, this is a new world."

So yes, to loop back to your question: if you give it guidance about "oh, it's important to put this kind of thing in," it will. At least not that we've seen — it won't necessarily discover completely new physical models from scratch, but it will certainly, if you tell it about interesting constraints about the world that are known, evolve.

They can make strange suggestions — I've used co-scientist for an interesting problem in geochemistry and I learned about a new kind of ion I didn't realize happened in magma. 参差不齐的边界（Jagged Frontier）

主持人： Going back — we were just talking about two years, 2.0 to 2.5, you already saw a leap, and now it's been another year or two and now we're at 3.5. But the question is: where are we on that?

John： I'm a big believer in the whole jagged frontier. So certainly there's some big spikes out in jaggedness in terms of coding ability and just gathering knowledge and finding related things — and that's huge and wonderful, which is great for scientists.

So far, it's less in terms of rigor. We can talk about things like the International Math Olympiad and math in general, but in terms of philosophy and creativity, it's still kind of not there.
