item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被遗忘的"早餐帝国"起源：疯人院是现代健康产业的子宫

最令人错愕的细节藏在几乎一带而过的一句话里——家乐氏（Kellogg's）玉米片，来自一家精神疗养院。今天全球超市货架上的早餐工业，其真正的祖先不是农业，而是 19 世纪基督复临安息日会为忧郁症患者建立的疗养所。当年林肯遗孀、亨利·福特、甚至泰山的作者都在那里"排毒、素食、通便"。

这揭示了一个几乎无人察觉的系统性真相：19 世纪美国的精神健康产业，就是今天"健康经济"（wellness economy）的原型——素食主义、肠道理论、断食、瑜伽式静养、"戒除刺激"——所有当代 biohacking 与 wellness influencer 的话术，早在 120 年前就以"神经衰弱疗法"的名义完整存在过。Silas Weir Mitchell 的《磨损与撕裂》（Wear and Tear）警告 19 世纪的人们：电报和铁路让神经系统"破产"。今天我们把"电报"换成"TikTok"，一字不差地重复同一套焦虑修辞。每一代人都相信自己是被科技毁掉的第一代人——这是一种周期性的文明性错觉。

二、精神分析的隐秘经济学：它其实是"工业过剩资本"的副产品

如果你把 Anna O、Rockefeller、McCormack、Mellon 这几个名字放在一张财务图上，会看到一个让人不安的模式：精神分析不是一个医学发现，它是一个由镀金时代美国工业遗产所资助的奢侈服务。国际收割机公司的继承人、洛克菲勒的女儿、梅隆家族——这些垄断资本的继承人不仅是荣格的病人，还是精神分析文献能被普林斯顿大学出版社出版的原因（靠梅隆基金会的补贴）。

这里有一个跨领域的连接值得警觉：Maslow 的需求层级理论反向解释了精神分析的诞生。只有在物质极度安全的阶层，"童年被压抑的性欲"才能成为一个需要五年、每周五小时深度挖掘的问题。Freud 却把这些富人的问题当作了普遍人性的模板。换句话说，20 世纪的"人性"，很大程度上是一小群维也纳中产和美国东岸继承人的病历合订本被误当作普适心理学。这与今天硅谷把"通过冥想优化生产力"当作全人类幸福方案，是同一种阶级性错认。

三、Freud 作为科学家失败，作为叙事技术家胜利——这解释了 AI 时代的许多事

访谈中一个被轻轻带过、其实极为致命的细节：Freud 自己承认，"我的病例读起来像短篇小说"，他为此感到遗憾，因为这让他显得不够科学。但真正的历史反讽是——这恰恰是他成功的原因。精神分析在医学上从未真正胜出（1930 年全北美只有 300 个分析师），却彻底占领了文学、电影、超现实主义绘画、戏剧和 20 世纪的自我理解方式。

这里藏着一个惊人的跨领域启示：Freud 不是一位失败的科学家，他是一位成功的"叙事技术"（narrative technology）发明者。他发明的不是治疗方法，而是一种解释人类的语法——"潜意识"、"压抑"、"童年创伤"、"口误"、"防御机制"——这些是认知基础设施，而非医学工具。一旦语言被改写，人就再也无法用旧方式思考自己。

这与今天正在发生的事情惊人相似：大语言模型也在成为一种"叙事技术"而非严格意义上的科学。它们能否通过图灵测试、是否"真的"理解，可能都不是关键——真正的历史效应是它们重写了我们描述自己思维的语法。Freud 用 30 年做到的事，AI 可能在 5 年内完成。

四、隐藏的百年循环：神经学 → 精神分析 → 药理学 → 神经科学

最后一个让人脊背发凉的模式：Freud 最初写过一篇《科学心理学计划》（Project for a Scientific Psychology），试图把心理学接回神经学——然后他放弃了。精神分析的奠基性动作，是对神经科学的绝望性撤退。100 年后，psychopharmacology 又把神经科学请回来推翻了精神分析。而今天的 fMRI、connectomics、脑机接口，正在完成 Freud 当年放弃的那本书。

心理学史不是进步史，而是一个钟摆——在"心是身体"和"心是叙事"之间摆动了至少 150 年。而每一次摆动的动力，都不是新证据，而是上一代范式的自我耗竭。这或许就是所有"科学革命"最不愿承认的秘密：革命的燃料常常不是发现，而是疲惫。

📝 转录文本

引子：交织的两条线索

Lex: We've been carrying multiple threads together. One of the threads that I think is really exciting to me and really important to the history of psychiatry is the psychotherapy side.

Scull: Okay.

Lex: We have mentioned the psychopharmacology that — it would be nice to discuss when the two clash and there's a revolution where psychopharmacology kind of wins over psychoanalysis.

Scull: For a time.

Lex: But let us start at somewhat the beginning — the 19th century, when talk therapy starts coming to life, maybe in the religious context with the Christian Science, and then psychoanalysis context.

一、19 世纪：精神病院之外的痛苦

Scull: Yes. So I'd mentioned late 19th century psychiatry — confined as it was to the mental hospital and to people incarcerated in those places — had become very biological. But there were people experiencing mental troubles of various kinds: sadness, confusion, loss of social relationships that were troubling them, grief, all sorts of things like that that didn't involve time in a mental hospital, but nonetheless involved a good deal of distress, as they continue to do.

And one of the things that was interesting about 19th century America is it spawned a number of new religions — sort of variants of Christianity. So you had 7th Day Adventists, a group that still exists, who actually spawned a sanitarium for their depressed congregants that was later taken over by two prominent members of the Adventist church, the Kellogg family. Everybody knows them through cereal, but they ran a huge sanitarium to which Abraham Lincoln's widow went, Tarzan went, Henry Ford went — lots of very prominent industrialists and politicians. It was kind of a farm to go and recover your mental stability and health. And it was all bound up also with beliefs about diet and defecation and all sorts of things.

So there were the Mormons or Church of Jesus Christ of the Latter-day Saints — many Christians don't believe they're really Christian, but they think they are and call themselves such. So you have a number of these, and one of them was Christian Science, which was the invention of a woman named Mary Baker Eddy. And it wasn't just about mental troubles: Mary Baker Eddy developed the idea — and there are still Christian Science churches and Christian Science reading rooms all across America — that there wasn't such a thing as disease, that it could be prayed away, that it was just a lack of sufficient faith.

So faith healing tended to work, I think, better if it worked at all for psychiatric problems than it did if you had, say, cancer. But Christian Science achieved a considerable number of followers, disproportionately women but not only women, and it began to treat many of the people suffering from what we would think of as the milder mental disorders. And it attracted both adherents and severe critics — Mark Twain, for example, was thoroughly dismissive of Mary Baker Eddy — but it was very successful for a time.

And there were other religiously based attempts to join in. The most important of which in New England was something called the Emmanuel movement, centered around the Church of the Emmanuel in Boston, which was an attempt actually initially to bring medical and religious approaches to helping the mentally troubled. But rather quickly the doctors involved decided this was veering too much in the direction of medically-based therapeutics, and they kind of withdrew from that enterprise and it dispensed. There were talk therapies, obviously with a strong religious component around them.

二、神经学的兴起与"休息疗法"

Scull: And this was also at a time when some — I guess we can call them psychiatrists, they were often neurologists — were beginning to get lots of patients with these kinds of difficult-to-treat disorders. Neurology had emerged in America after the Civil War. The Civil War provided a lot of naturalistic experiments on what happens to the human brain and the human nervous system when trauma affects — I don't mean psychological trauma, I mean bullets blowing holes in your brain. And so a group of new specialists emerged after the Civil War who claimed expertise in the brain and the nervous system.

Well, one of the other side parts of that is insanity, because insanity is also seen as a brain disease. So there is a conflict that erupts in the 1870s and 80s between neurologists and psychiatrists. But the neurologists can't for the most part get into the asylum where the most seriously ill patients are. And so gradually what comes to their waiting room, along with people suffering from things like multiple sclerosis, are people with functional mental disorders.

And so there's the beginning of an outpatient practice, which initially involves some drugs, the use of electricity — not ECT, but the use for example of static electricity, because it produces obvious physiological responses and electricity is seen as dominating the workings of the body — and sometimes tonics of one sort and another, and most notoriously of all something called the rest cure, which Silas Weir Mitchell, one of the leading lights of American neurology, developed. Which is complete bed rest, lots of calories, lots of food, complete lack of intellectual stimulation, and supposedly this is going to cure you — mainly aimed at women.

Lex: I feel like that's another uh evidence-backed technique [laughter] that works well. I've partaken in this and I know it has helped me. [laughter] Laying in bed doing nothing, eating snacks.

Scull: Virginia Woolf was one of the people subjected to this, and she claimed it practically drove her mad and made her worse.

Lex: Just to clarify, we're talking about laying in bed eating snacks.

Scull: Eating lots of snacks, a very high calorie. So Weir Mitchell wrote two popular bestsellers — self-help books, I suppose you'd call them in the modern genre. One was called Wear and Tear — so the pace of modern life, the telegraph, the railway, was all too much and your nervous system was overstressed. Either your batteries ran down (that was one analogy) or you overtaxed your system and went, you know, bankrupt. So Wear and Tear, that was the problem. And the solution was Fat and Blood — that was the title of the other book. So you got scrawny and all nervous and twitchy, and what you really needed was to build back up your strength, including your nervous strength.

Lex: Isn't it fascinating to look at that 120 years plus ago? They're talking about how anxiety-inducing society is, how much is going on. And we in the modern day talk in the exact same way about, you know, social media, the internet, all that kind of stuff.

Scull: It is. You know, we look back on the 19th century and think of it in idyllic terms of, you know, a much slower pace of life — and people, they thought it was stressful in exactly the ways we do.

三、1909：弗洛伊德登陆美国

Scull: So there was a class of potential patients. Some of them were seeking help in the neurologists and a few psychiatrists who moved out of the asylum. But there were also these mental healing groups that were religious, and they're all around at the beginning of the 20th century.

And in 1909, a Viennese gentleman and two of his close colleagues travel across the Atlantic on a German steamer and arrive in New York, and then transport themselves up to Worcester, Massachusetts, where Clark University is celebrating its 20th anniversary. Clark University was then set up — it still exists — but it was set up to copy the German research university. The only comparable example at the time was Johns Hopkins in Baltimore. And Hopkins developed the leading medical school of the time, borrowing from that German concept of mixing research and teaching and patient care.

Lex: I like how you're telling this in a cinematic way — the story of Sigmund Freud and Carl Jung coming to America to give a lecture. I like how it's like the movie opens and then here he is — you don't know who he is, he's fairly obscure. We should say the reason you're actually telling it that way is America has been a really defining place for psychiatry.

Scull: Yes.

Lex: And then Freud had his own views on America and so on. But this was —

Scull: In terms of the history of psychiatric medicine, America is central.

Lex: Right.

Scull: Many of the in-house histories of psychiatry portray this as Freud's conference. But it wasn't. Freud was almost an afterthought of the conference. The head of Clark was a psychologist and he was interested in Freud. But actually there were about 30 speakers at the Clark conference: two Nobel Prize winners in physics, Franz Boas, who was the leading anthropologist of his generation, and a host of other scholars, including a couple of Freud's fierce critics, one of whom — Stern — was on the same boat as him and they avoided one another like the plague.

But anyway, it's important to see that. And Freud — it's a mark of how important German science and German medical science was in the late 19th early 20th century, where it was the most advanced in the world — that Freud delivered his lectures in German, and the audience, that wasn't a problem for the audience because they'd all learned German so they could read German literature on medicine. So quite an extraordinary thing.

William James attends one of Freud's lectures and has a conversation with him. William James is one of the people thinking about the psychology of the human mind in interesting ways. He's not impressed by Freud, and he also has a bad heart condition — he dies not all that long afterwards — but he's not impressed by Freud.

A handful of people are — some of the neurologists — and Freud's lectures explicitly attack religiously based psychotherapy, says psychotherapy is like a surgical operation on the mind and only us doctors, or only us thoroughly trained people — because actually he doesn't believe that psychoanalysis is only something that can be practiced by the medically qualified…

Lex: But the lecture is on psychoanalysis.

Scull: Yes. It's five lectures, they're published subsequently, and he makes a very important convert there. James Jackson Putnam is a Boston Brahmin, one of the upper-class Bostonians, who's extremely well-connected and is professor of neurology at Harvard, and he becomes a Freudian at that conference.

So mainstream American psychiatry pays very little attention to Freud's arrival on the scene. And when he becomes a bit more visible, they tend to be very dismissive — they regard the idea of talk therapy for something they regard as a biological condition as a ridiculous idea.

四、弗洛伊德是谁？神经学家出身的分析师

Lex: Maybe just mention a few things. Freud, of course, is widely acknowledged to be the father of psychoanalysis, and he has a bunch of ideas — one of which is there's this unconscious mind that is the source of many of our behaviors, and then psychoanalysis is a way to delve deep into that mind.

Scull: And the tools you use to do that is talking. Yes. Freud was trained as a neurologist himself, and studied under the most famous late 19th century neurologist Charcot in Paris, and translated Charcot into German and endeared himself to Charcot by doing that — that's a clever way to help your career along. But his Viennese colleagues didn't think much of Charcot, and they didn't think much of Freud's ideas either. So he had a bit of a hard time.

But he did develop a successful practice, in the sense that patients came to him. He was accompanied by two of his close disciples to the Clark conference. One of them, Carl Jung, was then anointed the crown prince — he was supposed to inherit Freud's enterprise, until the men had a very serious falling out just a little bit later in 1913, and Freud and Jung went their separate ways. That's a complicated story.

Freud, as one of his close friends and collaborators put it, was a great hater. If you fell out with Freud, it was bad news.

Lex: Oh yeah, yeah.

Scull: You were excommunicated — if it was Adler, but Jung especially. Jung was Swiss and he worked in the major mental hospital in Zurich, and he was attracted to psychoanalysis and to Freud, and for the first few years there was this obvious close alliance. Anyway, so Jung was the person who actually persuaded Freud to go to America. Initially, Freud had a very low opinion of America. He said it should be renamed Dollaria, because it was only interested in the dollar, and American women were far too pushy and powerful, and American food was dreadful and it poisoned him, and on and on.

Lex: So as you said, Freud was a master hater.

Scull: Yeah, he was. [laughter] And one of the things he hated was America — even though America brought him some fairly rich patients. But the richest patients of all went to Jung, not to Freud. And I think that probably exacerbated this split.

五、精神分析的诞生：Anna O 与被压抑的记忆

Lex: Let's actually focus first, before the conference, on the actual ideas of psychoanalysis. So Freud was the originator of psychoanalysis — this is 19th century. So tell me about the original case of Anna O, and like — what is psychoanalysis?

Scull: So Freud's academic career had been failing in Vienna, and he faced a prospect of either having to immigrate to America — which he regarded with horror in the 1880s — or perhaps reviving his career by going and studying under the most famous neurologist of the era, Jean-Martin Charcot, who was then delivering lectures on hysteria in Paris. And so Freud went and spent some months there, and came back imbued with Charcot's ideas about hysteria and found a Viennese medical establishment.

He started a consulting career, and that involved — he had a close friend named Joseph Breuer, and Breuer was more senior, had a very large practice and referred patients to Freud. And the two of them began to be interested in this problem of hysteria. Breuer had treated a woman who's now known as the sort of foundation patient for psychoanalysis, who was known to us as Anna O. We actually know she was Bertha von Pappenheim, but that was hidden for a long time. A lot of these patients had pseudonyms, because obviously the cases exposed a lot about their inner psychology, and — quite reasonably even without the modern concerns about privacy — there was reluctance to identify them.

So Anna O had nursed her father — she was Breuer's patient, not Freud's. She'd nursed her father through an illness and he'd ended up dying. And she developed various physical symptoms that troubled her a great deal, and was also somewhat depressed. And Breuer and Freud dealt with that by developing a notion that what she was suffering from was repressed memories and trauma. And this would become central to psychoanalysis — the idea of half-forgotten memories lurking in your subconscious that emerged in distorted forms of psychological symptoms and ways of being in the world that were disruptive.

Freud of course developed a much more elaborate theory of this in years to come. Breuer and Freud collaborate on a book called Studies in Hysteria, and there are a series of case vignettes in there of patients Freud has treated. And he develops the notion that people have these past experiences — initially he thinks they're real, that for example they have been sexually assaulted as a child, and that they can't face that, and so they hide it away from themselves, but they can't completely, so it emerges in this tortured series of forms.

And as things develop, the notion of resistances emerges: that you can't easily retrieve these memories, and indeed you resist them surfacing, and you have a hard time acknowledging them, and only with long and painful work will it become possible — as you bring them from the unconscious into the conscious world, you learn to cope with them in a different way, and your personality is transformed and you're made better. But crucially, the stuff that happens in childhood is important.

Lex: Yes — that early experiences have a dramatic effect.

Scull: And I think even some biological psychiatrists would agree with that notion these days, that — to the extent we abolish this distinction between mind and body and acknowledge that they're closely tied together — traumatic experiences in childhood, various socialization experiences, loss and so on, deeply mark the human psyche, I think, and can have long-term effects that are very powerful.

Lex: Of course, Freud added a bunch of stuff in the realm of psychosexual stages of childhood.

Scull: Yes. As he begins to develop his theories, he more and more comes to see — at first the libido, which gets sort of transformed into the sex drive — and sexual experiences and repression of sexuality and the modification of sexuality as people grow. All of that enters the picture. It's one of the things that ends up dividing Freud and Jung somewhat, because Jung downplays that sexual side of things after the break.

六、心灵的三重结构：Id, Ego, Superego

Scull: So Freud develops a very complicated theory of mind. Initially reflecting his training as a neurologist, he tries to write an essay — which survives — called Project for a Scientific Psychology. And the scientific psychology is going to tie psychology back into neurology. But he abandons that. And once he's abandoned that, he goes on to develop an increasingly elaborate theory.

He writes The Interpretation of Dreams, for example, because he begins to regard dreams as an arena where these hidden memories, these suppressed things, re-emerge in disguised form in your dream life. And so that book marks an important step forward. He becomes interested in things like slips of the tongue — so-called Freudian mistakes — and sees those as revealing what really is hidden from you. And so there's this very elaborate dissection of things that relies upon long extended talk therapy.

Of course, underlying it, he's building a model of how this whole mind thing works. There's —

Lex: Yes — three interacting parts of the personality: - First the Id, which is the primitive, entirely unconscious, driven by pleasure principle, seeking immediate gratification of basic drives such as sex and aggression. - There's the Ego, which is the rational mediator operating on the reality principle, balancing the Id's demands with external reality. - And finally the Superego, which is the internalized moral standards and ideals, producing guilt or pride and striving for perfection.

So that's the structure.

Scull: Yes, that is broadly speaking the structure that Freud ends up with. And the conflicts between these entities and the ways they interact are obviously the thing that creates your mental universe, your way of being in the world, and in many cases creates pathology — which, through the process of psychoanalysis, you can transform grotesque unhappiness into ordinary unhappiness, or something like that. [laughter]

七、有钱的病人：荣格与洛克菲勒家族

Scull: So — yes, you get that. And initially Jung gets one of the heirs to the International Harvester fortune as a patient. And the McCormick family are as rich as the Rockefellers and the Carnegies and the Vanderbilts of that world. This guy is a US senator who ends up committing suicide in 1925 after a lot of treatment from Jung, when he fails to win re-election to the US Senate. He kills himself in Washington in the interregnum.

But he also gets another one of that brood. One of the Rockefeller daughters, Edith Rockefeller, marries a McCormick, and she has a lot of psychological issues, and she tries to get Jung to move to Chicago, promising him she'll set him up in a mansion with lots of her friends as his patients — and Jung has no interest. So then she finally persuades him to come to New York and accompany her on the liner across to Zurich to be treated. She's agoraphobic and so she has a hard time being out of her little cocoon. So she's treated there.

As an example of how peculiar she was: I mentioned the agoraphobia. So she occupies a huge array of suites with all her servants and so on in Zurich. And she takes her train journey with a stopping train, and her chauffeur follows the train in the Rolls-Royce, in case she has to jump out of the train at a station because she can't bear it anymore. And she becomes a Jungian analyst — but she's very wealthy and she writes big checks to Jung, which is the important thing. And then Jung attracts Paul Mellon and his wife Mary, and so Jung's works are published by Princeton University Press with the subvention from that Mellon foundation. So it's a long-running thing.

Freud doesn't get patients quite that rich. He gets some rich Americans.

八、一战、炮弹休克与文化上的接纳

Lex: We should say that Freud — his ideas became quite popular among the intellectual and artist class in the 1920s in America.

Scull: And another thing happened. World War I saw the breakdown of many soldiers from something that came to be labeled as shell shock. The label "shell shock" intimates the first theories about its origin — which was that shells bursting near you and bombs bursting near you shook up your body and your brain and created some physical damage that then accounted for the symptoms of shell shock: your mutism, your blindness, your constant shaking, your nightmares, all of that.

But it became increasingly apparent that shell shock was actually a psychological thing. The trauma of war, in a significant number of cases, brought about mental breakdowns. And in thinking about that, Freud's ideas about the unconscious mind and trauma and its connection to symptomatology acquired a new significance for a lot of people in that period.

And then after the war, you're absolutely right — among a certain smart section of society, those ideas developed a considerable purchase. Psychiatrists who were mostly stuck in the asylums dealing with psychotic patients wanted nothing to do with these ideas, that this talk therapy —

Lex: The mainstream psychiatry, which was mostly in a clinical setting…

Scull: Yeah. Freud's ideas were not popular. The only partial exception to that was the mental hospital in Washington DC, the only federal mental hospital, St. Elizabeths. William Alanson White, who was then the superintendent, was somewhat sympathetic to Freud's ideas and tried a bit — but you're talking about thousands of patients, and the idea of talk therapy for them is obviously out of reach. Plus they are much more severely disturbed.

So it does happen — novelists, painters, artists, playwrights, and the audience for those elite forms of culture do tend to embrace Freudian ideas. Sex sells, in the theater and on the movies, obviously. But beyond that, part of Freud's appeal to everybody — it was something he lamented at one point. He said, you know, my case histories read like short stories, like works of fiction, and in that sense people think they lack the stamp of serious science. But I'm driven to that because that's how I unpack what's going on.

Well, psychoanalysis is telling stories. It's getting people to recover stories, recover memories, to rebuild. And its elements of psychological conflict and hidden motives and so forth are naturally very appealing to people writing novels, people writing plays, people doing screenplays, and for artists of the modern sort. The idea that we can extract things from the subconscious — surrealism and the like, for example, are clearly very heavily influenced by Freudian ideas.

九、精神分析的现实局限

Scull: But it's important to know: circa 1930, there are probably 300 psychoanalysts in North America. If they each — classical psychoanalysis involving 5 hours a week — they can't treat that many patients. A few thousand, when there are hundreds of thousands in the hospitals.

Lex: Right.

Scull: So what changes… all right.

item.description:
## 一、被遗忘的"早餐帝国"起源：疯人院是现代健康产业的子宫
最令人错愕的细节藏在几乎一带而过的一句话里——**家乐氏（Kellogg's）玉米片，来自一家精神疗养院**。今天全球超市货架上的早餐工业，其真正的祖先不是农业，而是 19 世纪基督复临安息日会为忧郁症患者建立的疗养所。当年林肯遗孀、亨利·福特、甚至泰山的作者都在那里"排毒、素食、通便"。
这揭示了一个几乎无人察觉的系统性真相：**19 世纪美国的精神健康产业，就是今天"健康经济"（wellness economy）的原型**——素食主义、肠道理论、断食、瑜伽式静养、"戒除刺激"——所有当代 biohacking 与 wellness influencer 的话术，早在 120 年前就以"神经衰弱疗法"的名义完整存在过。Silas Weir Mitchell 的《磨损与撕裂》（Wear and Tear）警告 19 世纪的人们：电报和铁路让神经系统"破产"。今天我们把"电报"换成"TikTok"，一字不差地重复同一套焦虑修辞。**每一代人都相信自己是被科技毁掉的第一代人**——这是一种周期性的文明性错觉。

item.title: [Bits + Bips] An Oil Shock, a Boxed-In Fed, and Bitcoin at $85K
item.dc:creator: Bits + Bips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三个让人意外的系统性观察

1. 债务规模到达临界点后，加息竟然变成了"财政放水"——货币政策的相位反转

Austin 无意中说出了一个惊人的悖论：当美国债务达到 30 万亿美元级别、且短端占比极高、滚动极快时，加息 25bp 等于每年向美国居民注入 750 亿美元的利息现金流。这是一个连教科书都还没跟上的"相位反转"：传统上加息是紧缩，但在债务/GDP 超过某个阈值后，加息通过"利息支出→财政赤字→私人部门现金流"的传导链变成了扩张性政策。

这也解释了一个此前看似"反常"的现象——为什么比特币在 Fed 加息当天反而上涨 7%？市场不是在"逆基本面"，而是先于经济学家察觉到了政策工具的极性倒转。加密市场对流动性极度敏感的属性，让它成了这套新范式的第一个"验证器"。

2. USDe/稳定币的进化路径，与商业银行史惊人地同构——但它是压缩了 400 年的重放

节目开头 Guy Young 描述稳定币"把复杂性抽象在简单存款界面背后"时，其实无意中重演了 17 世纪威尼斯银行、18 世纪英格兰银行、20 世纪美联储三次金融基础设施迭代的共同叙事结构：底层资产越复杂 → 用户界面越简化 → 用户信任度越高 → 系统规模越大。

真正让人啊哈的是：Tether 不在乎 BTC 涨跌，因为它的商业模式已经"叛逃"到了传统金融。这与 19 世纪 J.P. Morgan 从铁路承销商蜕变成货币中心银行是同一种"母体切换"——一个行业最赚钱的玩家往往是那个最早认清"我到底在卖什么"的人。加密行业最赚钱的公司现在卖的是监管套利+美元利差，不是加密本身。这是全行业需要面对的存在性问题。

3. AI 与加密的"孪生结构"——它们其实在解决同一个哲学问题

Chris 提到"AI 有人在环、加密没有人在环"时，触碰到了一个更深的结构：中本聪当年用数学替代了央行行长，OpenAI 想用董事会替代上帝——一个已被证伪，一个正在试错。

跨领域连接：这与 20 世纪医学史上的"外科医生 vs 麻醉师"分工惊人相似——外科医生（AI 模型开发者）永远想保留最后决定权，而麻醉师（协议/规则）用无声的自动化让整个系统变得可扩展。加密不是 AI 的补充技术，加密是 AI 的免疫系统：它给 AI Agent 提供了一套"人类不能中途篡改"的执行环境，从而让 Agent 真正拥有"契约能力"而非"权限能力"。这意味着未来最有价值的加密协议，可能不是那些做 DeFi 的，而是那些做 agent-native 结算层的——一个目前几乎没人在正确定价的赛道。

隐藏的元模式

把这期节目从头到尾看完，你会发现一个反复出现的隐藏结构：每一个看似独立的话题——比特币短挤空、Fed 加息、OpenAI 债务、Meta 的 Muse——都在讲同一件事：中心化机构的"人类判断力"正在被市场系统性定价为负债。CLARITY 法案本身不重要，重要的是市场已经开始把"依赖立法者、依赖美联储主席、依赖 OpenAI CEO"都当作折价因子。这才是这一轮资金流的真正主旋律，而节目里没人明说。

📝 转录文本

An Oil Shock, a Boxed-In Fed, and Bitcoin at $85K

Bits + Bips

一、稳定币的隐形进化：USD 的风险其实在变低

The risk profile has changed quite a bit through time and the composition of what we do within USD. I would actually argue has become like safer through time, rather than more risky, which is kind of more slanted towards real-world assets lending in a secured way, you know, within qualified custodians, etc, etc.

And so yeah, I think if you compare some of the stuff that's sitting within USD now to where it started, many would make the argument that like holding a bunch of triple-A rated pieces of collateral was actually much safer than a basis trade on offshore exchanges.

银行账户式的抽象体验

The way I would like in very simple terms, sort of explaining it to the user on the other side is that the end user who's using a bank account doesn't really see the complexity of like a bank balance sheet that sits behind the whole thing. They kind of just see: I'm depositing my money and I'm getting a safe, reliable, dependable savings yield from my money within a deposit account.

And for us, I think it's obviously not the same in terms of like the risk profile of a bank, but the complication of everything that goes on within a bank is almost abstracted away from the user who just sees this very simple interface of a simple deposit with a reliable savings yield.

And so from our perspective, it's kind of like almost a new form of that, which is a tokenized form of different exposures that are sitting within USD, but simplified for the user as like a one-click experience for depositing dollars and getting a yield.

摆脱加密周期的依赖

Yeah, I think it's just because, you know, one of the big lessons that I think we've had in the last cycle is: you just don't want to be entirely reliant on just the crypto cycle as a business. And I think the very best businesses now in this space have tried to untether themselves from just the cyclicality of just "is Bitcoin price going up or down?"

As I think, you know, Hyperliquid here was a great example of, you know, kind of repositioning the business in some sense in the last year where RWA perps and the perps on equities and commodities actually grew to like more than 50 percent of their volumes, I think like a month or two ago. And that didn't even exist like nine months ago as like a category within the space.

The substance is that you're still seeing this CapEx which is 1.5 percent of GDP. It's driving growth. You know there were good arguments to be made that without that the economy would just be kind of limping along and weak, but it's very vibrant because of all this data center spend.

And you're right about OpenAI — thing is that's a company issue though, it's not a sector issue. So if OpenAI defaults on its debt obligations which they have a good chance of doing (I pointed out those $5 billion risks November last year), someone else will assume it. It's like foreclosure, right? 2008 someone doesn't pay their mortgage, someone says "gee I'll step in and I'll assume that" and it's going to be a firm like Meta, right? The stock went up 7 points today on this Muse thing because of their investment AI, or it might be another firm that wants to see faster inference and a better UX.

So one way or another the data center's getting built, the chips are being sold.

十一、Meta Muse：AI Agent 的主流时刻

I think there's a lot of opportunity for value accrual, right? It's an app — value accrual tends to go to apps over time. Massive unlock for crypto mind you, why? Because of the composability of various tokens and other assets, real-world assets, 24/7 markets. Like sorry guys, I'm going to go to sleep way too early at this point in my life but the agents are going to keep going. And so this is going to transform capital markets as we know them — trading, algorithms, liquidity, everything.

I feel like we're not there yet — I mean and I'm starting hearing it more and more talked about. I was at a cocktail party this weekend and that's what people were talking about: "oh I just got this new agent, it's doing this, it books travel for me, it did this and this." It's starting to slowly hit the mainstream — sometimes we live in a bubble.

I think the only thing that needs to be probably solved still is trust. You know when people first started working on these things what did we all do? We used our MetaMask right because we were very concerned about handing over the keys. People are starting to hand over the keys more and more. It really comes down to safety and security. I think there's going to be a couple bumps along the road, ultimately I think it gets figured out.

But a lot of value accrual is happening, elimination of arbitrage, crypto stands to benefit massively. Like the other thing about crypto because I'm a crypto guy is: AI's running around disrupting every single industry and institution. SaaS-pocalypse they said — and I think that was a little bit overblown frankly. I think great SaaS founders are going to figure out how to use AI. But what is the one technology that really complements AI? Yeah there's maybe a little security things that we're fixing right now, but it's a truly complementary technology — AI and crypto — and that is very different than the other industries that it's fundamentally disrupting.

Muse 的发布数据

Alright, we experienced mainstream, call it hobbyist phase, early adopters, and I want to give Meta a significant amount of credit here as we start, because Muse just hit.

And what's going on is Meta launched Muse on September 8th as a secure, private, personal AI agent that sends email, books travel, fills in forms, can buy things, keeps working after the app is closed. And notably within the release, if you read it carefully they said they're already working on privacy deployments for this — and I will remind everyone Moxie Marlinspike is over there now from Signal so I don't know that actually they're faking it on that one.

The way it works is Muse runs on a cloud computer and there's a second layer that approves every action that it takes on the internet. You can get a free tier, there's a $20 plan, there's a $100 plan, these are U.S. only for now. Go America.

It was number one on the U.S. iPhone chart on September 18th, 730,000 downloads in 10 days. ChatGPT had about 700,000 in its first eight, so running on about the same course.

Trust right now is the drag. There was an Oppenheimer survey that 8 percent of consumers would share their passwords with Meta, 30 percent with Google. Let me tell you right now for the love of God just use a password manager people.

Amazon 封杀 Muse

And this is provoking some commercial reactions. Amazon shut the door Sunday night. Shoppers using Muse on Amazon are getting a pop-up that continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon's conditions of use. Amazon said they asked Meta to leave it out, Muse doesn't identify itself and quote, "appears to capture and store customer credentials."

Amazon's statement was that third party agents should operate openly and respect the service provider decisions about whether or not to participate. Meta shot back that Muse has no visibility into people's passwords or payment methods, that they have other implementations for that, and noted that Amazon runs its own shopping agent, Alexa for shopping and buy for me, and took in more than 68 billion in advertising last year.

So legally can they do this? Amazon won and then lost an injunction against Perplexity's Comet, originally having it blocked from using their services while operating as an agent and then the Ninth Circuit vacated it. But Comet runs in a browser, Muse is running on Meta's servers, it's significantly more complex.

Agent 大战全景

There are some other things going on. xAI has Grok bots — they are a persistent cloud computer per bot that signs into apps. It's aimed much more at work, it's a more complex implementation, it's a multi-agent framework. Apple is shipping iOS 27 with a Siri that chains across apps. OpenAI hired Peter Steinberger from OpenClaw, the creator, to drive the next generation of personal agents.

And Stripe is getting involved — they are checkout behind Muse. Grok bot is working with Instinct through its Link wallet, and everybody is trying to win payments here, possibly using crypto. Basically the age of AI agents is hitting the mainstream.

Ram：Zuck、Dario、Sam 的排序

So Ram I want to start with you because you've been on the AI economics thing for a while. Meta has been spending money but not deploying too much, the Llama models are usable but certainly we're not at the top of the pack, and then out of nowhere Muse. What do you think of this, what is it telling you about the future of the space, what did it tell you about Meta?

Austin, before he answers, can I ask Ram, like — what do you think about Sam Altman, what does he think about Zuck?

I'm a Zuck fanboy. Yeah, I have a tremendous amount of respect for Zuck.

And where does Dario fit on that hierarchy?

I think Dario's incredibly talented for what he's accomplished. I just think how he deals with the U.S. government — he should change his presentation of AI to the American public. He's an extraordinary leader, you can't take that away from him of course.

So Zuck's number one, Dario's number two, Sam number three?

Steve Jobs is number one. Okay, Elon is on the list too, Zuck is a real champion. Jensen is up there too, I'm a big fan of founder-led CEOs in public markets. Anyway...

Sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt.

AI Agent 是新的"计算机形态"

No, no, all good. So yeah, look this is a big deal, this is a major, major deal. This is the rise of AI agents, I think are a bigger deal than computers. It's going to be transformational.

I was listening to some Steve Jobs wisdom over the weekend, which I do from time to time. And you know he developed the personal computer before there were color graphics, before there was a graphical user interface — we use a mouse and a pointer to click as an input into the PC. And you know when he passed away a couple decades later we have computers in the palm of our hands, in our pockets, and they're interactive and it plays music and it's multimedia — it's all these amazing things.

And AI agents are now this new form factor and they're helping people save money, make better decisions, meet them in their channel of their choice. Why do we need to use a mouse anymore? Why do we need to use a keyboard anymore? We just will and summon what we want and the AI starts doing it. We're moving at the speed of willpower more and more every day.

So I think this AI agent is an extraordinary development, it's why I think semiconductors are a great opportunity. And Meta's first out there but yeah Google is coming, Google Spark is in testing right now. It's going to be compelling. Apple sees this — everyone was going after the personal assistant AI, it was the obvious thing.

But there are other AIs coming — the personal concierge, the personal doctor, the personal wealth manager. It's what we're building at Lumida. All of these niches are going to get filled out. So I think it's super exciting if you're long the AI trade and we're going to be mainlining AI now to consumers. Right now it's been mostly infrastructure and compute story — this data center very abstract concepts. Now consumers are going to start seeing tangible value like when they first got their AOL CD and went on the internet. Right, that's what's happening now with these personal assistant agents.

十二、结语

So on that note, as always, thank you for joining us for this episode of Bits and Bips. We hope you're enjoying your agents and we'll be back in one week to discuss more about how the worlds of crypto and macro are colliding. As a reminder, we've got our own channels, please subscribe. Until then, everyone.

Thank you for watching and hope you enjoyed this episode of Bits and Bips. Just remember, nothing we say here is investment advice. And please check unchainedcrypto.com/bitsandbips for more disclosures.

item.description:
## 三个让人意外的系统性观察
### 1. 债务规模到达临界点后，加息竟然变成了"财政放水"——货币政策的相位反转 Austin 无意中说出了一个惊人的悖论：当美国债务达到 30 万亿美元级别、且短端占比极高、滚动极快时，**加息 25bp 等于每年向美国居民注入 750 亿美元的利息现金流**。这是一个连教科书都还没跟上的"相位反转"：传统上加息是紧缩，但在债务/GDP 超过某个阈值后，加息通过"利息支出→财政赤字→私人部门现金流"的传导链变成了扩张性政策。
这也解释了一个此前看似"反常"的现象——为什么比特币在 Fed 加息当天反而上涨 7%？市场不是在"逆基本面"，而是**先于经济学家察觉到了政策工具的极性倒转**。加密市场对流动性极度敏感的属性，让它成了这套新范式的第一个"验证器"。
### 2. USDe/稳定币的进化路径，与商业银行史惊人地同构——但它是压缩了 400 年的重放 节目开头 Guy Young 描述稳定币"把复杂性抽象在简单存款界面背后"时，其实无意中重演了 17 世纪威尼斯银行、18 世纪英格兰银行、20 世纪美联储三次金融基础设施迭代的**共同叙事

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被"抛弃"反而成了救命稻草：约束如何逆转为护城河

最反直觉的一幕，藏在 Blake 一句轻描淡写的自嘲里——"和 Rolls-Royce 公开分手"曾被所有人视为 Boom 的死刑判决。但真正的戏剧性反转是：一台专为 Mach 1.7、长时间高温运行而设计的超音速引擎，把风扇拆掉、装上发电机，就变成了 AI 数据中心梦寐以求的"不需要水冷的 42 兆瓦移动电站"。

这里有一个被大多数评论忽略的系统性真相：AI 算力泡沫正在悄悄补贴人类的超音速梦想。Blake 的商业模式实际上是"用 OpenAI / xAI 的 CapEx 焦虑，反向融资一条通向马赫 1.7 客机的道路"。这在能源史上不是孤例——早期铁路的过剩运力催生了标准时区，早期互联网骨干的过剩带宽催生了云计算。基础设施的"错配溢出"才是真正的创新引擎。当 Blake 说"从没见过这种需求"时，他其实是在描述一个由 Transformer 架构意外撬动的航空业二次融资通道。

二、Concord 的真正失败不是技术，而是"零售可及性"的缺失

Blake 的一句话点破了 50 年航空史的隐性诅咒："Concord 在安全、舒适、可负担这三个维度上是 0/3。" 这不是航空问题，这是产品设计的基本失败模式——用高价把技术锁进 1% 用户，让下一代注定被拒于门外，导致技术无法穿越"世代传递门槛"。

这里可以做一个惊人的跨领域连接：Concord 的死法和 Google Glass、Segway、以及早期 VR 头显是同一种死法——都是"精英专属的未来样品"，都因为无法制造出"童年记忆"而永远无法成为"成人常识"。Blake 讲述他女儿以为火箭必然会返回发射台的故事，实际上揭示了一个残酷的产品哲学：一项技术只有当孩子把它视为理所当然时，它才真正"活下来"。Concord 之所以能被取消而没人抗议，正是因为它从未进入过任何孩子的默认世界模型。Boom 要赢，不是要造出更快的飞机，而是要造出足够便宜到能被下一代当成"六小时横穿美国听起来像原始社会"的默认设施。

三、"专家陷阱"与"垂直整合的钟摆回归"——一场被误读的产业范式转移

Blake 说的"你成为专家的那一刻，你就浸泡在过去里，然后就完全没用了"——这句话被听众当成鸡汤，其实是一次对MBA 时代净资产回报率教条的宣战。过去 40 年主流商学院教的"外包一切非核心业务、最大化 RONA"，正在被硬科技领域集体反向证伪：SpaceX 自造引擎、Tesla 自造电池、Apple 自造芯片、Anthropic 自训模型、Boom 自造涡轮叶片。

这里有一个几乎无人提及的深层模式：所有"重新垂直整合"的公司，都在做同一件事——把"制造"重新变回"研发"的一部分。Blake 展示的那张涡轮叶片，本质上是在告诉观众：当设计工具（数字孪生）和制造工具（增材制造）的语言开始统一，"设计"和"制造"之间的分工就失去了经济合理性。这是自福特流水线以来最深的一次产业分工重构——不是"回到制造"，而是"制造工序被折叠回设计工序"。

最出人意料的推论：如果这个趋势成立，那么未来 10 年真正稀缺的不是工程师，也不是工厂，而是能同时理解物理学、拓扑优化算法和工艺参数的"三栖思维者"。这也解释了为什么 Boom 只用 50 个人就能造出一架超音速验证机——不是因为他们更勤奋，而是因为他们代表了一种新的"人均生产力单位"：一个能在 CAD、CFD、CAM 三层同时思考的工程师，其产出可能相当于传统航空公司的 20 个专业分工岗位。"50 人造飞机"不是奇迹，是新工业逻辑的第一个可见样本。

附：一个隐藏的时间线悖论

Blake 无意间说出的最重的一句话是："我们的实习生出生在波音上次推出新飞机之后。" 这不是产业观察，这是一种代际耻辱。请把这句话和另一条线索并置：Concord 停飞是 2003 年——恰好是 iPhone 前夜。过去 22 年，人类把所有加速的欲望都投射到了"信息移动"上，而彻底放弃了"身体移动"。Boom 真正在挑战的，不是波音，而是一个已经把"物理位移"从进步定义中悄悄删除的文明假设。

📝 转录文本

Blake Scholl 演讲与对谈｜Boom Supersonic

开场｜一个"不可能"的宣告

Set to fly at Mach 1.7, with 130 orders from major airlines. The founder and CEO of Boom Supersonic, Blake Scholl.

"Boeing hasn't built a new airplane in 20 years. I mean, it's David and Goliath, but Goliath is like asleep. We're here to bring back supersonic passenger travel and ultimately to make the planet dramatically more accessible. This whole airplane was built by essentially 50 people."

"By 50 people."

"The moment you become an expert, what you're steeped in is the past and then you're completely useless. Courage is not being fearless. Courage is acting despite the fear. If there's no boom at all, there's nothing to argue about. The world needs supersonic flight. Passengers deserve it."

Please welcome Blake Scholl.

一、"Houston, We Have a Problem"——半个世纪的停滞

Good morning. Houston, we have a problem.

In 1969, we landed on the moon and we flew an airliner through the sound barrier. Yet more than half a century later, we can't go to the moon and we can't fly faster than the speed of sound.

The legacy, the political legacy of Concord, was a ban on supersonic flight over the US. Boeing brought us into the jet age in 1957 with the 707. But fast forward to today, and their latest airliner is a literal carbon fiber copy of their first. By the way, we have interns born after the last time Boeing launched a new airplane in 2004. This is insane.

But imagine—imagine an alternate timeline in which innovation and flight had continued. What if we could cross the Atlantic in three and a half hours? What if Sydney were as accessible as Honolulu is today? What would that do for business, for culture, even for love?

二、从软件工程师到超音速创业者

Who could do something about this?

12 years ago, I was a software engineer and an ads guy from Amazon and Groupon. The idea that somebody with nothing more than a pilot's license could do something about this seemed laughable.

In 2015, I pitched my old big boss, Jeff Bezos, on Boom's seed round, and he passed. And then he wrote this in the 2015 Amazon shareholder letter:

"There are certain things that only large companies can do. No matter how good an entrepreneur you are, you're not going to build an all-composite airliner in your garage startup. Not one that you'd want to fly on anyway."

I took that a little personally. But I don't blame Jeff. This is what our garage looked like back then. And this—this was actually a slide from our pitch deck—that is in fact a supersonic airliner mockup made from cardboard, plywood, and seats from Office Depot.

But big things often have humble beginnings.

三、50 人造出一架超音速飞机

Fast forward to last year, and Boom became the first private company ever to build a supersonic jet.

Something that the big companies would have put thousands of people on—we did with just 50 really dedicated men and women.

And when we flew that airplane, we had the first supersonic installation of Starlink so people around the world could tune in—watching a video filmed on an iPhone, streamed via Starlink.

And my favorite part was the pictures that people started sending me from classrooms. Kids that would have tuned out on flight instead tuned in. Some of them stood up, and some of them even jumped up and down. Isn't that great?

One of those is a future chief engineer. I guarantee it.

四、重温 XB-1 突破音障的时刻

I'd like to invite you now to relive that moment with me.

From that fateful moment, the Kittyhawk. We strove to fly higher and faster. This pilot and this airplane are about to be the first ever to fly faster than the speed of sound. Concord showed us the future of passenger flight in 1969. In 2003, we lost all that. "Good morning. For the last time, Speedbird Concord 2." The sound barrier was back. But we are still pioneers, and humanity will always want to reach higher. A small team with a big dream. In 2025, XB-1 became the first privately developed jet to break the sound barrier. "You are go for Mach 1.1." But this time, we demonstrated that supersonic flight could be boomless. And now the sound barrier can stay broken.

Thank you. I thought that would get old, but it never does.

五、Boomless Cruise：让音爆消失的物理学

XB-1 uses actually a far simpler technique than others have talked about to solve sonic boom. We call it boomless cruise, and it uses the natural refractive power of the atmosphere to redirect the sonic boom upwards.

So it's like if a tree falls in a forest, but no one was there to hear it—did it really make a sound?

And we talked to the president shortly after breaking the sound barrier, and he agreed: if there's no sonic boom, there should be no ban on supersonic flight. So that ban that started in 1973 actually ended June 6th of last year.

But this was just an executive order, and theoretically some idiot could reverse it. So we went to Congress and we said: you should make that permanent. And the Supersonic Legalization Act passed the House.

Anybody guesses what the vote was? It's actually unanimous. It's unanimous—and it got out of Senate Congress unanimously recently, and now we have to get it through the rest of the Senate. And I think we should just do it unanimously, right? Because that's badass.

六、被宣告死亡之后：自研引擎的转机

So, okay. So it's all full speed ahead, right? And we get to look forward to supersonic passenger flights soon.

But wait, there was actually a problem.

Not that long ago, people declared Boom dead. One of the dumbest things I ever did was try to outsource our engine development to a big old company. And that plan didn't work out. We broke up with Rolls-Royce very publicly, and people said we were doomed.

So we decided to do the thing everyone said was really impossible: to make our own engine from scratch to pair perfectly with the airplane. Turns out that effort's actually working.

And we had an opportunity not just to build our own jet engine, but to reinvent how engines are designed with the world's most advanced digital design tools—and then to change how they are actually manufactured, also with the power of digital manufacturing.

So we're not just designing our own engines, we're not just making our own engines, we're making our own engine parts down to the turbine blades. I have one of those with me this morning. My girl was like, "Is that a turbine blade in your pocket, or are you happy to see me?"

Our philosophy is that engineering and manufacturing have to work together. If we want to re-industrialize America, we need to invent the next-generation manufacturing technology here—and use that to build the most incredible new products, not just try to bring back what we lost to China.

As we speak, our first vertically integrated jet engine core is getting assembled, and it's going to be in a test stand next month.

七、意想不到的支线：把超音速引擎装进数据中心

Now, in a bizarre twist of history, the thing that everyone said would kill us—that we didn't have a big company make us an engine—actually turns out to be the thing that makes a supersonic startup financially valuable.

Because it turns out, if we take our supersonic engine technology that's designed to run full duration at high power in a hot environment at Mach 1.7, and we take the fan off the front and instead we put a generator in the back—it does this.

So our first application of our engine isn't in the sky. It's actually on the ground for data centers.

We can wrap this up in a couple trailers and we can deploy 42 megawatts for behind-the-meter power generation with a supersonic engine core that's designed to run hot, so it doesn't need any water. I think we all know the water thing is kind of an objection—but why not make it go away?

八、最先进的涡轮工厂正在建设中

So as we speak, we are building in an undisclosed location the world's most advanced jet turbine factory. And our philosophy is the exact opposite of what you find at every legacy big company—with lots of outsourcing and a "return on net assets" philosophy that makes you spin out your crown jewels.

We are manufacturing our own engines at scale, starting from raw materials, then going to the parts, including the most difficult ones like blades and vanes, and then assembling them and then running on our own test stand.

The factory you're looking at here made its first parts last week, and it will scale to making multiple gigawatts per year. Over the next 5 years, we aim to add 10-plus gigawatts to the grid.

九、乘客能期待什么？

What this means is, as future passengers, we get to look forward to:

  • Flying faster than the speed of sound
  • Twice as fast over water
  • 50% faster over land, with no sonic boom
  • And doing it on what will actually be the most tested new jet engine ever made, thanks to being proven on the ground first

So there's still many, many hard problems to solve. Success is not guaranteed, but I think there's a lot of reason to be excited for a faster future, a more connected world, and American leadership in aviation.

十、对谈环节

Q1｜什么时候能坐上？多少钱？

"A date and a number. Right. These are my favorite questions. I'm sure your board asks once in a while."

The thing about faster flight is: everybody wants it, so long as it's safe, comfortable, and affordable. And Concord is really like zero out of three. And we should be able to do three out of three.

So, I'll give you the numbers. Round trip across the Atlantic at Mach 1.7, 3 hours, and the break-even fare is about $3,500. Round trip. That's the break-even. And of course it will probably go for more than that. But any dollar above that, United's making some good money.

Our goal is 4 years. But I've learned along the way it's more important to be fast than to be predictable. So how long will it actually take? I can't say with certainty, but we're moving as fast as we can, and we'll make sure that it's available at the earliest date that it's physically possible.

"So we're looking at potentially 2030, give or take, Blake, versus say Elon timing. So when you're doing the impossible magical thing, it can take a little extra."

Q2｜"Sonic Thump" 到底是什么？

"You keep talking about over oceans, but my understanding was that you're making it… the sonic boom is going to go away and become like a sonic thump or a sonic pow or something."

It's a sonic nothing, actually. Like, literally.

There are two different techniques that people use for boom mitigation, and the one we're using is called—we call it boomless cruise. The nerds call it Mach cutoff. The boom comes off the airplane, it's kind of a normal-strength boom, and it makes a big U-turn in the sky and never touches the ground.

That works up to about Mach 1.3, or you know, 50% faster than how we can fly today. So you can't go full speed boomless. But you could still go fast enough that you could leave New York, say, at 9:00 a.m. and land in San Francisco around 9:30 a.m. So it's still going to be pretty great.

And then over water, you can go full speed—but no one's there to hear a boom.

Q3｜数据中心业务的进展

"How is the data center project going? Do you have customers for this product already? … Is it printing money?"

It's an incredible money-printing business. I mean, I've never seen demand like this for anything else in my life.

"How many orders? Give us 10 customers."

Tens of gigawatts of demand in my inbox. We're going to run that first engine next month, and then we're going to auction it all off.

"Did you talk to Elon about it? Is he interested for the Colossus?" "You should ask Elon." "Okay, that's a yes. Okay, good enough."

Q4｜关于公司名"Boom"

"Do you ever think that as a name of a company for an airline, 'Boom' might be tempting the fates? I have a punch-up for you—how about Zoom?"

You know, no one's ever asked me about this before.

No, it's like—it's like Boom, and you're there. It's fun. And we called the company Boom because I thought the sonic boom was never going to be the blocker. So Boom is the company. The airplane is Overture. We wanted an innovative brand for the company, and something for the airplane itself that would have real gravitas.

Q5｜私人航空市场？

"Any chance at a private aviation option in the 2.0? … compete with Gulfstream and Falcon?"

Well, I hope the private jet guys will make a supersonic jet. They should. If they don't, I guess we'll do it.

Q6｜女儿与火箭：一个关于"世代期待"的故事

Let's talk about the future. I'll tell a story.

So my youngest daughter, who's four and a half now—when she was 18 months old, we'd watch rocket videos. When she was two and a half, I took her to watch a model Estes rocket. And I'm just the person I am—so I get the smallest little rocket and I put the big D motor in it, and so that thing goes and ends up in a tree three fields over.

I thought it was pretty cool, but she was upset. And it took me a moment to realize why she was upset: she expected the rocket to come back to the pad.

I had done nothing but watch rocket-landing videos with her, like literally her entire life.

And for supersonic, there's an analogous thing. We will have won when we've sped up flights for every passenger—from the president on a Supersonic Air Force One, to a supersonic private jet, to supersonic commercial flights that are available to every class of passenger.

So when you have to convince kids that it used to take 6 hours to cross the country, and they're like, "What are you talking about, Dad? Like, who would even do that? Like, New York's not worth it if it takes six hours to get there"—that's when we've won.

So that will take many generations of airplanes. But we're not giving up.

Q7｜与本届政府的合作

"The company's now getting close to 10 years." "12, in fact." "12, in fact. Yeah. Okay. So, very close, you passed it."

Well, first off, I think it's really cool that supersonic flight is not a partisan issue, and that we're able to get stuff through Congress unanimously.

That said, I love how fast this administration moves.

Literally—we broke the sound barrier on Monday. I tweeted about it. Elon reposted my tweet. I flew to DC that night to start the legalization campaign. By the time I landed, I had an invitation to the West Wing. So that's Tuesday. By Thursday, our airplane model has made it to the Oval Office.

And by the way, it's still there. It's like one of the greatest product placements of all time. Like, there's a supersonic jet model in the Oval Office. I kind of love it.

And then it took 115 days to get the executive order signed. To me, that felt slow, but it probably would have taken longer in a different administration.

"Yeah, I think Biden's going to call you back in about two or three weeks from when you called him eight years ago. It's a joke. Sounds fast. It's a Biden joke."

All right, let's give it up for Blake one more time. All right, great job.

item.description:
## 一、被"抛弃"反而成了救命稻草：约束如何逆转为护城河
最反直觉的一幕，藏在 Blake 一句轻描淡写的自嘲里——"和 Rolls-Royce 公开分手"曾被所有人视为 Boom 的死刑判决。但真正的戏剧性反转是：**一台专为 Mach 1.7、长时间高温运行而设计的超音速引擎，把风扇拆掉、装上发电机，就变成了 AI 数据中心梦寐以求的"不需要水冷的 42 兆瓦移动电站"**。
这里有一个被大多数评论忽略的系统性真相：**AI 算力泡沫正在悄悄补贴人类的超音速梦想**。Blake 的商业模式实际上是"用 OpenAI / xAI 的 CapEx 焦虑，反向融资一条通向马赫 1.7 客机的道路"。这在能源史上不是孤例——早期铁路的过剩运力催生了标准时区，早期互联网骨干的过剩带宽催生了云计算。**基础设施的"错配溢出"才是真正的创新引擎**。当 Blake 说"从没见过这种需求"时，他其实是在描述一个由 Transformer 架构意外撬动的航空业二次融资通道。
## 二、Concord 的真正失败不是技术，而是"零售可及性"的缺失
Blake 的一句话点破了 50 年航空史的

item.title: [Lex Clips] Side-effects of SSRI antidepressant drugs: Sex-life plummets | Andrew Scull and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"统计显著 vs 临床显著"陷阱——一场精心设计的语言魔术

Scull 提到的这一点看似技术性，其实揭露了整个现代循证医学体系的一个隐蔽裂缝：在60分量表上改善1-2分就能宣称"显著优于安慰剂"。这不是造假，这是合法的。药企与监管系统之间早已形成一种默契——用"statistically significant"这个词的模糊性，在患者听觉里替换成"clinically meaningful"。

跨领域联想：这与金融业的"风险调整后收益率"、社交媒体的"参与度指标"、AI基准测试中的"SOTA"，本质上是同一套认知机制——当一个领域找不到真正的突破时，就重新定义"进步"的度量单位。SSRI 的营销胜利，某种意义上，是一场发生在测量学层面而非药理学层面的胜利。

二、真正令人意外的观察：SSRI 制造了一种"哲学性副作用"，而不仅是生理副作用

大多数讨论 SSRI 副作用时聚焦于性功能障碍、戒断反应。但转录中一句话被轻轻带过、其实极具颠覆性："They flatten everything out. You can't experience the highs and lows that normally we take as part of human experience."

这不是副作用——这是存在论层面的截肢。

想想看：抑郁症被定义为"情绪低谷过多"，而治疗方案是"把整个情绪频谱压平"。这就像因为一个人在低音区痛苦，就把他所有的乐器都调成静音。这不是治愈，而是把人调成"人形的平均值"。

跨领域连接：这与硅谷"生产力优化文化"惊人地同构——用番茄钟、日程管理、专注力药物削平生活的波峰波谷，追求一种可预测的、可量化的、"稳定的自我"。SSRI 只是化学版本的"人生Excel化"。而丧失性欲，本质上是丧失了"生理上不可预测的、不服从议程的那部分自我"。药物没有治疗抑郁——它治疗的是"作为一个有起伏的人这件事本身"。

三、被系统性忽视的转折点：处方权的迁移是一场静默的政变

Scull 在最后随口提到一件被主流讨论忽略的事：SSRI 的诊断和处方权从精神科医生转移到了基层全科医生。

这句话的分量比它听起来大得多。它意味着： - 一个需要精神科专业判断的复杂决策，被压缩进 15 分钟的门诊； - 全科医生没有时间做 CBT 的转介评估，开药是最低阻力路径； - 抑郁的定义因此发生了漂移——从"精神科现象"变成"全科主诉"，就像高血压。

跨领域类比：这几乎完全复刻了Uber 对出租车行业的颠覆逻辑——不是产品更好，而是降低了从业者的门槛与决策成本。SSRI 的胜利不在药理学，而在分销学。它成为"心理健康领域的默认路由"。

最深的洞察：40% 无响应者、中间响应但被副作用捕获者、以及戒断困难者——这三类人加起来占大多数，但整个系统仍在扩张。为什么？因为系统衡量的不是"治愈率"，而是"处方量"。这不是医学失败，而是医学被商业指标殖民后的完美运行。真正令人不安的是：CBT 作为一线治疗方案在英国 NICE 指南里明确写着，但在美国依然是药物优先——同样的科学证据，在不同的支付结构下，导向截然相反的医疗行为。这才是暴露真相的核心事实。

📝 转录文本

SSRI 的诞生与"血清素神话"

In the late '80s, the drug companies came across a new class of antidepressants that didn't have those side effects. As we'll see, they had other side effects, but not those. And the most famous of those was Prozac. They were a class of drugs called SSRIs. And again, forgive the acronym, but what it means is selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.

Serotonin is something manufactured in our bodies, actually in our digestive system, and it performs a variety of functions in the body, but it's also one of the neurotransmitters in our brains. And the way these drugs worked was by slowing the reuptake of serotonin in the brain, which was marketed by the drug companies as the solution to depression—that when you got depressed, it was because you didn't have enough serotonin in your brain, and these pills solved that problem.

It was like—well, Tipper Gore, Al Gore's ex-wife, was like many politicians' wives, depressed for reasons I fully understand, or at least partially understand. And she went to her psychiatrist, and that was one of the things she was given, and she became one of the big public advocates for SSRIs, which still are the most prescribed antidepressants.

它们有效吗？副作用是什么？

Do they work, and what are the side effects?

Yeah. So, here's where we get into slippery territory. Every time you do a controlled study of these antidepressants, they beat placebo in a statistically significant margin, but not necessarily in a clinically significant margin.

And this is—when you see drug ads, be very careful. "This one significantly improves X or Y." Does that mean clinically or does it mean statistically? Because the fact—if you—when we measure improvement with depression, we tend to use rating scales of various sorts. And if you improve on one of the major scales that's used by one or two points on a 60-point scale, it may be enough to show statistical significance—this drug does a little better than placebo—but it doesn't really affect your quality of life much.

And for most patients, antidepressants are marginally better than placebo, but a lot of the effect is the placebo effect.

"麻木化"效应与性生活的消失

And they come with very difficult side effects. A lot of people describe them as numbing drugs. They flatten everything out. So you can't experience the highs and lows that normally we take as part of human experience.

And then the numbing extends elsewhere in your body. In particular, lots of patients find a complete loss of libido. They can't get an erection; if they're a woman, they can't climax; their sex life just goes away. And sometimes it doesn't come back after you stop the drugs.

戒断的地狱：被药物困住的人们

Next layer of problems: getting off the drugs, for some people, turns out to be hell on wheels. They get worse depression than they had before, they get terrible feelings. Their brain is sparking, something's wrong. And so many patients find themselves trapped on those drugs for a long time. And we don't know what the effects of that are going to be.

So, it's a very mixed picture. That's why I think groups like NICE in England are saying use CBT as the first line, not drugs.

三类人群：一场没有事先答案的赌博

But again, it's also fair to say—I think what we find, and there was a recent Lancet study that I think was revealing on this point—it's like this with both antipsychotics and antidepressants:

  • You have a group of people who respond pretty well. And the side effects for them are bearable, or even they don't experience them. That's great.
  • You have a group of people—and it's significant; with depressed patients, we're talking north of 40%—who aren't responding. Okay. So, drugs aren't doing anything for them and they're running a risk.
  • And then in the middle, you have a group of people who get some positive improvement, but they also get side effects.

And that's where this cost-benefit analysis, if we can call it that, comes into play. And it's very difficult—and the problem is, going in, you don't know which group you're going to fall in. And your doctor doesn't know which group you're going to fall in.

处方权的静默转移

And more importantly, one of the things that the drugs revolution did was it moved the diagnosis and the prescribing of things away from psychiatry alone. So, many of these things, particularly antidepressants, are dispensed by primary care docs, not psychiatrists.

观看原视频 →

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"金鱼记忆"背后的结构性脆弱：参与度悖论

小陶开篇那句"美股参与者的记忆只有一秒，比金鱼还短"其实揭示了一个远比情绪面更深的问题——指数创新高与市场参与度悖离。周一纳指破历史新高，但参与度只有60%，20日均线的参与度仍停留在25–35%的悲观区。他从这个数据得出"不该减仓"的结论是对的，但理由可能颠倒了：低参与度+指数新高恰恰是典型的"帕累托陷阱"——极少数个股承担了整个指数的上涨。这从系统论看不是"底部信号"，而是"结构性脆弱"信号。真正让市场在心态上像金鱼的原因，不是散户健忘，而是信息半衰期的坍缩——算法交易+短周期资金把每一条消息的"衰减常数"压到了以秒计。这也解释了为什么他会说"同样的表达，不同的人接收到的信息不一样"——在信息半衰期极短的环境里，注意力本身就是最稀缺的资源。

二、Amazon vs Meta：一场"注意力护城河"与"履约护城河"的时代对撞

这场 MUSE 被封的争执，表面是电商与社交平台的话语权之争，本质是两种护城河形态的正面对撞：Meta 代表的是无摩擦的注意力流量（无重资产、无库存、无物流），Amazon 代表的是有摩擦的物理履约（仓储、fulfillment center、最后一公里）。当 Agent 时代来临，注意力这一层被"抽空"——因为 Agent 不看广告、不被 UI 挽留——物理履约反而成为不可替代的下沉资产。这里有个跨领域的类比值得玩味：中世纪威尼斯商人控制地中海航线，任何想在东西方之间通商的人都得缴过路税。Amazon 的仓储物流网络就是数字时代的地中海航线，MUSE 想"过路"，就必须谈判。小陶提到"Shopify 想做线下仓库最终失败了因为是重资产行业"——这句话的重量被低估了：重资产在 AI 时代不是负担，是最后的定价权。这与市场普遍认知（"轻资产才是未来"）完全相反。

三、Agent 时代的"流量重定价"：一次 Google 广告模型的镜像反转

小陶提到未来 MUSE 向亚马逊和沃尔玛的智能体发请求"这个请求本身应该要付费"——这一句话被他一带而过，但它可能是整期视频最重要的洞见。过去 25 年的互联网商业模式建立在"免费流量+广告变现"这个公式上，Google 在 2000 年把它推到极致：用户免费搜索，商家为流量付费。而 Agent 时代把这个公式镜像翻转：Agent 付费查询，商家提供的是数据接口本身。也就是说，"搜索"从消费端的免费行为，变成了 B2B 的付费 API 调用。这个变化的第二阶效应更耐人寻味：一旦 API 调用有价，那么"平台上的内容"就必须重新定价（小陶提到"你把它想象成 Reddit"很关键——Reddit 卖数据给 OpenAI 就是先例）。这意味着未来的护城河不再是"用户数"而是"结构化数据的独占权"。从这个角度看，小陶把苹果换成谷歌+高通的操作暗含一个反直觉判断：iPhone 那个封闭生态的优势正在被"通用 Agent"稀释，而搜索/知识图谱这类"数据护城河"的先发优势反而被强化——这与 2010 年"移动互联网颠覆 PC"的叙事完全反向。历史不重复，但会押韵——只是这次押的是反韵。

📝 转录文本

开场：市场的"金鱼记忆"

上一周大家还在担心美联储再次打开了加息周期，对于接下去美股的影响。经过周一的这个反弹之后，市场可能已经忘了。如果说金鱼的记忆是两至三秒的话，我个人认为美股市场里面的参与者的记忆只有一秒，比金鱼还短。大家是不是认同我的这个观察？在留言区里面告诉我。

所以今天这新内容的前半部分主要还是从一个心态上、从市场参与度这个角度去出发。经过周一半导体板块比较大幅度的反弹之后，我们应该怎么去对于自己的仓位进行这个控制？应该加仓、应该减仓，还是说应该继续持有？——第一部分。

那第二部分，之所以周一的市场出现了比较大幅度的反弹，是因为 Meta 下面的 AI agent MUSE，正好有一条和 MUSE 相关的新闻——是亚马逊把 MUSE 给禁掉了，不让 MUSE 使用亚马逊的这个服务。背后到底发生了什么？对于这两家公司来说到底意味着什么？当我们进入智能体购物的这个时代，对于像亚马逊这类的电商公司意味着什么？

欢迎大家来到一个不单只聊新闻的专业美国频道，我是市场分析师小陶。那今天我就来回答前面的这两个问题：现在我们到底是应该怎么去做，加仓、减仓还是继续持有？在智能体购物的这个时代，对于亚马逊这类的公司意味着什么？好吗？那在开始之前，大家记得留言、点赞加转发，让更多的人可以看到我们这么专业的频道。大家说是不是。

一、周一市场回顾

先快速地回顾一下资产价格的走势。周一的市场美债收入这块波动并不大，但是10年期美债收入如预期地出现了下降，TOT 出现0.7的这个反弹。标普上涨的幅度不大，1.5%；纳指收盘应该是破了历史上的一个新高，收盘应该是收盘价格应该是破了历史上的一个新高，上涨2.3%。

那主要的这个纳指的涨幅全部——多数是来自于芯片板块的反弹，上涨4.9%；前七大科技股的反弹，上涨3.4%。如果手里没有芯片、没有大科技的话，你看一下标普的等权指数，周一只上涨了0.2%。

所以整个周一的市场，稍后有一张参与图可参——参与市场的一个参与率和大家分享。其实周一的市场的参与度并不是那么的高，没有指数所反映出来的那么的乐观。

那那随着前七大科技股的这个反弹之后，我们看一下 YTD——最后这一列这边——YTD 前七大科技股现在回报来到了11.1%，正式超过了 RSP。我记得在——对吧，也就是在7月初的时候，当时前七大科技股的一个涨幅 YTD 是负的2%，当时大家对于大科技非常的悲观。

那到现在为止，还还是首先先恭喜大家能够坚持下来。今天在我的 X 上面，有一位观众和我留言，自己的账户破了一个新高，然后非常感谢我怎么样。我说我说不用感谢我，为什么？我油管还是这么去做，X 还是这么去写，直播还是这么去做。我同样的一个表达，不同的人接收到的信息是不一样的，就非——哎就非常的奇怪。那所以大家账户能够做到哪里，完全是取决于大家自己对于风险的这个把控、对于仓位的这个把控。我就是一个市场分析师，那么尽量能够带给大家不同的视角，尽量能够能够给大家带来一个比较明确的一个前瞻性的视角。我不一定对，那么但是我一定会把我内心最真实的这个看法和大家分享。

二、硬件与软件板块的同步上涨

那我们还是回到市场这边。所以周一整个市场板块其实还是有分歧的：上涨比较多的芯片板块，然后前七大科技股。IGV 在周一上涨了2.7%。我在昨天的视频里面和大家分享了，我期待下半年我们应该能够看到硬件和软件板块同时上涨。结果市场非常的给面子的，在周一我们看到了 IGV 上涨了2.7%，芯片板块上涨了4.9。我们是在今年的上半年，包括今年前八个半月，我们很少会看到这样的一个走势。好吧，所以整个周一的市场其实反弹的幅度非常的好。

那黄金是出现了小幅的下跌。我看了一下，周一市场真实的美债十年期真实美债收率是出现上涨，那比特币出现了反弹，黄金是出现了小幅的下跌。那我并没有那么的担心。我的期待是，如果真实收益率、10年期美债收入这块持续下降的话，黄金应该还会继续往上走。

三、市场参与度分析

前面我讲到了市场参与度。我们看一下纳指3391只个股里边，在周一是1568只个股出现了上涨，1300只个股出现了下跌。所以上涨的幅度差不多就是在60%。通常来说，如果标普上涨1.5%、上涨2%左右的这种涨幅，其实市场参与度是比较高的，而其实我们在周一并没有看到非常高的参与度。

罗素两千也是一样：将近2000只个股，1084场上上出现了上升，829是出现了下跌，那上涨的幅度比例差不多也是在60%左右。标普也是一样：503只个股，291只个股出现了上涨，60%左右。

啊，所以整个市场上涨的幅度非常的高，但参与度其实没有那么的高，可以更高。那那主要上涨这个幅度是来自于半导体板块的大幅度反弹5%和前七大科技股的这个反弹。

周一收盘之后，我们来看一下市场参与度。20均线和50均线分别在32%和35%，处在一个中性偏悲观的位置，应该说处在一个悲观的位置，还没有到非常的悲观——我说30以下就是到非常的悲观了。罗素2000，29%和32%，就是正好在一个悲观的位置。标普500经过周一的反弹之后，20日均线的参与度仍然只在25%，仍然是在一个悲观的位置。

所以即使经过了周一的反弹之后，整个市场的参与度仍然是悲观的。你去看 CN 的恐慌贪婪指数，现在也是在一个恐慌的阶段，34。你去看 CN 恐慌贪婪指数里面的强度和广度都是在极度悲观。

四、加仓、减仓还是持有？

所以从这些参与度这个角度去出发，包括从现在市场——我没去更新估值，因为估值没有什么和更好更新的，你半导体板块上涨5%，估值无非就是从18倍，现在估值18倍啊，上涨5%，那就估值来到19倍。18倍是非常低的一个位置，那19倍还是在一个相对比较低的一个位置，所以并没有出——并不会出现非常大的一些改变，估值不会出现非常大的一些改变。那参与度还是在一个接近悲观的一个位置。

所以在这种情况下，我不知道为什么会有任何的理由去进行减仓。当然如果你从技术面角度，那是其他的一些判断标准。啊，但是如果大家比较认同我的这套系统，或者说我和大家分享的这些指标给大家是做一个参考的话，那从市场参与度这个角度去看，现在不可能去建仓（减仓）。

五、个股心态：为什么 AVGO 不涨？

那另外一个就是心态上的问题。在昨天视频下面有人问我，让我聊一下 AVGO。其实有啥好聊的，就是无非就是一天，到周一一天半导体板块上涨的幅度比较的大，然后 AVGO 就并没有跟涨。

当我们在投资个股的时候，我们必须要接受有一段时间，甚至比较长的这段时间，你手里所持有的这个标的本身没有这一个板块涨得要好。比如说我自己手里所持有的 Adobe，从 Adobe 我买到现在为止，可能就上涨了10%，但是 IGV 板块从最低点上涨的幅度已经很高了。包括软件板块里边的 Atlassian（对吧，Team），或者说你去看 CRM，它反弹的幅度、低点反弹的幅度都已经很高了。

那你说我拿着手里拿着 Adobe，是不是应该感觉到难受呢？我并不会感觉到难受。你只能以后告诫自己说 OK，以后也许在选标的上能够选到更好，能够尽量选到一个市场——呃，反弹比较好、或者市场比较喜欢的这些标题。这是没有办法。我投资个股，这是我们必须要接受的。

啊，所以怎么去分散这一个风险？我怎么去尽量去减少这个风险或者规避这个风险呢？那这个风险本身没办法规避，你只能去减、降低这个风险，就是通过仓位的这个配比。那尽量你手里持有最大比例的这些仓位，最大比例这些仓位本身是你信仰最高的，就是即使它在市场走得非常好的情况下，它如果不涨或者在横盘，你也能坚持得住。

所以并不是指数本身半导体上涨了5%，然后你手里所持有的半导体个股涨幅没有高过5%，然后你就认为这个标的本身基本面出了问题。那我们得反过头去看为什么周一像英伟达、像 ARM、那么像 AMD 出现了比较大幅度的一个涨幅，就市场的故事线是什么？是因为 Meta 的这个缪斯 agent，是因为它那个 AI agent。那市场在聊、是在交易这个故事线什么？CPU 对吧，那 CPU 只是半导体板块和硬件板块里面的一环。那么当市场在交易 A6的时候呢，可能就会牵扯到 AVGO 这一块；当市场在交易 CPU 的时候呢，可能就会牵扯到像英特尔啊、AMD 啊、ARM 这一类的标的身上。

那在我们布局个别标的的时候，我们一定要意识到，对吧，我们不可能我们手里所持有的这些——这个标的、这个公司本身永远是在一个热点上面，这不可能的。因为但是随着它——我们得相信长期来说，随着它基本面在慢慢变好，它的基本面一定会以财报的方式或者会以新闻的方式进入到大家的一个视野里边。

啊，所以不应该有这种焦躁的一个心理。如果有的话，那应该思考一下持有个股本身是不是适合我们，或者说这只个股身上的一个仓位是不是过大。因为本身来说市场在涨，然后你自己的仓位不涨，你会产生焦虑，可能是你的仓位过大了，那就是你的仓位本身和你对这一个标的的一个信仰、一个 conviction 是完全不匹配的。但你不应该放太多的仓位在这个标的身上。

六、Meta MUSE 与亚马逊：一场智能体大战

然后我们来聊一下下半部分，我们聊一下 Meta 下面的一个缪斯 AI Agent、AI Agent 和亚马逊之间的这个关系。

那今天有一条新闻是：亚马逊在其零售网站上屏蔽了 Meta 的一个缪斯 AI 代理。亚马逊禁止其他公司部署自动化工具在其网站上进行购物。今天是 Meta 下面的缪斯，明天可以是另外一家 Agent。购物者会看到弹出窗口称其使用违反了亚马逊的使用条款。

那么我们来讨论一下为什么亚马逊要去阻止 MUSE。

角度一：广告费用

首先第一个角度就是广告费用。因为亚马逊现在在电商这一块，它有很大一部分的收入是来自于广告费用。那这一部分广告费用，如果是 AI agent 去进行访问的话，广告费用这一块就会受到影响。因为人是会去看广告的，但是 agent 不会去看广告。呃，所以这是其中的一大部分的一个原因。

角度二：平台内容本身就是价值

第二部分的一个原因就是自己平台上的这个内容其实是价值。可能我们现在还难以去做出这样的一个理解，为什么？是因为我们现在每个人，你自己手——如果手动去上网、去上亚马逊的这个网站的话，我们完全可以看到亚马逊的网站上有哪些 promotion、然后有哪些商品，免费的。就你去浏览他们那个网站就是免费的。

但是未来如果 agent 要去浏览他们的这个网站的话，那这个网站这个平台上的一个内容就是有价值的。那么因为 agent 他可能不单浏览了亚马逊网站上的内容，他也可能去沃尔玛上浏览了沃尔玛网站上的这个内容，他可能去搜遍了整个——包括他可能还去了 Shopify。那这三家公司一对比下来之后，针对客户、针对用户的这个需求，这一个 agent、这一个购物的一个 AI agent 本身可能就知道到底最终应该挑选哪个商品。

在整个这一套思考的一个过程里面，亚马逊提供了什么？好像最后如果最后没有选选亚马逊的话，那亚马逊其实没有任何的一个收获。亚马逊平台上的这些内容本身其实是有价值的。你把它想象成 Reddit 就没有那么的抽象。

角度三：Meta vs 亚马逊，谁更有话语权？

那第二个问题就是也是市场讨论度非常高的：那究竟是 Meta 还是亚马逊会更有话语权？因为我今天看到在老外社区里面有很多的老外都在说，亚马逊选择把 MUSE 给办掉是一个非常错误的一个决定。因为同时 Shopee 宣布和 Meta 之间合作。那虽然 Shopee 也是电商，但是很多人误以为——我我不认为这两者之间有非常大的一些关系。就是市场理解的就是 OK，Shopify 和 MUSE、和 Meta 之间这个合作，然后亚马逊选择不和 Meta 之间这个合作，所以 Shopify 是走在了 AI 支付的一个前端。

我不认为可以把 Shopify 和亚马逊之间放在一起去做一个对比。为什么？因为这两家公司亚马逊那个户审核在哪？亚马逊的户审核是在它的一个 fulfillment center，是在它整套的一个物流系统。而原来 Shopify 是想去做线下的，它是想去布局的自己一个仓库，最后他们失败了，因为这是一个重资产的一个行业。

那亚马逊在电商它有——到了今天基本上在全世界的这个范围之内，唯一有可能可以挑战亚马逊电商这一块的谁？沃尔玛。啊，但是沃尔玛现在自己本身也在开发这个广告业务。

所以市场的一个担心是亚马逊的这个选择是错误的，因为他们今天如果不选择和 Meta 之间合作的话，那明天沃尔玛就会和 Meta 之间合作。但是你会发现沃尔玛如果和 Meta 之间合作的话，沃尔玛这一部分的广告业务是不是也会受到 Meta 的这个影响？所以市场的一个假设是这一个话语权更多的是在 Meta 这边。

但是我可能会有一些不同的看法。因为电商本身你是没办法破坏的，线下的这个电商——我说电商不但是只是一个网店而已，它最后它背后有一个存储、有压货，然后有整个物流系统，包括送货等等。这不是一般的互联网公司是可以进来的，那它背后有非常深的这个护城河在那边。

所以我认为反而亚马逊是有这个话语权在那边的，包括沃尔玛也是一样的。我认为沃尔玛和亚马逊两者是有非常大的一个话语权在那边。因为未来的 agent 绝对不不会只有 MUSE 这一家。未来谷歌也会有自己的这个 agent，然后苹果也会有自己这个 agent。那你今天 Meta 你可以选择不和亚马逊之间合作，你可以和它降下去，你可以选择用 Shopify，啊，但是如果明天苹果或者谷歌他们选择和亚马逊之间进行这个合作，而你作为这个 agent、你的这个 agent 却没有办法在亚马逊上去进行购物的话，那你的 agent 所能够执行的这一个使用场景是不如其他 agent 的。那这一点对于你的用户来说——你的，你觉得你的用——因为最终是会抢用户的。那 Meta 有 Meta 的这个生态，然后谷歌有谷歌的生态，苹果有苹果的生态。

所以关于第二个问题，暂时来说，我认为这——我相信这两者之间最后是会有一个 settlement，但是中间的这个利益的一个牵涉应该会需要一些协议在中间。

七、Agent to Agent：未来的购物场景

然后第三点就是未来的这个发展。亚马逊的这个广告业务所面临的风险点是类似于就市场现在的一个定价，有点可能类似于当时两年多前吧，市场对于谷歌在广告业务这一块可能会受到破坏的一个担心。

那我个人认为亚马逊是要推出自己的这个购物 Agent，那不再是站内——现现在亚马逊其实有一个 A Agent 在那边，但是这个 Agent 更多的是站内的这个智能搜索。但是未来亚马逊旗下的这个 Agent，我认为要对接其他的一些智能体，实现 Agent to Agent，就是智能体和智能体之间的这个沟通。

因为我认为未来这种场景就是——我以前其实我以前就聊过这样的一个场景：每一个人都会有属于自己的这个个人智能体，然后个人的智能体，你会根据不同的场景去会——智能体本身去会和另一个场景里面的专业智能体进行交流。那在网购这一块，亚马逊就会有自己的这个专业的网购智能体。

也就是我认为未来的这条路径应该是：我们个人有一个需求，和我们个人智能体进行交流，比如说 MUSE。那 MUSE 会去亚马逊的这个网站上，和亚马逊的这个网购智能体进行交流；同时它有可能再会发一个 request 请求，和沃尔玛的这个网购智能体去进行交流。然后比如说他问了两个智能体——问了亚马逊和问了沃尔玛，那沃尔玛和亚马逊分别会给我——MUSE 这个智能体会给一个答案，最后 MUSE 去进行、根据我的这个需求，去在这两家公司之间或者这两个智能体之间去进行选择。

但是你每去提交一个请求，这个请求本身是应该要付费的。

当然，Agent to Agent 的这种场景，我认为还是有一段距离的，而现在市场就已经做了这个线性外推了。我当然了，今天就周一的这个市场，亚马逊并没有出现下跌，上涨的幅度还是 OK 的，和市场的一个涨幅几乎是类似的，我还是比较意外的。就单纯根据市场的一些参与者对于亚马逊的这个担心来说，我有点意外亚马逊在周一其实并没有出现下跌。

啊，所以这是我自己对于这件事情的一些看法。

八、AI Agent 布局与仓位调整

那最后一点，这件事——这个问题本身我还没有思考完全清楚。是我今天在思考的是 A 啦，未来在 AI agent 这一块的一个布局。

那我在上周五和大家分享过、昨天视频和大家分享过，在上周五的时候，我是把苹果卖了，然后把苹果的仓位转了很大一部分转到谷歌上面，然后还加了一些谷歌的这个仓位。所以现在我自己个人在 AI Agent 这一块的布局——那除了英特尔不算，英特尔是 CPU 这一块——在 AI Agent 这一块的布局主要是两家公司：一家是谷歌，一家是高通。

我其实我在几个月之前我就有聊过，我认为未来 AI Agent 这一块的落地可能在四家公司身上，对吧：谷歌、苹果和高通，然后还有一个是 Meta。这四家公司我认为都是有机会的。因为一开始我是说了三家公司，然后高通是后面该加进去的。

那现在呢，苹——Meta 我现在自己手里是没有的，然后苹果我认为现在是比较贵的，那剩下的这两家公司我可能会进行加仓。那这个仓位来自于哪，我还没有完全思考好。那这个仓位有可能会来自于亚马逊。

好吗？所以等我思考完之后，我会做一期视频，然后我来和大家解释一下接下去一些布局的仓位变动。不会太大，可能就是在3~4个点左右的一个变动。

结尾：赞助商与结语

最后是我们今天的活动来自于 Vivo 微牛证券。那微牛证券在美国的体量是非常的大，现在有一个我们这个频道的独家福利：美国市场这边通过开户且入境，只需要入境100美金啊，就可以获得12股免费股票的这个抽取。如果去官网上的话，是没有12股的。总共的这个金额从36美金最高可以高达3600美金，然后在这个基础上还可以获得一个月威牛 Premium 的订阅。加拿大市场这边通过开户且入金，最高可以获得价值250加币的这个返现。大家如果感兴趣的话，可以在置顶的留言里边找到开户的链接。

那今天这期内容就到这边，下期见。

## 一、"金鱼记忆"背后的结构性脆弱：参与度悖论
小陶开篇那句"美股参与者的记忆只有一秒，比金鱼还短"其实揭示了一个远比情绪面更深的问题——**指数创新高与市场参与度悖离**。周一纳指破历史新高，但参与度只有60%，20日均线的参与度仍停留在25–35%的悲观区。他从这个数据得出"不该减仓"的结论是对的，但**理由可能颠倒了**：低参与度+指数新高恰恰是典型的"帕累托陷阱"——极少数个股承担了整个指数的上涨。这从系统论看不是"底部信号"，而是"结构性脆弱"信号。真正让市场在心态上像金鱼的原因，不是散户健忘，而是**信息半衰期的坍缩**——算法交易+短周期资金把每一条消息的"衰减常数"压到了以秒计。这也解释了为什么他会说"同样的表达，不同的人接收到的信息不一样"——在信息半衰期极短的环境里，注意力本身就是最稀缺的资源。
## 二、Amazon vs Meta：一场"注意力护城河"与"履约护城河"的时代对撞
这场 MUSE 被封的争执，表面是电商与社交平台的话语权之争，本质是**两种护城河形态的正面对撞**：Meta 代表的是**无摩擦的注意力流量**（无重资产、无库存、无物流），
