item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一位无神论者的护身符：Constâncio 悖论

这段访谈最耐人寻味的时刻，不在他反复宣称的"黄金是神话"，而是他不经意的一句自白——葡萄牙央行的黄金储备排名全球第十二。一位刚刚论证黄金"非理性、迷信、无收益"的前央行行长，坐镇于一个人均持金量惊人的国家。这就像一位无神论哲学家，抽屉里始终放着一枚圣物。他把这称为"集体非理性向个体理性的转化"，但这个用词本身就是一次无意识的降维——他用"非理性"命名了一种他所在体制无法建模的价值维度。

他的论证里藏着黄金最好的辩护词

Constâncio 定义资产价值为"未来现金流的贴现"，因此黄金"没有收益流 = 投机品"。但他随后自己拆解了这个定义：谈到"安全资产"时，他承认——没有任何资产是绝对安全的，安全性来自"低通胀""法治""对财产权的保护""对机构可信度的信任"。也就是说，他推崇的"安全"完全寄生于制度信任。而黄金的全部特征恰恰是：它是唯一一种"制度信任崩塌时依然工作"的资产。当他说新兴市场买金是因为"美元资产会被冻结制裁"时，他等于承认了：黄金正在履行的，正是他框架里根本无法定价的功能——制度失灵时的救生舱期权。跨领域看，这与信息论中的"香农熵"异曲同工：黄金的价值不在于它产生什么，而在于它不会衰减为什么。它是货币系统中的"暗物质"——不发光，但决定引力。

央行的隐性宗教战争

Constâncio 反复使用"magic""mythology""myth""black magic"这些词，人类学味道极重。但真正引人深思的是：他把 fiat 货币视为科学，把黄金视为神话——而这两者其实是两套并存的信仰系统，只是布道者不同。法币系统由央行祭司主持（他曾经就是），依靠仪式（利率决议）、经文（Taylor 规则）和圣殿（法兰克福）；黄金系统则更古老、更去中心化、无需教士。中央银行家们对黄金的鄙夷，与其说是经济学判断，不如说是祭司阶层对旧神的驱魔。这也解释了一个隐藏的模式：他对法国财政风险的语气是"可控、有工具"，对黄金上涨的语气却是"灾难、绝对不能发生"。前者威胁的是数字，后者威胁的是叙事的垄断权。他愿意面对可量化风险，却抗拒面对本体论风险——这不是经济学分歧，是神学冲突。

一个未被追问的裂缝

他说美元的主导地位"根深蒂固、无可替代"，同一段又承认"特朗普政策正在侵蚀美元根基"、"美元贬值可期"、"美国财政赤字 6.5% 不可持续"。这两句话不能同时为真而不产生代价。他解决这个张力的方式是把时间尺度拉长——"侵蚀会发生，但要几十年"。而黄金市场的定价，恰恰是把这几十年的尾部风险贴现到今天。所以当他问"你怎么解释金价新高"，答案其实就藏在他自己的分析里：市场不是在赌黄金变成锚，而是在为他描述的那个"缓慢侵蚀"过程购买保险。他看到了病灶，却否认了处方——这在临床心理学里叫做"知性防御"（intellectualization）：用精确的分析回避一个情感上无法接受的结论。

📝 转录文本

Cold Open — The Verdict

"No, there is no magic in gold. I mean, it's really just because people believe in magic. It's a myth."

— Do you see a revival of gold as an anchor?

"No, not at all. It would be a disaster if that would happen. It won't happen."

"The presence of more gold and less dollars in the reserves of those central banks has no consequences for the international monetary system. It's there because people have all these magic ideas about gold — is mythology, is whatever you can call it — is irrational."

— Well, what is rational then?

"If everyone or most people are irrational, then it is rational that I also have that, because it's guaranteed that the value will go up."

Introduction

Interviewer: Well, it's an absolute pleasure to be speaking with Vítor Constâncio. You've been Governor of the Banco de Portugal — if I pronounced it correctly — from 2000 until 2010. And then afterwards, you've been Vice President of the European Central Bank from 2011 until 2018.

Constâncio: Okay, I started in 2010, but…

Interviewer: 2010, exactly.

Constâncio: Yes.

Interviewer: So we're here at the event hosted by [the organizer], entitled The G-Economic Landscape. For the viewers, it's also a great opportunity to speak with someone who — I don't think there are many central bankers within the European Central Bank, or perhaps globally, who have gathered as much experience as yourself. So I'm curious to get your take on many of the topics we might touch on today.

Lessons from the Post-2008 Era at the ECB

Interviewer: In your view, how has the post-global-financial-crisis era reshaped the balance between monetary stability and financial risk in the Eurozone? What lessons do you draw looking back at your tenure at the ECB?

Constâncio: At the ECB, it was a period of crisis to start with, and it was difficult to stabilize. So we had to embark on unconventional monetary policies, as we know, and it was necessary and it was done. Then finally we could stabilize the situation, despite the — minor in terms of significance — crisis in 2015 around Greece, which was a very localized problem, but which by itself created a sort of existential crisis. Whereas the crisis after 2008, and the next few years after that, was broader and more, say, existential.

Then we stabilized the situation, and I think that the euro proved — and Europe proved — that it could be resilient enough. Many new institutions had to be created, the ESM and so on, in order to stabilize the situation. Meaning that a monetary union among such heterogeneous countries would require a mechanism to attend to possible temporary shocks of liquidity stress in particular countries, and that mechanism was not there when the euro was conceived.

So lots of reforms had to be introduced, and not just by the ECB. Of course, we provided the liquidity assistance and the decisions to sustain the financial system and avoid a collapse of the European banks, which was indeed avoided.

Fiscal Heterogeneity and the France Question

Interviewer: If you look at the design of the euro — there's much criticism, and it was also a topic brought up today — that in the monetary union, the way debt is treated among countries can differ. The Nordic countries have a much more pragmatic approach than others. There might be differences that during the Greek crisis were even more exacerbated. How do you see that evolving into the future, looking also at France recently being in distress — even rumors of calling for IMF bailout help? How do you see this developing?

Constâncio: Well, the situation is different in many ways. In the first place, there are instruments within the monetary union. The ESM is there, prepared for assistance if need be. The ECB has two programs — the OMT, which is also associated with the ESM, the European Stabilization Mechanism, and there is also the TPI, a possible intervention in the sovereign debt market, provided the country is respecting the Stability Pact — which is not the case of France right now. So the TPI would not be appropriate.

Either the OMT or the ESM mechanism would involve an adjustment program that France would have to negotiate, accept, and implement to receive that assistance — which, of course, won't be easy for a country like France to recognize, if it comes to that. Because it's not there yet. It's a possibility, in view of what happened in the past to other countries, so there is no justification right now. But if the situation would worsen, then those mechanisms are there and could be used by France to stabilize the situation. That can be done within the euro — it's nothing that puts into jeopardy or difficulty the euro itself.

The Original Design Flaws of the Euro

Interviewer: Looking at the viability of the design of the euro, do you see anything that could be the biggest challenge on its design in terms of a monetary union going forward?

Constâncio: The one that was revealed by several episodes of crisis of different intensity was precisely the fact that the initial design did not contemplate that the financial integration of monetary and financial markets would be so quick and complete. Because during the initial stages, the debt of the different member countries was traded in the markets as if there was equal risk — which was not adequate. But that sort of integration then, when shocks appeared, precisely connected with the big financial crisis — suddenly that smooth functioning was totally changed, and there were no mechanisms foreseen to deal with such a liquidity crisis. They had to be created under pressure, and we had to embark on extraordinary monetary policy. So that was a mistake of the initial design: it didn't count with that financial integration going so far as, in the end, it went.

The other thing is that nothing was foreseen in terms of a fiscal tool that could help in moments of recession to the whole area, to complement monetary policy. Because one of the lessons of that long period was that monetary policy can be very asymmetric. It is efficient to control inflation — because it's just restricting, increasing interest rates and restricting the economy. But if it is a recessionary shock, it's not so simple. We can, and we did, lower the interest rates, but that was not enough to convince private agents to invest more. Monetary policy is asymmetric in its effects, and in periods of recession, the help of fiscal policy becomes evident. Again, it was not there — that tool — and it's still not there, by the way. Other tools were created in terms of loans to countries to assist them in such situations, but this fiscal tool is also, I think, a shortcoming of the initial design of the euro.

The Euro's Global Role — Clarifying the Record

Interviewer: You've actually talked about this right before this interview — the role of the euro in the global markets and the global monetary order. You've said something like: the euro shouldn't be a global reserve. Am I correct?

Constâncio: Well, I will correct you just to be precise, but okay.

Interviewer: It shouldn't be global, in order to make it more competitive? Or not?

Constâncio: No, no, no. That's not exactly what I said. The point is the following. The euro became the second currency in the world economy. In broad figures, in terms of the international role of currencies, we have now the dollar at a general index of usage as the international currency of 66%; the euro is at 24%; the Chinese currency is at 3%; the Japanese yen is at 4%. So all the rest is very, very small. The euro is a regional currency of importance. It already is — around 60% of the trade that the euro area does with neighboring countries is done in euros, which reveals the significance of the euro, even cross-border with the neighboring countries. And that's okay — that situation was to be expected, and it is important that that number, a little higher than 20%, has been stable over the years. So it's a stable situation.

Then, some Europeans think that the euro area should aim at increasing the euro's role in the international monetary system, approaching more and more the dollar. What I said is: in order to increase our economic performance of the euro area, in order to increase our productivity — which is the basis of the level of living that we can offer European citizens — to do that, we don't need the euro to become more important in the global monetary system. It's not necessary. It's not the priority.

It may happen that it will increase. It will depend also on what will be the policies of the US. Right now the dollar is depreciating, there are doubts internationally in many countries about the reliability of US policies, and even US institutions — if the government can really control the central bank, the Fed. That, of course, would undermine the fundamentals that have made the dollar the dominant currency in the world.

That situation cannot change too much, because there is no substitute. The dollar is entrenched over decades in all the international markets and payments — in payments, in the issuance of international debt (mostly done in dollars), the transactions in the foreign exchange market (mostly done via the dollar). That cannot be dismantled or replaced readily, and there is no real alternative.

What the Euro Is Missing to Rival the Dollar

Because the euro is missing at least two ingredients to become much more important in its international role.

One is: it must have an integration of the European bond markets, with a European safe asset that would be broad enough — sizable enough — so that the market would be liquid and deep, so that international foreign investors could come in, buy those instruments, and then get out because the market would be deep and liquid. Without that, no currency can become a global currency in a very significant way. And we don't have that. That is connected, of course, with more political integration — and we don't have political union in Europe. It's not envisaged that this is going to happen in the visible horizon. It may happen one day, but many things will have to happen for that to be reached. That's the first ingredient, which is not there.

The second one is that, as history proves, the country that becomes the issuer of the dominant international currency, or a currency with a big participation in the international monetary system, has to be a great power — including in military terms — has to project a notion of power, of credibility. It has to have institutions, it has to have the rule of law, so that foreign investors feel confident they can put their assets there, and that the rights will be protected by credible institutions. Those are conditions. Europe has that, and that's why the euro has expanded a little bit — but it is missing those two other ingredients, and they are not going to happen anytime soon.

What I was saying was: look, that is the reality, but in order for our economy to grow more, to improve our productivity, our technology and so on, we don't need the euro to be more important than what it is in the international arena. That objective should not be a priority. The priority is to improve our performance in terms of productivity, because that's the basis of the level of living.

Why "Competitiveness" Is the Wrong Frame

It's not competitiveness — because competitiveness among nations is totally different from competitiveness among firms. In firms, you have a market, and with your sales you compete with other firms to increase your share of the market. That's not what happens in international trade. The fact that other countries also perform better does not harm the possibility of our country also increasing its productivity. Having separate currencies means that competitiveness is smoothed out by movements in the exchange rate. So what matters is internal policies and the increase in real productivity in each country. Competitiveness is the wrong concept. But okay — governments and media like to see this as a race, as a competition. It's not like that that the whole thing works.

The OECD many years ago defined exactly what, economically, can count to assess a country being internationally competitive. The definition is the following: the economy is growing — which includes also productivity growing — in a context of openness to international trade and international capital flows. That's a condition. And at the same time, respecting broadly the macroeconomic equilibria — meaning the public deficits and public debt, and the current account. If a country is doing that under those conditions, it's because it is competitive.

We — the euro area — qualify, with some deviations, but we broadly qualify under this definition. We are growing (small, well, not very high), productivity is growing (again, very low), and our public finance situation on average and our current account has a surplus, and the budget deficits also have been reduced — much below, in both cases, than the US, for instance. So we can say that the European economy, the euro area economy, is competitive in this fundamental economic sense of the OECD definition.

The Euro's Share Doesn't Need to Grow — But…

Interviewer: So it doesn't necessarily need to increase its global share of reserves.

Constâncio: No, it doesn't need to increase. But it also cannot really decrease too much either. I was pointing out to you that since its creation in 1999 until now, the importance of the euro in the different international roles has been stable, around 20-odd percent, despite all the crises and stresses. Which is an important reminder that the monetary union has worked fundamentally, with some ups and downs — yes — but that were not reflected in the international usage of the euro.

Interviewer: But if we look overall — because you just mentioned that deficit spending is pretty much under control, but we've seen with France recently, and Italy, and other countries, that this risk kind of got back on track more or less compared to what it used to be. A lot of analyst projections see the euro faltering. What also came forward is the potential for a boost of investment in technological competitiveness.

Constâncio: Well, different things there. You are referring now basically to France, because the other countries don't have that sort of fiscal situation anymore, including Italy. Italy reduced a lot its budget deficit — it's now around 3%, if not a little bit lower. Greece, Spain, Portugal — everyone has lower than 3%. Portugal has even a positive balance, not a deficit, for some years now. So the adjustments that were made served as a lesson for many countries that went through the crisis many years ago.

France is a different situation, which got out of hand. In fact, because they do have a very, very high level of public expenditure in relation to GDP, and now they have deficits and they have political difficulties to really reduce them. So they are under pressure. That's true. It's a cause of concern. No doubt. But that does not put into question the euro itself. And the euro has not been affected in that international role. As I mentioned, it continues the same.

So we have to make the distinction between a particular country and a particular stress — which right now is France — and the overall picture.

Sovereign Debt Risk in Europe vs. Japanification

Interviewer: Overall, you don't see any potential of… because there's the US situation, Japan there for kind of giving us a glimpse of what the quote-unquote "Japanification"… you don't see any risks or any troubles when it comes to sovereign debt in Europe in general?

Constâncio: Well, I'm not saying that. Things can always move sometimes quickly, and the French situation is a cause of concern. So far, it has not had spillovers over other countries. So no contagion from France to Italy or Spain or whatever. No, that's not happening.

But the situation in France can go worse, because they do have a political impasse to have a government that can really address the situation. Yes, situation can worsen, contagion can occur, but it will never be the same as what happened in 2010, '11, '12, '13. Why? Because then there were no mechanisms of assistance, and markets put a lot of pressure, and there was a big disturbance — indeed, a sort of existential crisis of the euro. That will not happen this time. The instruments are there. They have to be used, if that is the case. Not yet necessary, but they are there if they will become necessary.

So yes, the situation can go worse, and stress can increase, and we may have even a global financial crisis, because the situation in the US has also its own problems. By the way, the deficits in the US are much higher than in Europe. In Europe overall, the euro area is slightly below 3%. The US is at 6.5% deficits that we can project for many years ahead. So they have also a debt that is now above 100%. And if it continues with deficits of 6%, by 2030, 2035, it will be very, very high. If nothing is done — and apparently no government in the US feels that they have to do something about the fiscal situation, because the dollar has this international dominance and they think that that will last forever and that they can finance their deficits easily.

So if that happens that way — but it's also a risk. And also they have the situation in the equity market, which is of course overstretched by all measures and indicators. We don't know what will happen in the near future if there is some sort of problem with the earnings of the big tech firms — perhaps they will not continue to grow the same amounts as they have been growing. All those things can happen. We are not totally protected from financial stresses that may happen.

Growth Outlook: Demographics, Productivity, and AI

Interviewer: How would you forecast the growth of the economy in Europe for the next decade?

Constâncio: Well, the decade I don't know, but I can tell you: the more recent forecast for growth this year is 1.2%; 2% for next year — 1.3. And also I can tell you that the measure of the maximum growth rate of potential output — potential, if the economy would operate at potential, meaning the maximum use of resources — the potential growth rate of the euro area long-term is 1.1–1.2%. Why? Because our population is decreasing — I mean, the working-age population is decreasing — and to offset that, productivity would have to increase much more, because the two things add up together to the growth rate of GDP.

So — can we increase productivity to offset that new demographic negative? Yeah, we should, and we must do it. And we need some change of policies to do that. Just to remind, also, the potential growth rate of the US is around 1.7–1.8%. So it's higher, but not dramatically higher than in Europe. The countries have gone back to a situation of so-called lower growth that has prevailed, because both economies are now mature — have progressed a lot.

We don't know — and no one knows — what will be exactly the effect of artificial intelligence on further growth. We know that it can increase productivity a lot. We don't have to be the ones that invent everything about AI. We have to be good enough to be good users of that. That would be enough. If we are very close to the technological frontier — which we have in Europe, all the conditions to be — that may indeed increase productivity a lot. It may create a problem of jobs, if that increase is too quick. But even the increase is enough. If it happens in a very significant and very quick way — no one knows.

There are economists that hope, there are economists that say "well, no, it's not like that overall, it will increase productivity in certain sectors but not overall in the economy to really run away again with growth rates of 3% in real terms or more." There is a debate, and no one knows. But it may happen — that this sort of supply shock, increasing productivity, may happen — and both a job problem and an income distribution problem will develop, if AI will have that huge effect that some experts predict.

Gold: "A Disaster If It Happened"

Interviewer: We've seen that central banks since 2008 have been net purchasers of gold, and the trend is going parabolic. We've seen all-time highs — the 36th all-time high, I think, this year of the price of gold. I want to know your perspective on how you see the role of gold in the monetary system as a whole. Do you see a revival of gold as an anchor?

Constâncio: No, not at all. It would be a disaster if that would happen. It won't happen. I tell you — in the first place, the European central banks are not doing that. It's mostly Asian central banks and other emerging countries that are increasing their gold reserves. So that's a point to be underlined.

And secondly, the presence of more gold and less dollars in the reserves of those central banks has no consequences for the international monetary system.

A History Lesson: How the Dollar Became Entrenched

Central bank reserves were important for the international monetary system during the initial stages of the Bretton Woods system after the Second World War, because international official liquidity was created by central banks. It was the Fed that was creating dollars, and no one else could do it. So there started to be a liquidity problem in the international monetary system — because of the so-called Triffin dilemma. In order to supply more dollars, the US would have to have higher current account deficits to issue more dollars, and that in itself would create suspicions about the dollar. So it was not sustainable.

But the solution came — and the solution came that it was the private sector that started to create international liquidity. The Eurodollar system started basically — well, it started in 1958 — then it was very small, then it developed. It's the system of deposits denominated in dollars outside the US. Now, not only in dollars, in other currencies, but outside the countries of issuance. That Eurodollar system expanded very quickly, because there is a multiplier: dollars started to be deposited in European banks in Europe for regulatory reasons and other reasons; and then banks would have dollars here in Europe, started to make loans; and like in any banking system, when the banks are doing that, it's a fractional reserve system. So by granting more credits, they create deposits. There is a multiplier — and so the Eurodollar market expanded and became the core of the international private-liquidity system, with all the functions of providing liquidity, giving loans, and then came the derivatives. All that expanded to huge amounts, and most of it is in dollars. Also, the network of banks that are connected and do transactions among them operate mostly in dollars.

So the dollar is entrenched in this private-sector system in a way that is difficult to substitute. If it happens one day, there will be some erosion, but it will take a long time. It cannot be done just like that.

Which means, going to the initial question: the amount of gold or dollars in the reserves of central banks does not matter for this mechanism. This mechanism is there. It expands according to the needs, because giving more credit in dollars outside the US creates deposits in dollars, and so on. From time to time, the Fed has to give some support to the market.

The market initially, for many years, was just a correspondent market — meaning that the banks had lines of credit among themselves purely on trust. Then SWIFT came with the messaging system. But then, after in particular the financial crisis, trust disappeared among banks, and then repos — secured lending among banks — became the crucial safety net of the international system. And repos are mostly overnight, so they are risky, because they just last 24 hours. That's a big problem from time to time. Repos are done mostly on Treasuries — US debt. Again, it's the dollar and US securities that are the basis of the international system.

So it's nothing to do with the reserves of central banks. When we say "well, the dollar is the reserve currency" — well, it's not that that is important. What is important is all these broad markets. It's the fact that the dollar is the invoice currency of almost two-thirds of world trade; that it's also the same percentage for the issuers of international debt (it's in dollars); that the transactions in the foreign exchange market, 88% are in dollars. It's all this that makes the international system, and no connection with reserves.

The international role of a currency has no really significant linkage with the composition of reserves of central banks anymore. It was important at the beginning, when the liquidity was only official liquidity. That has changed completely since the '60s, the '70s. By the beginning of the 2000s, the amount of dollars in banks outside the US was bigger than the total deposits in the US itself. It's not anymore like that, but just to give you an example of the expansion of this international monetary system and the role of the dollar there.

Why Emerging Central Banks Are Actually Buying Gold

So gold has no role. What is happening — why are these emerging countries and Asian central banks buying more gold?

Well, there is a certain element of balance sheet protection, because the dollar is depreciating and there is indeed the risk that the dollar will continue to depreciate for quite a while. So to have only dollars, or lots of dollars, in the balance sheet means that you may — and will — incur losses. So they are buying gold. That's one reason.

But then there are political objectives, of two types. One is that emerging countries — and many of those countries have the experience that their assets in dollars were seized, were object of sanctions and were frozen. And with gold, it's more difficult to do that. It depends where you have the gold, but it's more difficult to happen. So to have more gold, for types of countries that can be subject to sanctions, there is a reason to buy more gold.

The second political reason is: they do that to undermine the dollar and try to create alternatives in the monetary system. It won't succeed. And if you wish, I can [explain why].

Why the Renminbi Won't Replace the Dollar (Anytime Soon)

Interviewer: Yeah, I sensed that.

Constâncio: Well, for the following reasons. Take China — which would be the prime candidate to develop a currency with an international role. It's around 3% now. For a currency to become an important currency in international payments, loans, credit, securities and so on, it has to have a list of conditions.

Rule of law. The first list of conditions includes rule of law — and foreigners trust completely the judicial system and the legal system to protect their rights when they have their assets there. China is not seen by foreign investors the same way that Europe or the US is seen. The US is undermining their position, but not yet — I mean, not comparable. But yes, if Mr. Trump's policies will continue for long in the same direction, well, it can do a job of undermining the credibility of US institutions for this purpose. But we…

Interviewer: …started before Trump.

Constâncio: It started before Trump. Well, a bit — but okay, now it has really exploded. So that is still not there.

Capital controls. Then China has capital controls. You put money in, but you don't know — in the first place, you don't know if you enter, and especially, that you can withdraw it at will without any bureaucratic complications. So that's a very important aspect of the thing.

Size, stability, and deep markets. The country has to be big, of course. The country has to ensure low inflation stability as much as possible — because if people want to hold that currency, they would prefer that. Then the country also has to ensure that it has domestic deep, liquid financial markets. Because if they are not big — the financial markets, both equities and bonds — then whenever a sizable foreign investor goes in, it affects the prices, or the other way around. So it is necessary that those markets are deep, sizable, liquid enough for investors to come in and out without affecting too much the prices. China has not that.

Geopolitical projection. Then, a country to have the currency in that very important role has to be a geopolitical power. It has to project power, which includes military power — which is one of the missing things for the euro that I mentioned before, but China has it. But doesn't have the other things.

Regional acceptance. Then, for the other countries of the same group to accept the renminbi as the international currency, they have to give up their own goals. India also would like the rupee to have a broader and bigger international role. So it's a competitor. It's not a country willing to say "well, yes, let's have the renminbi just like that." No.

Then to create a sufficient commonality of use of a currency in one area, we also have to trust enough that you can get out and in in their financial system — because not all the countries have the same level of external deficits or surplus, and either they trust enough to accept a currency that is international for the settlement… if they are not trusting enough, and they may not trust yet the renminbi and China to have that — it means that if they have unbalanced trade and financial relationships with China, they don't want to be paid in yuan or renminbi. For that to change, it will take a lot of time.

CIPS vs. SWIFT. So the fact that China is also expanding the messaging among banks, which is called CIPS — the equivalent of the SWIFT — was built by China and connects already banks in certain parts of the world. But there is no common currency that is widely accepted in that system.

Interviewer: You mentioned CIPS?

Constâncio: CIPS. Yes. Right.

Constâncio: Just to say that it will take a long time, and many changes, for China to be able to bring the role of the renminbi from 3% to 30% or more. So it may happen gradually. It depends on a lot of trust with other countries that also have aspirations.

If the US continues to misbehave internationally and be hostile with everyone, yeah, that will speed up that process of erosion of the dollar. It will take a long time, because as I explained, the dollar is entrenched so much that it's difficult to just say "now we take the dollar and we get renminbi." And the euro is also not a full candidate.

Why We're Not Going Back to a Gold Standard

Interviewer: So if I try to summarize, as you clearly [said]…

Constâncio: So the price of gold is going up for this political reason, and also because of the recent depreciation of the dollar. But the fact that it is increasing in the central banks of many countries does not mean that we'll have a monetary role again. We are not going back to a sort of gold-standard regime of international payments — because that would be a total disaster for the world economy.

Because as economies grow and trade more in absolute terms, even if the rate of growth decelerates — trade more in absolute terms — we need money to expand. A system based on gold has not the flexibility of money creation that would accompany the growth of the economies and trade. And we saw in the 19th century, and then again just before the big crisis of 1929–1930, that the gold standard created a depressionist situation in the world economy — and also in the UK, in the US — and indeed they had to abandon the link with gold: the UK in '31, and then later on President Roosevelt had to do the same with the dollar. So gold lost gradually any role in the monetary system, and we are not going back to that.

People may invest in gold instead of other things because they sense that they will have capital gains. So it's a profit motive.

Gold as a Speculative Asset — And the "Irrational Rationality"

Well, the price of gold is outside of economics — because economics and finance say, fundamentally, that the value of an asset is just the discounted present value of the stream of income that the asset generates over time. That's the fundamental definition of the price, of the value of an asset. Difficult to calculate, because it implies the future, the long term, and the use of the interest rate to calculate the present value.

The problem is that gold — and even less so bitcoin — does not generate an income stream to discount. It is a speculative asset.

Interviewer: Does it need to?

Constâncio: Does it need to? It should — I mean, to be just an economic calculus that would be behind the value of an asset. The value of an asset is the discounted-to-the-present-moment of the expected income stream that the asset will generate in the future. That's the definition of fundamental economic value of an asset. So if an asset has no regular income stream, it's just a speculative asset — in the sense that you just earn or lose capital gains or capital losses with the fluctuation of the prices. You don't have income. So it's a pure speculative — which is even more true about Bitcoin. No income stream whatsoever. Gold has a small income stream for central banks — but it's very small, it's not significant.

The "Black Magic" of Gold Leasing

Interviewer: What about leasing?

Constâncio: Are you talking about leasing more?

Interviewer: Yes, leasing — modern leasing.

Constâncio: It's a consequence of the black magic operated by lawyers and accountants that permits central banks to lend their gold to investment banks and other things that then use that gold to enter into derivatives, in order to hedge the price of gold, which is of their interest to do.

But the magic of lawyers and accountants allow that the central banks lend that gold, but continue to register in their balance sheets as if the gold is still in their balance sheet and in their ownership. I am not a lawyer, and I was never explained how is this possible — that someone lends… it happens also in shorting equities. People lend the thing, the other party uses the thing, but the thing continues to be in the ownership of the institution that lent those securities or gold or whatever. And then there is a fee by having this operation. And it's risky, because sometimes the institutions intermediary of this business — of this lending business — fail. And if they fail, then it is revealed that lending gold or whatever to that institution was really a risk. The ownership was not kept.

But okay, lawyers and accountants have some magic to go around the issue and permitting this sort of operations, and keeping the fiction that the object being lent continues to be in the ownership of the institution that lends. But okay — that provides then fee and income. But it's not relevant in the case of gold.

Bitcoin is out of this consideration. So that is a pure speculative — the value depends on the eye of the beholder. And that's it. Which is, in pure economic terms, irrational.

But if many, many, many people believe in that irrationality, then it becomes rational that I also buy gold or other things — because I can anticipate that I will have a capital gain, because the prices will go up if everyone, at a certain moment of stress, starts to buy gold. And it was to be expected that after Trump won the elections last November, that the stress would come to the world economy and to the dollar, and so the price of gold would go up necessarily. And you know, it moonshot since then to very high prices.

So it's rational to play the game, if we assume that most people are irrational — of buying gold. Everyone is just playing on capital gains, and I hope to avoid capital losses, because sometimes the things crash. But no role — no monetary role for gold. That's not happening.

Then Why Do Central Banks Hold Gold at All?

Interviewer: This is what I'm surprised about when you say this. Because then, why do central banks have gold at all? Why don't you just sell it all?

Constâncio: Ah — it's balance sheet protection. It's gaming on capital gains and capital… well, losses may happen. But over time, they think that the gold guarantees stability in the value of the balance sheet. So that's one of the reasons.

Well, then with time, many central banks realize: "you know, this earns virtually nothing in those basis points of those lending operations. We can have dollars or other currencies and earn some income." And they started to sell gold. So much so that some countries sold practically all the gold they had — the UK, for instance.

Interviewer: And Canada as well.

Constâncio: And Canada, and so on. We sold a bit, but still, in our small size, we are the 12th country in the world in terms of tons of gold in the central bank — which is irrational, especially for a country that no longer has its own currency. It's irrational, but okay — it's there because people have all these magic ideas about gold. It's mythology, it's whatever you can call it. It's irrational.

Interviewer: Well, what is rational then?

Constâncio: No, no, no — I mean, as I say, if everyone, or most people, are irrational, then it is rational that I also have that, because it's guaranteed that the value will go up. Okay? So the collective irrationality is transformed into individual rationality. That's the irony of that situation.

Then What Is a Safe Asset?

Interviewer: But then I'm really perplexed. Because if gold is what you say it is, then what is a safe asset? What is keeping value?

Constâncio: Ah, what is a safe asset? A financial safe asset is an asset that — you can believe, for reasons — its value will not be very much eroded by inflation, because the country behaves well in terms of keeping low inflation. That's why stability and low inflation is a condition for a currency to have an international role. And you believe that about certain countries, and not about other countries.

So that's one reason. And then you earn some income, and you have that condition of stability. Also, you can rely on the laws of that country, that will respect your property, and so on. That's why then you consider that a safe asset.

Everything is relative, of course. There is nothing that is absolutely safe. Even the gold — it can be stolen, it can be seized if you don't import the gold to your own vault. So there is no 100% guarantee of safety. It's relative. A safe asset is the asset that is more safe than all others. That's the definition. That's what counts.

Closing: Playing the Game You Don't Believe In

Interviewer: So what would be, today for you, in this context, in this current global monetary system…

Constâncio: Let's say — if most investors are irrational and prefer gold, I will have to include gold in my portfolio, because I know it's going to increase in value. And then hope that I will be smart enough to start selling when it will go down — because it will go down again. It has been like that.

Only very recently, in real terms, discounted for inflation, the price of gold — very recently, one month or something — attained the same real value as the value of gold in 1980. Exactly 1980. So you see, it goes up and down in real terms. It's now equal to 1980.

Interviewer: So what does it say about the supply of…

Constâncio: The supply is limited, but…

Interviewer: M2 in that sense — the fact that it could have…

Constâncio: So if you had bought gold in 1980, and now you look at it, you have no profit. Because to have the profit, you have to sell it. But if you have it still — no profit. If you had invested in the stock exchange, you would have gained a lot — thousands — from 1980 until now. So the investment in gold was a very, very bad investment. Even Treasury bills would have earned more than the gold that you had from 1980 until now.

That's it. You have to be smart enough to buy, believing that the price of gold is going to increase a lot, and that you will be smart enough to sell in the good moment — otherwise it's a bad investment. Over the years, it's a bad investment.

Interviewer: Well, over the course of the euro's creation, it's been outperforming pretty much anything else — even the S&P.

Constâncio: No, no — outperforming the S&P?

Interviewer: Yeah — maybe because the S&P had the financial crisis and so on.

Constâncio: There were ups and downs. If you take a longer period of time, that would not be the case.

Interviewer: But at least its purchasing power kept its…

Constâncio: Yeah, it kept — but you only benefit if you sell it. Otherwise, it's just there.

Interviewer: Well, a lot of people would say, in central banks too, that they don't do it to make a profit. And this is what also [others say]…

Constâncio: Then, if that's your answer, don't pretend that the central banks do well by having lots of gold, because it is not — because they don't care about the profits. They don't care that they had the gold in 1980, they didn't sell, and now the gold that they had in 1980 values the same as it valued in 1980. And they missed a lot of income, if they had reserves in securities.

It's so difficult to really reason about the value of assets, you know. Gold does not generate a stream of income. Only capital gains. And okay — moments of stress build belief. Well, "historically it has been like that, gold is scarce, so let's have gold because the price will go up." Yeah, okay. Goes up and goes down, as my comparison illustrates.

Interviewer: Your position on gold is very clear.

Constâncio: As I told you — as most people have these magic views about gold, and so they put up the prices in moments of stress, it is rational for me also to invest in gold.

Interviewer: But all central banks have gold.

Constâncio: Well, some have sold almost everything…

Interviewer: So how did their balance sheet do since then? Canada, the UK.

Constâncio: Well, it depends on the time frame. Maybe. But I don't know the calculations, of course. And then — let's do the calculations 10 years from now. The gold may come down again a lot. No one knows.

So no — there is no magic in gold. It's really just because people believe in magic. It's a myth.

Interviewer: But you could say that about silver, bonds, stocks — everything.

Constâncio: I know, I know. But as I said, there is no 100% safe asset at all. That doesn't exist.

Interviewer: Well, that's very reassuring.

Constâncio: No, it doesn't exist. It's just relative, and depends on the time frame and many other things. So that's what it is. It's hard to accept — but that's what it is.

item.description:
## 一位无神论者的护身符：Constâncio 悖论
这段访谈最耐人寻味的时刻，不在他反复宣称的"黄金是神话"，而是他不经意的一句自白——**葡萄牙央行的黄金储备排名全球第十二**。一位刚刚论证黄金"非理性、迷信、无收益"的前央行行长，坐镇于一个人均持金量惊人的国家。这就像一位无神论哲学家，抽屉里始终放着一枚圣物。他把这称为"集体非理性向个体理性的转化"，但这个用词本身就是一次无意识的降维——他用"非理性"命名了一种他所在体制无法建模的**价值维度**。
## 他的论证里藏着黄金最好的辩护词
Constâncio 定义资产价值为"未来现金流的贴现"，因此黄金"没有收益流 = 投机品"。**但他随后自己拆解了这个定义**：谈到"安全资产"时，他承认——没有任何资产是绝对安全的，安全性来自"低通胀""法治""对财产权的保护""对机构可信度的信任"。也就是说，他推崇的"安全"完全**寄生于制度信任**。而黄金的全部特征恰恰是：它是唯一一种"制度信任崩塌时依然工作"的资产。当他说新兴市场买金是因为"美元资产会被冻结制裁"时，他等于承认了：黄金正在履行的，正是他框架里根本无法定价的功能—

item.title: [a16z] Why the People Who Built Hip-Hop Ended Up With Nothing
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：这不是慈善，是"债务的迟到清算"

大多数人会把 Paid in Full 基金会读成"富人回馈给穷艺术家"的温情叙事。但看完整段，你会发现一个更冷峻的真相——Ben Horowitz 反复强调的关键词不是"给予"，而是"credit where credit is due"（该归谁的功劳就归谁）。他花 10 美元买的一张专辑，让他在硅谷创业地狱里挺过来，最终转化成 500 万美元的商业价值——这是一笔从未被记账的知识产权授权费。

真正让我意外的是 Nas 那句"在 hip-hop 里你不能直接给钱"。这句话表面是文化敏感性，深层其实是产权哲学：当你直接给钱，等于承认对方是"受救济者"；当你以"荣誉"的形式支付，等于承认这笔钱本来就该是他的版税。基金会的整个仪式设计，是一次对未签署合同的追溯性履约——他们不是在扶贫，是在补交欠了 40 年的许可费。

二、跨领域连接：Tommy Hilfiger、Adidas 与"未被资本化的文化 alpha"

访谈中最惊人的一段是 Steve Stoute 讲 Tommy Hilfiger 开车穿越 Harlem，看到年轻人露出 Calvin Klein 内裤边——于是他把自己的 logo 放大放在腰带上，救活了整个品牌。这个细节看似八卦，其实揭示了一个至今仍未被主流经济学建模的现象：

文化生产者（hip-hop 艺术家）持续为消费品牌生成"隐性 beta 因子"，但资本市场把这笔 alpha 全部算在了品牌方的市值里。

Adidas 在美国的市场份额从 2% 起飞、Hilfiger 从卖领带到街头之王、Louis Vuitton 请 Virgil Abloh——这些商业史转折点的因果贡献者从未被列入损益表。这和什么现象结构相同？开源软件维护者与万亿美元云计算产业的关系。Linux 内核维护者的处境和 Grandmaster Caz 的处境是同一个数学问题：基础设施提供者被系统性地从价值分配链中除名。

Ben Horowitz 作为顶级 VC 干这件事的深层动机，很可能不只是"报恩"——他见过太多技术领域的"Grandmaster Caz"，他知道一个不奖励基础层的生态系统最终会枯萎。Paid in Full 本质上是一次针对文化产业的"OSS Sustainability Fund"实验。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：为什么"骄傲"比"贫穷"更难解决

访谈里最容易被略过、但最有分析价值的一个细节是：有些老艺术家收到电话时不相信是真的，甚至有人拒绝领奖——"我不需要施舍"。Ben 说他们"很难帮助人"。

这是一个经典的博弈论悲剧：当一个群体被系统性伤害了 40 年，接受帮助的心理成本会高于继续贫穷的物质成本。这个现象在心理学叫"defensive pessimism"，在博弈论叫"信任崩溃后的次优均衡"。基金会真正的天才设计不是筹钱，而是用"荣誉"这个语义包装解构了防御性骄傲——你不是在收钱，你是在被加冕。

更深一层的观察：Nas 在场是关键的"信号发射器"。Ben 一个白人科技富豪打电话，会被当骗子；但 Nas 出现在董事会名单上，等于给整个项目盖上了文化 KYC 的印章。这是一个用"社会资本"启动"金融资本"流动的完美案例——放在 crypto/DeFi 领域，几乎就是一次"文化 DAO"的原型。

四、彩蛋洞察：Ben 那句"从'正确'开始，而不是从'可能'开始"

这句话在访谈末尾轻轻一带，但它其实是 Ben Horowitz 整个投资哲学的暗号——a16z 押注加密货币、AI Agent、生物科技这些"看起来不可能但正确"的赛道，用的是同一个决策框架。Paid in Full 不是他的副业，是他的世界观在低风险场景下的一次公开演示。你可以把这个基金会看作 Ben Horowitz 的一份"人格白皮书"。

📝 转录文本

开场：为什么要做这件事

Ben Horowitz: I think in life it's impossible to do anything great if you start with what's possible. You have to start with what's right. Hip-hop's not that big. Like the guys who made the art form are not that many. And so why can't we honor them?

Steve Stoute: Acknowledging and celebrating and then bringing this group of people together is something that the industry should have done a long time ago.

Grandmaster Caz: When people see me and they see my passion, this [ __ ] still got it. He's still doing it because I have to. Hip-hop don't have social security. You have to work.

Nas: The whole thing about hip-hop is about to grow to be better. And I think we are living our lyrics — paid in full.

Steve Stoute: I want everybody to know around the world what Grandmaster Caz looks like and to celebrate him and applaud this man for what he's done and celebrate Roxanne and celebrate Melly and the DOC and everybody else who's had these achievements. The thing is the honor. The thing is putting you in the light that you deserve to be in. If you're watching this and love hip hop.

一、基金会的缘起：一张 10 美元的专辑，与一笔无法偿还的债

主持人: So, this is the first time this group has gotten together to publicly talk about the Paid in Full Foundation. Guys, welcome to the podcast.

All: Thank you. Yeah.

主持人: So, Ben, why don't you introduce the foundation and maybe let's get into the origin story as far back as you want to go as to how this came to be.

Ben Horowitz: Yeah. So, Paid in Full is an organization meant to honor the legacy of the people who created one of the most important musical art forms of all time, hip-hop, and make sure that they're paid in full — financially, spiritually, and culturally.

The idea kind of started with me, Steve and Nas. It always bothered me that, you know, I bought Paid in Full — the album — for $10, and in my career (those of you in tech know this) I probably got at least $5 million worth of value out of that record. But there was no way to pay it back. And it needed to be paid back.

So I had the idea originally, and I called Steve. Steve and I have been friends for many, many years, and I said, "Steve, I have this idea, what do you think?" And he said, "Well, it's not only a good idea, but it's a very timely idea because people are talking about this right now — but they're not doing anything." So, like if you listen to the podcasts, people are saying, "Oh, these rappers, these old guys, they don't have any money. They're dusty, they're this, they're that." And these are very, very important guys. But nobody's doing anything. And so, I thought, well, let's do something.

And then the next call I made was to Nas. And Nas had a great insight — a lot of the concept was inspired by our dear friend Quincy Jones, who had a thing called the Jazz Foundation where he would get money to the old jazz guys. And I told it to Nas, and Nas said, "You know, that's not going to work that way in hip-hop, because in hip-hop you can't just give somebody money. It has to be more than that. It has to be a recognition of what they did and who they are."

And so that's when we got the idea of, well, let's have a big award show — have this idea of the Grandmaster Award for the true greats of hip-hop — and invite everybody to honor these guys. And we started it off with two all-time greats: Scarface and Rakim.

二、Scarface 的电话：当"荣誉"遇上"救命"

Steve Stoute: Before we even got to the first show, it was also timely because Scarface was going through a medical condition.

Ben Horowitz: Yes.

Steve Stoute: And I remember I was in the south of France, and I called him — he needed to get his kidney, to get his kidney from his son, a kidney transplant, and it wasn't the right doctors. There was a lot of care and concern on that anyway, but more specific was the money and the doctor who was performing the surgery. And I called him — I've known Scarface for years — but when I called him literally from the south of France in June, and he got that phone call from me about what we were going to do, he was in shock.

I mean, just imagine — a phone call coming randomly from a guy you hadn't spoken to in two years, and I'm calling you about your medical condition and I'm telling you that we got you financially, we're going to help you. And I remember calling Ben after that and saying, "Look, I spoke to Scarface, man, and he was in disbelief."

In fact, early on, people were in such disbelief they didn't believe that it was real.

Ben Horowitz: Yeah. We had a hard time actually helping people because they didn't believe it. I have some stories on that — I don't even know if I can mention the names, but we had people who literally didn't get the award because they thought it was a scam. They just didn't want to mess with it.

And that's actually what reinforced the belief that if you celebrated the artist — and it didn't feel like you were giving them reparations, but you were actually celebrating them and giving them the honor and dignity they deserve that they had not received properly — then that would be the way it would be accepted and celebrated.

It wasn't until we did the first one — and, you know, like any other startup, duct tape and whatever we got to do to get this thing going — but we had Scarface and Rakim, and obviously the support of the board, having Nas on the board, that all helped. Then it started to go through the community: "There is something that's happening." And that's when it worked. But literally, it was disbelief from the initial phone calls.

Ben Horowitz: Yeah. Well, it's one of those things where somebody's got to step up at some point. Ben Horowitz: Okay, let me give the plug. paidinfullfoundation.org. You can come and be a part of it. Felicia and I match every donation two-and-a-half to one, which means that all your money goes to the artist. There are no paid employees at the foundation. Everything is volunteer. If you want to be part of it, if you want to contribute, paidinfull.org. That's my plug.

And I want to ask Caz —

Nas: That was pretty good. That's like a radio.

Ben Horowitz: Thank you. Caz, we've been talking about it — but as a recipient, what has it meant to you from an honor standpoint, from a financial standpoint? How did it affect you?

十七、Grandmaster Caz 亲述：它买了我一间房，也买了我的尊严

Grandmaster Caz: I definitely was gonna address that at some point, because it's not specifics — like, yo, this and that, this one gets that. It's like you get a grant, so to speak, and it's over a five-year period. And it's helped change my life.

I was on a path to self-improvement, trying to get things. LL Cool J called me a few years back and was like, "Yo, it's time. I want you on the radio." But when Paid in Full called me, it was like, "Yo, now this is going to change your life."

I bought a house.

Ben Horowitz: Wow.

Grandmaster Caz: I moved out the projects. And I've lived in the Bronx all my life. I only did a three-year stint in Cali for a while, but I lived in the Bronx all my life. And I thought I would always end up here. And my last thoughts in my head for the last like 10, 15 years — I don't want to die in the projects. I don't want to end here. I don't want it to end here.

And it didn't. You know what I mean? I got a nice house in Pennsylvania. Me and my wife. And my life has improved drastically. I got a comfort, I got a cushion that I never had. Everything was day-to-day. Everything was run out, grind, hustle.

And when people see me and they see my passion — this [ __ ] still got it. He's still doing it because I have to. I didn't have no — hip-hop don't have social security. Hip-hop don't have no health benefits or none of that. You have to work. You got to stay out there. For me anyway, I got to keep working. So when you see me on radio, you see me doing park jams, you see me doing hip-hop sightseeing tours — all that was to maintain, to keep me up and at it.

And I think my attitude that went along with it, and the way that I deal with people, kept me in people's consciousness — which I'm so [ __ ] grateful for. Like I said, I can't speak for everybody, but I'm sure what it's done for me, it's done for everybody.

One thing I want to say — I don't want to say what person — but when you was talking about some people didn't know if it was a scam or whatever, a couple people thought was like, "Yo, I don't need this. Like, I'm good." Like a handout — "I don't need nobody to give me." Nah, it's not about that. It's not all about that. That's a part of it. The thing is the honor. The thing is putting you in the light that you deserve to be in.

And I got to salute LL Cool J for that, too. He put us — he put Shai Rock on the radio — when he didn't have to. He created a whole lane. He's like, "Now that's y'all, go. Monday through Friday, y'all on the air." So that kind of recognition, it resonates. And when people see important people giving you your props, they feel obligated — like, "Yo, I got to say that."

What this does — how you just ended it — is it brings recognition. And that's the gift that keeps giving, because it's done out of love. And it inspires more people to think that we can do things like this, too. We got to remember: let's take care of each other.

I'll say this. I was getting reached out to by a few hip-hop artists for a while, probably the later end of the 90s on. And I would do things for different artists — won't say it, won't mention the names. Even up to someone who passed away recently, a musical hip-hop producer. I was there. And I wonder how many more of us were doing that — but it's on the low. This is on the high. This is on an even bigger level. And you can show the world: we're taking care of our own. We're taking care of the thing that took care of us.

十八、隐藏的商业史：Adidas、Tommy Hilfiger 与 Hip-hop 的未支付版税

Grandmaster Caz: In Ben's book, he has pieces of lyrics that inspired him. These things are important, because if we forget, if we sweep it all under the rug — if you don't know that Puba took Hilfiger to another level, if you don't know —

Nas: Sprite.

Grandmaster Caz: Sprite — the fashion industry, period.

Steve Stoute: By the way, that's exactly why I wrote The Tanning of America. It was specifically so that all of the things that hip-hop created —

Ben Horowitz: In your book, when you talk about the Run-DMC concert — I go from — everybody holds up their Adidas. What that did for Adidas.

Steve Stoute: Adidas was kind of dead at the time.

Nas: Hold on. Dead.

Steve Stoute: Oh yeah. 2% market share in America.

Ben Horowitz: 2% market share in America. And three-quarters of that 2% was coming from the Northeast region. And all they knew is that — why is everybody up there buying this one specific SKU, and why are they throwing away the shoelaces?

Nas: Hip-hop, baby.

Steve Stoute: But — Puba: "Obey your thirst" is his line.

Nas: "First things first, obey your thirst." That's his line. That's their tagline.

Steve Stoute: No one would ever pay attention to these things. These guys are pioneers above and beyond hip-hop. They created the culture around the music that lives on to this day. The fashion, the language, the brands that only exist as a result of their contribution.

I love Tommy Hilfiger. Tommy Hilfiger is a great guy. He's done a lot with artists. He should be part of contributing to Paid in Full. If it wasn't for hip-hop, he was dead in the water. They were selling ties. He says that he was selling ties. He was trying to be Ralph Lauren. And they were like, "You're not Ralph Lauren, dog."

And on his way home — because he lived in Greenwich — when you leave the city you can obviously get to Greenwich by the traditional way taking the highway, or you can cut through Harlem and get up to Westchester. So he's cutting through Harlem, and he sees everybody wearing their pants low and their Calvin Klein — the top of the Calvin Klein brief showing. And literally that's where he got the idea to make underwear and use that where Calvin the — the top —

Ben Horowitz: Yeah, and put Tommy there. Whatever this [ __ ] is called — the elastic band. And he put Tommy Hilfiger there and made the waistband bigger, thicker, so that you could really see it.

Steve Stoute: And that's how the whole thing got going. Seriously — literally — and he talks about it. He'd seen it driving through Harlem.

Nas: That's crazy.

Steve Stoute: And that's when the brand took off — and went from selling ties that wasn't working to now selling streetwear. The hottest fashion trend in the world. Streetwear. That Louis Vuitton sells, designed by skateboard P. You know what I'm saying?

Ben Horowitz: God bless. And Virgil.

Steve Stoute: These are the things that these guys have been a part of contributing that they never got their fair share of.

And by the way — what we're doing is, we're just trying to get momentum. We're not trying to solve the world's problem here. We need others to either come and donate to the organization, or start other organizations that also have the same motive: to help celebrate, give back to the guys who have helped contribute to your business, to inspire you — on some real, with love and respect.

Nas: With love and respect.

十九、Felicia 与 Scarface 的开胸手术

Ben Horowitz: And actually, on that, I want to tell a story. Because the love and respect part goes beyond even the award.

So Scarface had a heart condition. And, you know — look, he comes from a place where people don't even really go to the doctor, let alone go in for open-heart surgery, which is what he needed. And he was on the phone with my wife Felicia, and she knew he was scared. And she flew out to Houston to see him before he went to the doctor. And he didn't want to go in. He's like, "No, I don't want to go to the doctor. I'm not going to the doctor."

And she said, "No." And he calls her "the bully." She's about 5 feet tall, weighs maybe a buck 05. And she says, "No, I'm taking you to the doctor right now."

And right as they got into the doctor, his aorta burst — and they got him in just in time and saved his life. And that doesn't happen without her caring so much about him.

And a lot of what the foundation is about — because she runs it, he's the president — is how much she cares about these artists and how much she's committed to taking care of them regardless. Forget the award, forget what the actual contract is and all that kind of thing. She's going to do that work. And that creates the whole culture of the thing — which is why that feeling at the award is so different.

Grandmaster Caz: Agreed. Definitely kudos to Felicia. None more serious than that. She makes it — like it's love involved here. Beyond the award, beyond the check. It's not over. You'll get a call — "How are you doing? How's your wife?" "Oh, she's sick." "Give me your address." She sends — the next day flowers come. The next day like some Dior glasses come. That's how Felicia is. And it's not about what's going on. She'll randomly call you just to check on you, to see if everything's good. And that's the difference between this and anything I've ever experienced in an award, grant, foundation. The love. The genuine love.

I just can't speak enough about the event that's coming up — the next Hip-Hop Grandmaster Awards. It's going to be monumental. And if you haven't been abreast of what's going on with Paid in Full, definitely check in this year, and then look back at what we've done in the past four years. And then get on board. Don't play with it. Stay with it.

Nas: Yes, sir.

二十、结尾：Nas 的父亲、Quincy Jones、以及被隐藏的谱系

主持人: Now Steve, I'm curious — if you could talk about when was the moment you knew that you and Ben were going to be friends for life?

Nas: Steve invited me to a dinner years ago. That's the craziest — way up.

Steve Stoute: Oh yeah, it was an interesting room of people, right? He put together a great room, great restaurant.

Nas: It was Mr. Chow's downtown. Mr. Freddy. Yeah. So this room was dope, right? And he put this together. And I heard about Ben through him, and I met Ben right there. And our love for music and love for food was a thing that connected me and Ben at that point. And we just been cool since then.

Ben Horowitz: Yeah. Some of my best times listening to Rakim with Nas. By the way, Nas hears things in Rakim songs that nobody else hears. It's unbelievable. And then listening to Prince. We listen to Prince together — and then break it down. Going and visit triple OG Quincy Jones together. Music fans who just — Nas is like, as great an artist as he is, he's that great a music fan.

Nas: By the way — I was at Quincy's house when he had just moved into the house. Or redecorated the house, rather. And it was me and Chris Tucker. And he goes and shows — he was showing us the casting tapes for The Color Purple.

Ben Horowitz: The Color Purple.

Nas: Right. He's showing us — and there was Whoopi Goldberg. And she's talking. She's just talking to the camera like this or whatever. And then she starts reading the script — and then within a second starts crying. I was like, "Oh." It was the first time I seen acting and I was like, "Oh, I mean — I knew for a fact this is a skill that is beyond." She was like, regular normal talking — and they said, "All right." And Steven Spielberg's holding the camera. And boom, she just starts crying.

Ben Horowitz: Yeah, she was great in that role, by the way.

Nas: So anyhow — Chris Tucker, we all were blown away by the fact that she did that. And we just started talking about a bunch of different [ __ ], and I bring up Nas — I bring up my dad, Olu Dara. Yo, this guy — Quincy Jones at that age was still moving very quickly, like a quick guy — quickly went and grabbed a bunch of vinyls and came back with pictures. And he showed me a picture of him with Nas's dad in Saint-Tropez in the 60s.

Ben Horowitz: That's amazing.

Nas: I was like, "Holy shit." Like, I knew Nas's dad was obviously a jazz legend, but I didn't know at what level it was that these guys were running around.

Grandmaster Caz: He would tell me stories of people he'd been around, but I didn't listen. I'm like, "Oh, yeah. Okay, pop." Yo, my pop told me — about Mtume. The song Juicy came out. He's like, "Yo, that's my man." I'm like, "Come on. You probably met him in passing." I ain't thinking nothing about it. What year was that? 83, 84 or something. I got into the rap game and I met Mtume — and he's like, "Yo, your dad is my man." And I said — I didn't believe him when he told me that. Not that he's a liar or anything, but I didn't know it was like y'all were like that. He was like, "That's my guy, man." I was like, yo, you understand? Juicy Fruit was the biggest song in the world. So how could I believe that at the time? I'm a kid. I don't know. I think he's just trying to make me feel good or something. But he knew a lot of people when he was younger, man. Quincy knew everybody.

Ben Horowitz: Everybody. Everybody knows your kids.

Nas: Yeah, we know. But the fact that Olu — now you got to understand, like in anything else, the DNA thing, right? Your dad's a famous football player, right? The son. This I didn't know. I mean, obviously I know Nas is a brilliant artist. I had no idea the connection was that his dad was that level of brilliant. I thought his dad — I didn't know it was that level of brilliant, that Quincy Jones within a second go find a picture of them together. And I'm like — these guys were in Saint-Tropez in the 60s doing their thing.

The whole thing was profound to me — that whole evening of going from The Color Purple to Olu Dara, and then reflecting on the fact that Nas comes from this great lineage of talent.

Nas: Yeah. They come from Mississippi. My pops. He comes from Natchez, Mississippi, and his dad was in a band. And it just — music in the family.

Ben Horowitz: Yeah. It's crazy.

尾声

主持人: So, one more time. Paid in Full.

Ben Horowitz: paidinfullfoundation.org. All your money goes directly to the artists. And it is — everybody who's ever been to it will tell you it's the greatest charitable event in the world. Like, there's nothing like it. I guarantee nobody's ever gone and not had a great time. And a time that will be a memory for the rest of your life.

主持人: Oof. All right. Thank you guys. That was great.
