item.description:
## 一、"80%治愈率"作为一种人类学化石
Scull不经意间抛出了一个惊人的模式：**"80%这个数字在这些疗法中反复出现"**。这不是巧合，而是一个未被言说的社会心理学常数。为什么不是95%？不是100%？因为80%正好落在**"奇迹阈值"与"合理性阈值"的交界带**——高到足以震撼、传播、吸引投资，低到足以为失败案例留出解释空间（"那20%本来就无药可救"）。
这个数字与庞氏骗局承诺的年化回报率、邪教宣称的"觉醒率"、创业孵化器吹嘘的"成功率"惊人吻合。**80%不是医学数据，是一种叙事货币**——它是骗子、狂热者、真诚的错误者共同发现的"最优说服比例"。萨克尔从德国戒毒所走到纽约诊所、从治疗诈骗中挣到200万美元（1960年代币值，约合今天2000万美元）的整个轨迹，本质上是这个数字的社会学套利。
## 二、萨克尔的"精神分裂脑细胞"辩护：一个思维病理学标本
当被告知胰岛素休克疗法杀死脑细胞时，萨克尔答："**是的，它们在杀死精神分裂的脑细胞。**"
这句话值得被写进认知科学教科书。它展示了一个完整的**自我封闭系统（closed epistemic loop）**

item.title: [Alan Chen加州生活号] 加息25个基点，市场却开始挤空：AI下一轮领涨已经换人 | 美股圆桌｜
item.dc:creator: Alan Chen加州生活号
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、隐藏在租金里的"暗物质"：AI 商业周期的相位切换

这期节目最容易被听众忽略、但真正值钱的信号，其实藏在 NBIS 那个几乎被一笔带过的细节里——CPU 租金涨幅超过 GPU。

大多数人还在用"训练时代"的心智模型看这轮 AI 行情：Nvidia 是唯一的太阳，其他都是绕着转的行星。但租金曲线其实在悄悄告诉你另一个故事：AI 已经从"造模型"进入"跑模型"的相位。Alan 那个"CPU 是车间主任、GPU 是工程师"的比喻其实很惊人——推理需要的是编排、调度、事务性逻辑，不是暴力算力。这意味着 AMD、Intel、Arm、AMAT 这些被市场视为"上一代"的公司，实际上是在被下一代需求重新召回的老兵，而不是在追赶潮流。

跨领域连接：这个模式跟电力工业史惊人相似。1900 年代初期，所有资本都追捧发电机制造商（相当于今天的 GPU 厂），但真正跑赢 30 年的公司是变压器、电表、配电盘——它们对应的正是"让电真正被用起来"的基础设施。今天 CPU 租金反超 GPU，就是那个"电已经发出来了，接下来看谁把它送到千家万户"的转折点信号。

二、"预期已满"的量子态：加息利空为何变利多

节目里 Alan 说"上涨的预期已经 fully priced in"，这句话背后是一个被反复验证但很少被讲清楚的市场悖论：在信息市场里，被观察的风险会失去破坏力。

Fear & Greed 指数触及 Extreme Fear、20 日均线上方个股跌到 20%——这些不是超卖信号，这是"所有人都已经把最坏情况想到"的市场共识指纹。当 FOMC 真的加了 25bp，反而释放了一个更强的元信号：所有人担心的那件事，已经不能再吓到任何人。

这个现象跟量子力学的"退相干"是同构的：叠加态一旦被观察，就坍缩成确定态。市场也是这样——一件事只要被充分讨论、充分交易、充分定价，它就从"变量"变成了"常数"。真正需要警惕的从来不是被讨论最多的风险（关税、加息、AI 泡沫），而是当前完全没人在讨论的东西——比如今天 10 年期和 30 年期国债在股市反弹时依然阴涨，这个反相关的裂缝，才是被市场遗漏的量子态。

三、川普输中期选举 = 股市的"稳态悖论"

节目末尾那个反直觉观点很值得深挖：川普赢中期选举反而是股市的利空。听起来违反商业媒体的常识，但它其实揭示了资本市场一个更深的规律——市场爱的不是政策取向，是政策边界。

一党独大意味着单方向政策可以无阻力推行，这在数学上等同于方差扩大：能推行的政策空间变宽，市场无法用制衡逻辑收敛出预期。而"两党对峙"看似低效，却给市场提供了一个天然的贝叶斯先验：任何激进政策都会被稀释、被延迟、被谈判。

跨领域连接：生态学里有个"多样性—稳定性假说"——物种越单一的生态系统对扰动越敏感（想想爱尔兰土豆饥荒）。政治权力结构对市场的作用完全同构：制衡不是低效，是抗脆弱性的定价机制。所以 2018 年中期选举后市场那个"12 月 20% 反弹"的老故事，本质不是"川普失去众议院"这个事件本身，而是方差被重新压缩的重定价。

四、彩蛋：S-1 文件本身就是催化剂

最后一个容易被跳过的洞察——Anthropic 递交 S-1 后，供应链会先涨。这不是"利好兑现"，而是一个更微妙的机制：S-1 是公开知识的诞生。

在博弈论里，"共同知识（common knowledge）"和"每个人都知道"是两回事。私下都知道 Anthropic 增长很快，跟"所有人都知道所有人都知道 Anthropic 的 ARR"，是完全不同的两个市场状态。前者不会改变行为，后者会立刻改变所有下游厂商的采购、议价、扩产决策。IPO 招股书的价值，从来不是融资本身，而是它把"私人信念"升级为"公共协调点"。这也是为什么 SpaceX 当年临近上市传闻时，太空板块一次次爆发——共同知识的形成，本身就是最强的多因子催化剂。

📝 转录文本

开场

Hello everyone, welcome back to our Meizhou Meigu Yuan Zhuo。上周我跟 Will 聊了 AI 小作文，市场当时非常 panic。这一周有一些大的波动，大市和股市都上下颠簸。周三 FOMC 加息 25 个基点——上周我预测可能会加，Will 预测可能不加。稍后我们会回顾各自的思路。本周要聊的东西很多，今天先从 FOMC 说起。

一、FOMC 25bp：为什么市场反应还算体面

我们上周先请你（Will）复盘一下思路，包括为什么这次加 25bp 的市场反应其实是可以接受的。

  • 过去一年多以来，指数已经处在比较低的位置；
  • 20 日均线之上的个股占比只有 20% 左右；
  • 这种位置一般是需要反弹的，此时再去追空，废纸的可能性会更大。

二、点阵图 vs. 市场预期：分歧才是机会

第二点是看点阵图。我觉得可以补充一些细节：

  • 其实点阵图释放的信息并不等于市场预期；
  • 点阵图只释放了后续再加两次的信号；
  • 但市场（看 WATCH 工具）预期到明年年底其实是 3–4 次的加息（原文口误，语境为"降息"）。

所以真实情况没有预期得那么糟。在这个背景下，超卖的、擅长做多的人就跳了出来，现在的大盘就是一个超卖反弹。

不过我依然是"加 0.25"的那个观点——上周我就说了，市场已经把 25bp 打满在 WOS 里；如果他选择加，影响不会太大；但如果他不加，可能会影响到他的 credibility。所以我当时判断他会加 25bp，同时维持美联储的独立性。

三、风险偏好的信号：QQQ 未创新低、标普创了

我觉得市场表现挺好。周三我们社区 Q&A 的时候我就跟大家说过：QQQ 没有创新低，但标普创了。整体来说是一个 risk-on 的好信号。

我们也聊到了 Fear & Greed Index，已经触及 Almost Extreme Fear，包括收盘时依然处在 panic 状态。美元上涨之前，我也在 X 上贴过自己的观点：当前的恐慌情绪已经很到位，价格不会跌破 25、也不会跌破 50——预期已经 fully priced in。

其实 9 月 18 日的波动可能比 FOMC 本身更大。目前来看，这是一个 miss。

四、大牛市结构与半导体估值

我们上周聊过，无论是标普还是纳斯达克，整体都在走一个高位牛市结构，对吧？我记得那之后我们做了一波多头。当时我们就说过——

我们整个 SOXX 半导体板块，也在这样一个正面背景下：估值非常、非常有吸引力。即使已经涨了一周，当前估值仍然很强，让那些还没上车的朋友仍然可以继续考虑。这就是我们在言宝社区里的判断。

调研中还有很多可以分享的内容，包括 SMH 从技术形态上是一个比较标准的头肩底形态，这些都在兑现之中。感兴趣的会员朋友可以在 ALANTSLA.com 上看到我们中线、国内和长线所有过往交易，包括哪些股票具体输了、赢了。

五、网络安全 & AI 小作文余波

本周（包括昨天）一些个股上涨，其实和上周发生的事情关系很大：

  • 一是网络安全板块从周一开始起涨；
  • 我们周日聊过 AI 小作文，Dario 开始吓人；周一、周三 all-in summit 出来之后，情绪有所反弹；
  • 尤其是周一，NBIS（Nubi 博士）说要涨价，把整条半导体产业链的情绪都带起来了，包括"订单删除"的情绪。

六、NBIS 涨租的秘密：CPU > GPU

我们发现一个很有意思的现象。Will，你帮大家梳理一下——我说太多了。

这条信息其实非常关键：本周 NBIS 的新租约，不管是 GPU 还是 CPU，租金都在涨；而且 CPU 涨得比 GPU 还要多。

第一，大厂并没有跑路，基本上都还在——因为全场的控制逻辑是"折旧被高估"。但如果我的老芯片、老显卡还在涨，那它的会计算盘就是合情合理、有利有节的。

第二，CPU 和 GPU 的需求都在持续增长，尤其是 CPU。CPU 是做什么的？我们在报告里说过——CPU 在推理阶段的需求非常高，因为推理的占比越来越大。CPU 就像车间里的一个"主任"，需要管理软件和其他方方面面的事情，才能让推理顺利跑起来。

（此处为一段较长的转录静默段，从略。）

七、大厂建新数据中心背后的隐含预期

我们都知道，建一个 data center 的工地至少要 3–5 年。原本纯 CAPEX 是压在今年年底的，但如果他们真的认为 PIX（peak capex）就在今年年底，为什么还愿意投钱去建新的 internal 技术？

所以我们此前的假设需要改一改，还需要进一步研究。但今天，包括 AMD、Intel、Cadence 这样的半导体公司——

八、半导体的"50 军线"与内部分化

关于这个半导体板块，我可以多说几句。这大概是你在外面、如果没人告诉你，可能不太理解的：

整个半导体板块给人的感觉像是"50 军线"刚刚站上——但在这条线里面，其实有很多个明显强于其他公司的强者。

比如为什么我们刚才聊到"推理未来的需求可能高于训练"？——你就能清楚地看到，那些沾 CPU 的公司，跑得比纯 GPU 的更好。

  • AMD 为什么今天接近历史高点？可能下周就要突破？因为它主要做的就是这方面业务；
  • Intel 两周前就已经在早期启动；
  • 包括 Arm——今天也是。它开始发展这一模式，也刚发布了新产品 CBR4 Rebus，同样基于推理。

所以如果你把这些串起来：订单 → 存储 → AMAT → 其他硬件，你就能更清楚地判断谁会是这一轮的 leader、哪个版本、哪些标的。我们会在社区里跟会员详细讨论。

九、比特币反弹与 RWA

这周（包括今天）更大的一件事，是比特币又涨了：今天涨了大约 6%，看起来风险情绪回来了。

主要原因是本周 Clarity Act 失败，失败之后先大跌，休息了两天，今天似乎是通过美股链上的 RWA（Real World Assets）实现了这样的交易。所以他们的 leader、Yang Hu——市场愿意再承担一些风险。

十、前方的不确定性事件

但前方还有很多不确定事件：

  • 下周有 APEC（原文"春节"疑为口误）；上次他们在北京开会时美股大跌，会后如何仍不确定；
  • 中期选举：现在只剩不到两个月，市场已经很早地开始定价"民主党回归"；
  • 伊朗战争：德国等会尝试拿掉一些共和党席位——因为能源价格仍然偏高，尽管有企稳趋势；上周我们也提过原油。

看起来 OK，但又有一点"不太合理"。

十一、债市的"裂缝"

本周还有一些点值得注意，包括 30 年和 10 年国债：虽然走势偏稳，但今天也在涨——股市和债市同时上涨。

这说明债市对通胀是否被完全控制仍然有些担忧。因为如果没有担忧，它应该在加息之后与股市呈负相关——毕竟这次是 0.25bp。

今天如果 equity 表现这么好、债券反而下跌，我们会更放心。但目前来看，市场可能更在乎的是——川普是否在跟伊朗释放利好？油价是否会下来？——市场好像有一种"抢跑"的感觉。

十二、川普外交的"猜谜"

这个挺有意思的：他之前说选举结束之后战争才会结束。但现在的问题是——战争没有结束，选举基本已经结束了。所以我不知道他现在在打什么算盘。

刚看到几分钟前他又发消息说要和习达成很多协议。我们还需要更多信息，才能知道他在葫芦里卖什么药。你还带了一堆中国企业家。但问题是：如果你不让他们投资美国，那这些中国企业家来是占便宜的。

表面上关系看起来还可以接受，但实际上更多的是继续 decoupling。

十三、Anthropic IPO 猜想

所以还有一件即将发生的事——Anthropic（AdRabic）的招股与落地即将官宣。

我们之前也聊过：SpaceX 上市前是被选中的公司；Anthropic、OpenAI 和 SpaceX 基本上是同一量级的公司。看看这次会不会发生。

这里有个很有意思的观察：一旦它宣布要发 S-1，这件事本身就更有利可图——因为你的 S-1 会披露 ARR、营收、增长、指引。理论上下游会得到更多订单：存储、光模块、GPU、CPU，以及各种光机等等，都会受益。

那么等到它真正 IPO 的时候，可能就会出现类似 SpaceX 上市时那种少见的现象。所以短期来看，这应该会让这些 AI 相关板块再涨一轮。

个人观点：我更看好 DaFan（大范）。至少下周，我觉得还是 OK 的。过程会更痛苦，因为要走长期；但总体在这个位置，仍然是不错的一段时间。

十四、季节性与中期选举的历史类比

除了大选年，9–10 月这段一般都比较危险。除了 2018 年——那一年大盘也在中期附近，从 12 月一路涨。当时也很出人意料：结果 12 月出现了 20% 的反弹，把大家都吓出去了。

如果控制多数席位——川普会没有人能够监管他；但如果民主党回来，又可能在经济发展方面带来担忧。到底会不会……

我个人认为，川普中期选举失利，其实对股市是好事——市场不喜欢不确定性。但如果他失去这个能力……

十五、技术面展望

从技术指标看，我认为我们应该会有另一次挑战前高的机会。但能涨多少，我们不知道；能不能走到终点，我们不知道。

这里有一种"不确定性恐惧"——因为每一次中期选举，都会给人一种"要出大反馈"的感觉。市场要么会安心，要么想等等看，看测试结果如何。所以我觉得我们也可以关注这样一种可能性。但在那些恐惧真正开始之前——

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、隐藏在租金里的"暗物质"：AI 商业周期的相位切换
这期节目最容易被听众忽略、但真正值钱的信号，其实藏在 NBIS 那个几乎被一笔带过的细节里——**CPU 租金涨幅超过 GPU**。
大多数人还在用"训练时代"的心智模型看这轮 AI 行情：Nvidia 是唯一的太阳，其他都是绕着转的行星。但租金曲线其实在悄悄告诉你另一个故事：**AI 已经从"造模型"进入"跑模型"的相位**。Alan 那个"CPU 是车间主任、GPU 是工程师"的比喻其实很惊人——推理需要的是编排、调度、事务性逻辑，不是暴力算力。这意味着 AMD、Intel、Arm、AMAT 这些被市场视为"上一代"的公司，实际上是**在被下一代需求重新召回**的老兵，而不是在追赶潮流。
跨领域连接：这个模式跟**电力工业史**惊人相似。1900 年代初期，所有资本都追捧发电机制造商（相当于今天的 GPU 厂），但真正跑赢 30 年的公司是**变压器、电表、配电盘**——它们对应的正是"让电真正被用起来"的基础设施。今天 CPU 租金反超 GPU，就是那个"电已经发出来了，接下来看谁把它送到千家万户"的转折点信号。

item.title: [All-In Podcast] Bill Gurley: Searching for Feynman
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

关于 Bill Gurley「寻找费曼」演讲的系统性观察

一、这是一场关于「搜索算法失效」的演讲，而非关于新冠

表面上 Gurley 在讲根因分析，但更深层的结构是：他在用费曼的方法论去寻找一个费曼。这是一个递归自指的问题——当科学体制本身成为被调查对象时，谁来做调查者？他列举的五个灾难中，都有独立于当事机构的「第三方节点」（NIST、NSF、参议院、学术委员会、独立记者），构成了一个分布式验证网络。而新冠事件的独特之处在于：所有本该充当独立验证节点的机构，都与被调查对象共享同一个知识网络。

用密码学的语言说，这是典型的拜占庭容错崩溃：当超过 1/3 的验证者被同一利益污染，整个共识系统失效。Gurley 三年前讲「监管俘获」（regulatory capture），今天讲的其实是科学俘获（scientific capture）——一个更危险的升级版本，因为科学声称自己是终极仲裁者。

二、一个几乎无人提及的观察：性别的完美镜像

Gurley 展示的五位「阻拦者」（Collins、Fauci、Daszak、Farrar、Baric）全部为男性，且全部是同一代际、同一学术圈的内部人；而他致敬的五位「搜索者」（Chan、Eban、Kopp、Tufekci、Young）全部为女性，且分散在分子生物学、财经记者、非营利组织、社会学、调查记者五个完全不同的领域。

这不是巧合，而是一个系统性信号。跨领域连接：这个模式在其他历史时刻反复出现——沙利度胺灾难中的 Frances Kelsey、安然事件中的 Sherron Watkins、Theranos 事件中的 Erika Cheung、烟草诉讼中的 Jeffrey Wigand（男性但为局外人）。当核心圈层高度同质化并共享既得利益时，突破性的真相往往由「结构上的局外人」揭示——他们既没有社交资本要保护，也没有被邀请进入"共识制造"的房间。女性在科学体制中的边缘地位，反而使她们成为最可靠的搜索节点。

这里有个反直觉的推论：多样性不仅是道德议题，而是认知安全议题。同质化的专家网络在正常时期高效，在危机时期危险。

三、规模的悖论——伤害越大，调查越少

Gurley 提到一个惊人的数字：新冠的死亡人数是他列举的所有其他五个灾难总和的 3000 倍，但投入调查的人力资源大约是 1/1000。这看起来违反直觉，但如果你把它建模成一个「institutional flight response」（机构逃逸响应）函数，就完全合理了：

调查强度 ≈ (公众关注 × 记者独立性) / (被调查方规模 × 意识形态载荷)

飓风卡特里娜的调查对象是陆军工程兵团——一个可以被围剿的、政治上安全的目标。而新冠的调查对象是整个全球生物医学建制，加上一个战略竞争对手（中国），加上一个已被极化的政治议题。分母膨胀到无穷大时，分子再大也趋于零。

四、跨领域连接：这场演讲预示了 AI 时代的核心风险

最令我意外的是 Gurley 在演讲末尾看似顺带的一句话：「我的 P(second COVID) 远高于我的 P(doom)」。这句话轻描淡写，但颠覆了整个 AI 安全叙事的框架。

主流 AI 风险讨论聚焦于「模型能力失控」，但 Gurley 指出了一个更近迫、也更被忽视的风险：制造共识的机制已经被证明可以在没有 AI 帮助的情况下扭曲全球集体认知。Proximal Origins 论文一周内写成，绕过了正常的科学审议，成为维基百科的引用锚点，让整个话题变成禁忌——这已经是前 AI 时代的信息战完美案例。

推论：真正需要担心的不是 AI 会不会说谎，而是当这套「制造共识」的社会机制被 AI 加速 1000 倍时，人类的分布式验证系统是否还能运作。Gurley 演讲的真正议题，其实是「知识论的抗审查性」（epistemic censorship-resistance）——这与比特币解决的问题在深层结构上同构。

五、一个隐藏的元讽刺

Gurley 在演讲中把自己反复归入「读过顶级 1% 资料的人」——这是他给自己颁发的信誉徽章。但整场演讲的核心论点恰恰是：权威徽章不是真相的来源，独立搜索才是。他必须援引徽章来让台下的风险投资人听进去，但他真正想传达的信息是「不要相信徽章」。

这个内在张力揭示了一个更深的系统性困境：在一个低信任社会中，即便你要传播「打破权威」的信息，你也必须先建立自己的权威。这是所有改革者的双重束缚，也是为什么真正的范式转换往往需要一代人的时间——因为老一代必须先死去，新一代才能在没有旧权威负担的情况下重新开始搜索。

一个具体行动建议：如果你相信 Gurley 的框架，最有杠杆的干预点不是捐款给某个调查组织，而是降低「搜索者」的社会成本。每一次公开为 Alina Chan 或 Zeynep Tufekci 的观点辩护（即使你不完全同意），都是在给系统的搜索能力增加冗余节点。反之，每一次沉默都是在验证「围剿有效」这一策略。

📝 转录文本

Bill Gurley: Searching for Feynman

开场介绍

Silicon Valley royalty. Legendary investor Bill Gurley.

Track record's incredible.

The legend who backed Uber and Zillow, who's lived through every major tech cycle for over 25 years.

You're not just a commentator, right? You've been an operator.

I'd love to unlock this latent human potential. There's been no time in the history of the world where you can learn faster. You can increase your surface area for luck. I'm not a big fan of these dystopian narrative. The thing to do right now is to run as fast as you can.

Please welcome Bill Gurley.

主题引入

It's good to be here again. Three years ago, I gave a talk on regulatory capture and this group was quite kind and how they reacted and how that video was promoted. And I'm very happy we got that word out into the public discourse. Obviously today you hear it quite a bit.

Um, I have a different topic I'm going to talk to you about today. It's not — I'm not going to talk about AI. Um, it's a serious topic and so there might not be as many fun joke parts in it. Um, but it's something that's been weighing on my mind for the past five or six years, and I'm thankful that the team here allowed me to come to talk to you about it, and I'm hopeful that we can have an impact by getting the word out on this as well.

I'm going to start by talking to you about some catastrophes that have happened in the world and how humans normally respond to them.

案例一：Surfside 公寓倒塌（2021）

This is the Chamberlain Towers in Surfside, Florida. You may remember in June of 2021 when the building suddenly collapsed, 98 people died. What happened?

There were design areas from the very beginning. There's poor maintenance schedule. And then the board of the condominium did not listen to an inspection report that said they needed to take care of this. Three different things. That's kind of the institutional failure.

The technical failure was different. And you can see it here. This is a New York Times article. Hopefully they can push play so you can see. It's a 3D article. If they can't make it play, you'll have to watch it on your own. Um, here we go.

But the reason I want you to see this isn't to talk about the details of exactly how this collapsed. It turned out the pool deck was exposed to saltwater air. It corroded. The pool deck collapsed into the basement, which took out the structural columns, and the building came down.

But what I want you to take away from this is the New York Times and its investigative team had excruciating detail about how this happened, which comes from doing primary investigative work.

五路调查者

There were four other parallel investigations that happened.

  • NIST — the National Institute of Standards and Technology. After 9/11, they were assigned as a federal agency to go investigate what happens in a building collapse. These two individuals, Matrini, Risner and Bell, would spend five years on this.
  • Allan Kilshimer — the wolf of building collapses. He's who you call when you want to figure out what happened. The town of Surfside hired him.
  • Judge Randall would convene a grand jury in the state of Florida to investigate this.
  • 17 victim lawsuits which got put under a single class. Tropin was the defender or the litigant, and Hodsman was the judge that did that.

All of these different groups were doing investigations on their own. Sometimes running into each other, sometimes helping each other out, but all trying to get at what caused the failure.

迈阿密先驱报的英雄行动

One particularly heroic group was the Miami Herald. They had just gone through bankruptcy. They had a new executive editor named Monica Richardson, but they went after this hard.

The beat reporter, Alan Liuititz, was on the scene within two hours. Sarah Blaski would lead an investigative team. They would eventually find Don Leman, who's a professor at the University of Washington. She would join the team. They would staff up to 37 people on this. They have a 3D model that's equally impressive to the New York Times one, and they would deservedly win a Pulitzer Prize for the work that they did.

When they won it, Monica Richardson, the executive editor, who also won an award for executive editor of the year from her peers, said:

"We will continue to investigate the collapse to find answers to how this happened to ensure a tragedy like this never happens again."

Now, finding the failure cause doesn't help if you don't prevent. This is a list of some of the changes that went into all the condominium rules in Florida. And thankfully, multiple other states, especially coastal states, adopted them. So you have change that causes prevention. That's what you want to have happen when these things happen.

案例二：737 Max 坠机（2018–2019）

737 Max crash. Unfortunately, there were two crashes, October 2018 and March 2019. For those of you who don't know what happened, let me give you the really short version.

Airbus had come out with a plane that was incredibly fuel efficient and they were starting to take share from Boeing. Boeing wanted to respond. If they built a new plane, it required tons of hours of teaching and training, and that makes it harder to sell. So, they decided they would attach a fuel efficient engine to an old plane, the 737. That's how you get the name 737 Max.

The problem is the engine was too big and they had to move it forward on the wing. When you move it forward on the wing, the plane is imbalanced, and they had this problem during test flights when it would occasionally tip up. So they wrote a piece of software, secret software called MCAS, MCCast, and they put it in there without telling anybody. And if the sensor went off and told him the plane was tipping up, the autopilot would push it down.

The poor pilot that was flying the Ethiopian Airways flight, his sensor malfunctioned. The software thought that the plane was tilting up and it pushed it into the ground. That's what happened.

六路搜索者

There were many people that investigated this. I call them the six searchers.

  • The US government did a Senate Commission, a House Commission, and the DOJ went after it.
  • KNKT is the Indonesian agency that had the right to inspect the black boxes. They could tell very quickly the pilot was fighting the autopilot.
  • The press played a key role. Dominique Gates had followed Boeing for the Seattle Times for 16 years. He would win a Pulitzer for his work here. Peter Robersonson wrote a book called Flying Blind. You can tell why it would have that title.
  • 57 whistleblowers sent letters into the Senate to tell on Boeing.
  • The victim's family showed up and were ever present and put pressure on Congress to make sure something happened.
  • The head of the pilot union was very upset that they had put this piece of software in there and not told the pilots. Boeing tried to come have a sit down with the pilots union and they secretly recorded what Boeing said and gave it to the press. And then when they wouldn't respond to Boeing's request, the pilots union issued FOIA requests against Boeing. It's unheard of.

阻拦者与「围剿反应」

Now, in these situations where you have six searchers, you also have blockers. And unfortunately, in this case, both Boeing and the FAA were being unhelpful in trying to find out what happened. Boeing initially accused the pilots of not being trained well enough. The FAA refused document requests to the Senate panel.

And one thing I would tell you about these big organizations, when you put a spotlight on them, they can feel the weight of that spotlight and they circle the wagons. I think part of it's institutional. I don't think they're necessarily evil. They're just — they have a sick sense about how to respond when they're put on the spot like that.

The other thing that's interesting here is a lot of people came to think that Boeing and the FAA were working as one. Senator Ted Cruz, when he had the head of the FAA in front of the Senate, literally accused him of being captured. There's our favorite word again. And he even said to him, "Sir, do you know you don't work for Boeing?"

One of the real failures here in this case: 45 days after the first crash, almost everyone knew the MCAST software was at fault and no one grounded the plane. Boeing didn't ground the plane. The FAA didn't ground the plane. And the second crash — I mean, the first crash should have never happened because that piece of software should have been identified, which would have required retraining, but the second crash should have really never happened.

I wanted to share with you — I don't want to go through this in detail — but these are the two different committees in the House and the Senate. And I just want to highlight that they were decidedly bipartisan. DeFazio was the head of the House committee, very active. Ted Cruz and Wicker were super active. No one thought this was anything that should be partisan, nor should it be.

CAPA 方法论

It turns out the scientific community has a process they use when they want to do failure analysis. It's called CAPA — Corrective and Preventive Action. And there are five steps: you detect, you investigate, confirm root cause, correct, and prevent. And it's all about prevention. You want to stop this from happening again. But you can't skip root cause. That's a requirement. You don't know how to fix it if you don't know actually what happened.

CAPA is required by law by the FDA in pharmaceuticals and medical devices. The aerospace industry has regulations that require this type of process if you have a failure.

案例三：Hurricane Katrina（2005）

Now, let's move on. Hurricane Katrina 2005. Look at these stats. They're horrible. 1,800 deaths, 400,000 people displaced, damage $125 billion.

What happened here? Well, the Army Corps of Engineers that built the levees want you to believe that the water went over the levees, but that's, you know, an act of God, natural disaster. But this was only a hurricane or category 3 level hurricane. What in fact happened was the levees gave way from underneath. They washed under. And that's what's unfortunate — this was a preventable accident as well.

As with these others, you have searchers and blockers.

  • The House had a commission. The Senate had a commission.
  • The press played a key role. Mark Slestein and John Mcuade had written a series three years earlier about how this could happen. They would win two Pulitzers. I actually had a chance to talk with John about it.
  • The NSF, the National Science Foundation, cared so much about this, they did a bake off to have another team doing investigation, and these two professors from the University of California led that.
  • And then the state of Louisiana hired a team out of LSU, and they all investigated.

I talked to John. Sometimes once again running into each other, sometimes blocking, sometimes sharing notes, but they all came to the exact same conclusion — that this was a man-made error.

被俘获的 ASCE

The US Corps of Engineers is the one that built the levees, and they naturally, as I talked about, are going to act as blockers. What's weird here is they asked the American Society of Civil Engineers if they would join the investigation, join the internal investigation. They paid them a million dollars. And over time they would just get kind of encapsulated inside the Army Corps and become blockers themselves.

When this dust all settled, Raymond Seed, the professor from UCal, he wrote a 42-page report to the ASCE explaining all the times that they blocked. That document's on the internet. You can go see it. Like 42 pages, that's a lot of blocking.

The other thing that happened here that's great is prevention. These different investigations led to 90 recommendations. Those changes were made and the seawalls have held. It was $15 billion. Seawalls have held now for 20 years, which is great.

案例四：Fukushima（2011）

Let me move through a couple more real quickly. This is Fukushima. 2,200 deaths, 154,000 displaced, 200 billion in cleanup.

What happened here is pretty simple. The seawall in front of the nuclear plant was 5.7 m. The water went over the wall, took out the generators, the cores started to melt down. There was no way to cool them, and the disaster happened.

There were internal documents that showed they expected tsunamis in a 30-year window to be in the 10 to 15 m range and they buried the report. So, if you had simply raised the wall, this never happens. But it didn't happen. And in a lot of these cases, there's a combination of a technical failure and an institutional failure. The technical failure is what happens to the product or the surface of the building or the seawall. The institutional failure — why did the humans let that become a weak point here?

As with the others, there are searchers and blockers.

  • The press played a role. Martin Fler at the New York Times spent 20 years in the Tokyo bureau. He would be a Pulitzer finalist. Mr. Yorimitsu took the third-place paper and added 20 investigators to his staff to go after this. Had a huge impact, won two awards.
  • The Japanese citizens were out in force both protesting and filing claims.
  • And just like the FAA and Boeing, TEPCO was the company running the power plant. NISA was the regulator, and they blocked and they blocked and they got in the way. And in fact, the failure was partially just a result of regulatory capture once again — that they weren't playing the right role of regulator and regulated. They had almost become friends.

英雄 Kurokawa

Now, the real hero of this story is a guy named Kiyoshi Kurokawa. He was asked by the Japanese Parliament to lead the first ever private investigation they've ever had in their country's history. And they had a lot of power. They were told that no one on the committee could have any institutional connection to the regulator or the power company. They had the full authority to go after anybody in any way. And they had a ton of meetings.

Kurokawa, when he kicked this off, said he had three mandates that he wanted to adhere to: 1. He cared about human safety. He didn't want it to be a battle about nuclear energy. 2. He said the investigation should definitely result in recommendations. 3. He knew the weight of this because of Three Mile Island and Chernobyl from a global perspective, and he cared about that.

Now, interestingly, he's a medical doctor. He's not a nuclear physicist, but he led this commission with a level of grace and professionalism that makes him a hero from my perspective. All these searchers are heroes from my perspective.

He would publish a report 7 months later. Interestingly, they chose to publish it in English first because they were worried about global transparency and how they were perceived. And in the first sentence, he says:

"The accident at the power plant cannot be regarded as a natural disaster. It was profoundly man-made, and it could have and should have been prevented."

Powerful.

案例五：Challenger 航天飞机灾难（1986）

One last one. This is the Challenger Shuttle disaster. January 1986. I remember where I was. It was a Tuesday. I was in college. It was a long time ago.

Everyone, if you've seen the documentaries, you know what happened here. The O-rings on the solid rocket boosters weren't designed for cold. Turns out it was cold that morning in Florida, and that flaw caused a problem. Unfortunately, the subcontractor that had worked on that piece tried to object the night before that they shouldn't launch, and he got shut down. So, you have a technical failure and institutional failure once again.

费曼登场

Now, I could talk about a lot of searchers and blockers, but I'm just going to talk about one — Richard Feynman, who was already mentioned during the All-In conference this week.

Richard Feynman was a professor at Caltech. When the shuttle Challenger blew up, Ronald Reagan created the Rogers Commission and they added mostly insiders — Neil Armstrong, they had astronauts, they had generals, they had people from Washington, people from NASA executives, but someone had the idea that they should put Feynman on there. And I think they wanted like a stamp of approval from a physicist. The good news is it made a lot of sense. He's one of the most famous scientists of all time. He won a Nobel Prize and he worked on the Manhattan Project, so he had a lot of credibility.

What they didn't know is he's fiercely independent. He's highly truth-seeking, and he has zero time for unnecessary diplomacy. They didn't know that was coming.

He didn't want to do it. He said he hated Washington. I kind of get that. His wife talked him into it, but once he did it, he cleared his schedule. He took everything off his calendar for 6 months into the future. None of the other commission members did that, and he started doing investigation on his own before he ever went to Washington. He's showing up at NASA facilities and asking to meet with people. And when he got to Washington, none of the other members wanted to act that way. In fact, Neil Armstrong told him, "You know, we just evaluate. We don't investigate." It was too late. He was already doing it.

三个费曼趣事

Now, three fun facts about this:

  1. There's a famous story. If you watch any of the documentaries where Rogers runs into Neil Armstrong in the bathroom and says, "Feynman's being a real pain in the ass."
  2. He staged a stunt on live television. He found some material that was similar to the O-ring, and in front of everybody, he dipped it in his cold ice water in front of him and pulled it out and cracked it to show the failure. It infuriated the rest of the commission.
  3. When he submitted all his notes to the commission, they wrote a final report. They really kind of smoothed over everything, and he was pissed. And so he called Rogers and said, "You know what? Take my name off of it." Of course, he'd already done the thing on TV. There's no way they could take their name off of it. They caved. Appendix F to the report is all of his notes included in their entirety.

转向：为什么讲这些？——COVID-19

Now, why am I talking to you about all these catastrophes and searchers and blockers and heroes like Kurokawa and Feynman? Because I want to talk to you about COVID-19.

In December of 2019, COVID-19 caused 15 million deaths, disrupted every life on the planet, and cost our globe $45 trillion. It was particularly hard on children. You've read about learning loss. My kids were in high school and college and missed three years of the most formative years of your life. I never want to live through this thing again in my life.

But guess what? For all the other catastrophes, I told you what root cause is. 6 years later, we don't know. So, forgive me if I'm unafraid of what some AI guy's chatbot is going to do to humanity when you can't tell me what this thing already did. My P(second COVID) is way higher than my P(doom). And if their models are so smart, tell me what happened here. Let's get them working on this problem.

规模对比

I want to put this in perspective. I've added up all the deaths and cost of the five catastrophes I walked through with you and you get to 5,000 deaths and $349 billion. COVID is 3,000 times bigger than that.

Feynman in one of the documentaries said someone was telling him he needed to be nicer, and he said, "But seven people died." If you have to get through niceties and seek truth when seven people died, how are you supposed to behave when 15 million people die?

I can take it even further. I add up all plane accidents, all hurricanes, all nuclear accidents, all building collapses, all space accidents. You still only get one-third of the way to what happened with COVID. We should want to know what happened here so we can stop this from happening again.

没有发生的事

Here's what didn't happen. And this is shocking because all these wonderful people, all these well-intended people did this in the other cases which were much smaller. And they did it in a purposeful and meaningful way.

  • There's no committed newsroom with over 30 investigators on COVID. None of the major papers did that.
  • There was no Gates or Schelestein or Flacker — like a dogged investigative reporter that had the backing of his newsroom going after this.
  • No bipartisan Senate congressional committees like you had in Katrina and 737 Max.
  • You didn't have a standalone investigation with someone like Feynman or Kurokawa.
  • There was no science-funded investigation. The NIST and the NSF launched them in these other two cases. NIH didn't fund a third-party investigation here.
  • And no massive victims lawsuit to figure out what happened.

谁是「专家」——还是阻拦者？

So, what went wrong? I'm going to share some thoughts with you, and I want you to be aware of a couple pieces of information that I think are kind of new or new to be understood.

I want to make one qualification. This has been bothering me for a long time. I've read a ton. I'm sure there are people that are smarter than me on this, but I'm gotta be top 1% in terms of how much information I've consumed.

The first thing I would tell you is these five people were relied on as experts:

  • Francis Collins
  • Anthony Fauci
  • Peter Daszak — runs something called the EcoHealth Alliance. It's a nonprofit that did virology research.
  • Jeremy Farrar — the head of the Wellcome Trust that funded a lot of this stuff and went on to work at the WHO.
  • Ralph Baric — the top virologist in the US at the University of North Carolina.

What I'm here to tell you is they weren't experts. They were blockers. They acted exactly like FAA and Boeing and NASA did in these other situations.

四条判定他们是阻拦者的理由

  1. They're virology insiders. So, as I said, there's going to be a natural instinct to circle the wagons when someone shines a spotlight on you.
  2. They led a misinformation campaign to take us off the lead and to tell us not to search. I'm going to tell you about that in a second.
  3. They were all outspoken gain-of-function advocates prior to COVID coming along. And if you don't know what gain of function is — it's when you take a virus and you make it intentionally more dangerous to animals or humans. They felt that that was smart to do. Obama had outlawed it. They were constantly promoting to try and make it happen more often. Fauci in 2011 wrote an article in the Washington Post, an editorial, where he said the pros outweigh the cons. Now, if you talk to any behavioral psychologist, if you've told the world "we should definitely do this and the pros outweigh the cons," there's zero chance you can be impartial when it comes to figuring out what happened. Because to go home at night and think that something you did contributed to the death of 15 million people would be impossible to go to bed. Your brain's much more likely to trick you into just thinking it didn't happen. You wouldn't be allowed on a jury if you had that kind of bias.
  4. They didn't search. I tell you they stopped searching, but they never started searching and they should have been searching. They should still be searching.

谁在真正搜索——五位英雄

There are people that did search. They're not at large institutions.

  • DRASTIC — a loosely affiliated group of scientists that come together and share information. They have a website. You should follow them. It's like 20 Nick Shirley's that are all virologists or scientists.
  • US Right to Know — a nonprofit that's filed the majority of the FOIA claims here. You can donate to them. I have.

But I want to tell you about these five heroes. They're heroes of mine that have been actively trying to find out what happened from the very beginning.

  1. Alina Chan — one of the first molecular biologists that realized that the virus looks like it was designed for humans. She wrote a book with Matt Ridley. And here's some really good news: in the past couple of years, the New York Times has published two of her op-eds. I would rather it be the investigative team at the New York Times, but it's a start. They're really good. Read both of them.
  2. Katherine Eban — the first person to really stick their neck out and say, "We're not looking at this the right way." She published an article, oddly in Vanity Fair, titled The Fight to Discover COVID Origins. I think the title is important because the fight was about the discovery process.
  3. Emily Kopp — worked for US Right to Know. She may know more than anybody. She's been the one uncovering all of these documents, and we've been getting more and more documents each and every day. So, we're learning more.
  4. Zeynep Tufekci — a professor at Princeton who also writes sometimes for the New York Times. I'm going to tell you something she did recently that I think is super important.
  5. Alison Young — wrote a book called Pandora's Gamble that looks at all of the lab leak failures that have happened prior to COVID, which is an interesting and relevant data point to study if you want to consider whether or not that was part of the problem.

These five women have been attacked for sticking their neck out. Some of them directly by the men on the previous slide. And I think that's completely unreasonable. I think they're heroes.

两个必须知道的信息点

Now, there's two things I want to tell you about and then I'll wrap it up. There's two pieces of information you should know about.

一、被制造的共识

I said earlier that the five experts/blockers had created a misinformation campaign to take us off the lead. I think that's an understatement on what they created — a highly successful misinformation campaign to convince everyone that animal spillover was a decidedly determined cause of this and that anyone that considered a lab leak — even thought about it or asked a single question — was a conspiracy theorist. And they were successful at it.

They leveraged the scientific journal community, which they understood. The Proximal Origins paper went out like this — this thing was written in like a week. There's no way you did an investigation. They just wanted to get it out there. And then the Lancet had a similar one. These papers have been cited over and over again. If you try and like go through Wikipedia, you just always end up going back to them. So they were highly successful.

They also somehow made this thing partisan. Using the word "conspiracy theory" with Trump back. I don't know how it happened, but they were able to get people in their surveys and polls — "What do you think caused COVID?" — and if you're Democrat or Republican, you have a different answer. That's nuts. Like there's no way that should be relevant in this discussion.

Recently, more and more of this information's come out, and so you have more understanding of how they came to write these papers, and you can see inconsistencies between what they think and what they wrote.

Zeynep put this on Twitter 45 days ago and I think she chose her words very carefully. She said:

"Incontrovertible proof of a conspiracy to cover up and deny the possibility it well may be a lab mishap orchestrated from the highest levels of the scientific establishment and a self-serving group of scientists who deliberately misled the public."

Those are strong words. She put that up 45 days ago. It has 400,000 views and zero community notes. At least today. Maybe tomorrow we'll have some.

Katherine Eban was more terse but equally opinionated. She calls it manufactured consensus. If you feel strongly you think you know what happened in COVID, you need to understand that this happened. It took people off the scent.

二、DEFUSE 提案

Three years after COVID, the DRASTIC team uncovered this document. It's called the DEFUSE proposal. Who's heard of the DEFUSE proposal? Raise your hand. This is nuts. Look, it's like three people. Okay.

No major journals ever covered the DEFUSE proposal. There was a survey of scientists who said "animal spillover" as the cause, and they were asked "Have you heard of DEFUSE?" Only 22% had. 78% said they had never heard of it.

What's the DEFUSE proposal? Three years after COVID, DRASTIC uncovered this document. You can go download it. It's real. It was a proposal by EcoHealth Alliance, Peter Daszak's company, that connects the top virologist at Duke in North Carolina with the top virologist at Wuhan, the bat lady, Jun Lee. And there's a proposal that they're going to insert a furin cleavage site at the S1/S2 junction of a bat coronavirus because they think it'll make it more viral in animals. And it's in a document.

I went to AI. I said, "Let's do a clean session AI." That means don't look at anything I've ever told you before. "If I were interested in helping to solve the origin of COVID and I was using the scientific principles of CAPA to guide me, how would I react to finding the DEFUSE proposal?"

Look at these answers: direct investigational lead, highly critical, major investigative lead. Yes, that would be a high priority piece of evidence. Primary document evidence, highest tier evidence class.

Most people don't know about this thing. And I would make an assertion: had this document been exposed in January of 2020, we would have had a very different conversation back then. But it wasn't. The searchers are aware of the document. Rand Paul's aware of the document. Hopefully now you're all aware of the document.

One other thing I need to say. If you ask these AI bots, "What would you do next in your CAPA process?" — they say you would go after documents at Duke University and University of North Carolina. And the searchers have been doing that. Unfortunately, the University of North Carolina and the state of North Carolina are blockers. They're refusing to deliver the documents. And I would encourage — if any of you have connections to UNC or know anyone on the board, I would encourage you to make them think about whatever they're protecting and whether that's more important than preventing the next one of these.

If you want to learn more about this, Matt Ridley just did an interview last March with Jay Bhattacharya at NIH. It's a great way to catch up on everything people have been learning.

号召：支持搜索者

As we look forward — and this is where I'd love your help — let's support the searchers. We have to find a root cause to this thing. We don't want this to happen again.

I can't tell you that I speak for science like Anthony Fauci did, but I can tell you I speak for scientific inquiry. There's no one that should be telling you you can't search. That makes no sense whatsoever. You're not a bad person if you search. You're a good person if you search.

You have to move through and around the blockers. I don't think you want to attack the blockers. I think Rand Paul's making a mistake making it about prosecution. We should make it about root cause and prevention.

This isn't partisan and should have never been. If your view on what caused COVID is because of who you vote for, please reconsider that.

I would ask the newsrooms to dive in, be like Monica Richardson, and then let's put a truly independent commission together. Let's find our Kurokawa or Feynman.

I'm going to leave you with a quote. I'm way over time. I'm going to leave you with a quote that's attributed to Plato that sums up what I've been thinking here:

"We can easily forgive a child who is afraid of the dark. The real tragedy in life is when men are afraid of the light."

Thank you.

问答环节

Wow. I got to ask a question. Stay out here. No. No. Stay out here. Stay out here. Can I do a question?

Another standing ovation here. Um, Bill, wow. Uh, you put a tremendous amount of effort into this. Uh, we've known each other for 30 years. I've seen you emotional, I think, two other times. One was a Jason Isbell concert. Another time you your top set got counterfeited or something. But this is emotional and this is personal for you. What they did to our kids is really clearly impacted you. Maybe you could talk about why it's so important that we consider the damage that was done to this generation.

Well, I mean, for me, it's all back to prevention. Like, you have to stop it from happening again. I have zero confidence right now that if another pandemic started tomorrow, we'd have any better way to navigate it. I think we might do worse —

because of the misinformation campaigns cause a lack of trust. Next time you're not going to listen to them.

There's not going to be ability for anybody to lead. And I'm struck, as you can tell by the presentation, by the difference between the attitude of the people that searched in these other catastrophes, how they were viewed as heroes, and what happened to the people that were looking here.

Yes. And you repeatedly talk about the power of journalism, Pulitzers and investigative journalism specifically, which is different than clickbait journalism. There is something very virtuous about investigative journalism and those type of journals. Maybe you could speak to that and then explain to us why people didn't go after the Pulitzer here, why they didn't put a large amount of resources to — because that seems incredibly suspicious. And I seem to have a recollection of Fauci getting a pardon, which also seems to be a red flag that you didn't bring up. So take those two issues.

Well, yeah. So on the investigative part, I mean, one of the reasons I mentioned all the Pulitzers was just to highlight that fact, right? There's a wonderful video on YouTube, if you're interested in this topic, at the Brookings Institute — three or four of the ladies that I showed led a panel to talk about why the press missed this. And both Katherine and Emily Kopp pointed back to the misinformation campaign by the virology experts and how they kind of made it like a faux pas to actually ask questions. But considering the scale of the outcome, it's just horrible that that happened. And I would once again encourage them — like, there's still work to do. There's still information coming out. We're getting closer. Like, come on in.

Yeah. And there's something really tragic here in that if you asked questions this time, you were put into a conspiracy theorist who didn't trust the experts, and you were the damage.

Yeah.

For asking questions. This is pure evil.

It's crazy.

I mean, it's pure evil to take the people who just say, "Hey, is it possible this came out of the Wuhan?" — guys have, if you in fact funded gain of research, why is that such a hard question for them to answer?

Well, I said — I think a behavioral psychologist would tell you you're able to fool yourself to keep your own sanity.

Yeah. Now, I'll just end with this. Knowing what you've known — you've put thousands of hours into this. You and I have been talking about this for three or four years now, and this has been a passion project of yours, and I really appreciate you sharing it with the audience. What do you believe, based on what you know now, is the most likely scenario of how COVID originated, and what we can learn from it, just based on you being in the —

I would tell you I intentionally didn't take a side on that here. Because we haven't found root cause. And I would celebrate — you know, anyone that's 100% convinced it's animal spillover, to do research there — I funded US Right to Know. If you want to go search for the animals, I'll fund that, too. You should know China has tested 80,000 animals and not found a single crossover. And they have a huge incentive to find one if they could.

Yes. The wet market theory would be — absolutely free them from having fingerprints —

Right. So there's a massive incentive. Why hasn't — But if you want to keep looking, go look. Fauci in these documents that have been uncovered admitted there were multiple cases prior to the spreader event at the wet market, which also is another problem you have to deal with.

Yeah. Uh, listen, Bill, I think this could wind up being the most important work of your life, and as your friend, I'm just in awe of your passion and your doggedness. And any way we can support it — I think everybody here and in the audience at All-In would love to donate to more research being done. So, we'll tweet that in the future. Let's give it up one more time for Bill Gurley.

Thank you.

Thank you, brother. You crush it.

# 关于 Bill Gurley「寻找费曼」演讲的系统性观察
## 一、这是一场关于「搜索算法失效」的演讲，而非关于新冠
表面上 Gurley 在讲根因分析，但更深层的结构是：**他在用费曼的方法论去寻找一个费曼**。这是一个递归自指的问题——当科学体制本身成为被调查对象时，谁来做调查者？他列举的五个灾难中，都有独立于当事机构的「第三方节点」（NIST、NSF、参议院、学术委员会、独立记者），构成了一个分布式验证网络。而新冠事件的独特之处在于：**所有本该充当独立验证节点的机构，都与被调查对象共享同一个知识网络**。
用密码学的语言说，这是典型的**拜占庭容错崩溃**：当超过 1/3 的验证者被同一利益污染，整个共识系统失效。Gurley 三年前讲「监管俘获」（regulatory capture），今天讲的其实是**科学俘获**（scientific capture）——一个更危险的升级版本，因为科学声称自己是终极仲裁者。
## 二、一个几乎无人提及的观察：性别的完美镜像
Gurley 展示的五位「阻拦者」（Collins、Fauci、Daszak、Farrar、Baric

item.title: [Lex Clips] Fraud in psychiatry - The Rosenhan Experiment | Andrew Scull and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个"必要的谎言"：欺诈如何催生了正确的改革

这段访谈埋着一个精妙的递归悖论：Rosenhan 的实验本身是一场学术欺诈，但正是它推动了 DSM-III 的诞生——而 DSM-III 的核心缺陷（可靠性有余、有效性不足），恰恰又是如果 Rosenhan 实验是真的，它本会揭露的问题。换句话说，精神医学被一个假证据推着走上了改革之路，而这条路最终产生的系统，正是那个假证据本该批判的对象。制度性变革不需要真相，只需要一个可信的故事——这一点在科学史、法律史、金融史里反复出现，但很少有案例像这样自我指涉。

可靠性 vs. 有效性：一个被严重低估的跨领域裂缝

Scull 提到的 reliability/validity 之分，看似是精神病学的内部术语，但它其实是现代文明所有分类系统的通病。想一想： - LLM 基准测试（MMLU、HumanEval）高度可靠——同一模型每次得分接近——但它们衡量的是"智能"吗？ - FICO 信用分具备极高的银行间一致性，但它究竟测的是"还款能力"，还是"过去被信贷系统接纳的程度"？ - 大学 GPA 在不同评分者之间可复现，但它测的是学习，还是服从？

DSM 的"打勾诊断"和这些系统同构：当我们无法直接测量一个真实存在但难以定义的东西时，我们发明一套可复现的替代物，然后集体假装替代物就是本体。药厂、保险公司、患者家属之所以拥抱 DSM，不是因为它真、而是因为它稳定——稳定的错误比不稳定的真相更适合搭建产业。这是一种协调陷阱（coordination trap），和法币、学历、编程语言标准一样：一旦建立，就没有人有单方面推翻它的激励。

那个让我意外的观察：Insel 的 200 亿美元寓言

$20B 花完之后精神病人的处境毫无改善——这不是"科学失败"，而是抽象层错位（level-of-abstraction error）的典型病例。它和阿尔茨海默的淀粉样蛋白假说、癌症"战争"、甚至早期 AI 的符号主义研究是同一种失败：假设疾病的因果层就是可见的物质层。如果精神障碍不是一个"东西"、而是一个过程（就像 18 世纪的 "fever" 一样是一堆不同现象的集合名词），那么无论对着大脑投入多少神经科学与遗传学，都会像用望远镜研究一段音乐——工具本身没错，只是问错了问题。

一个跨领域的连接：18 世纪的 "fever" 和今天的 "AI hallucination"

Scull 类比 DSM 标签像 18 世纪的 "dropsy" 和 "fever"——把一堆不同的东西装进一个词——这不是历史怀旧，而是现在进行时。"AI 幻觉"、"注意力经济"、"心理健康危机"、"algorithmic bias" 这些词都在扮演同样的角色：一个尚未被科学分解的语言容器，方便我们组织资金、政策和情感反应。每个时代都有它的 "fever"——语言先于科学，产业先于理解，改革先于真相。Rosenhan 的欺诈之所以能改变精神病学，是因为它给了当时的 "fever" 一个可以被处理的形状。今天的 AI 讨论正处于同一阶段——我们讨论的不是一个已被理解的现象，而是一个等待被分解的词。

📝 转录文本

The Rosenhan Fraud and the Birth of DSM-III

Psychiatrists had a very hard time agreeing with one another about what was wrong with somebody. And that became embarrassingly clear — first in the professional literature, which outsiders didn't read, and then via a very famous study that's a scientific fraud by David Rosenhan called On Being Sane in Insane Places, where he claimed to have sent in pseudo-patients to the hospital, and they all were diagnosed as schizophrenic — all but one diagnosed as schizophrenic, the other as somebody with bipolar disorder. And they were fake patients.

So, almost in a panic after that study appeared in Science, and because there was an abundant professional literature from the 1960s showing the same thing — that diagnosis was a very erratic process — the DSM-III task force led by Robert Spitzer, who was then at Columbia, was explicitly set up to try to create a sort of tick-the-boxes approach to deciding which box a patient belonged in. Were you schizophrenic? Were you this type of schizophrenic or that type of schizophrenic? Were you manic-depressive or bipolar? Did you have various forms of depression?

The Symptom-Checklist System and Its Stakeholders

And to construct those boxes, what they relied upon was a list of symptoms. And if you had more than a certain number — if you had more than six of ten, six of ten or more symptoms of a certain sort — you could be diagnosed with major depression, for example.

So, that system came into being. It was partially embedded because it appealed to drug companies who were developing drugs to treat these various disorders. It appealed to insurance companies, because it gave them a stable basis to look at. It appealed, as diagnosis always does, to patients and their families who are scrambling to deal with these enormous upsets in the mental life of either themselves or a family member. So it provided some sense of certainty around diagnosis.

But that was always based simply on symptoms — in the way an 18th-century doctor might diagnose dropsy or diagnose some other kind of disease or fever, for example. Well, fever and other diseases they talked about in the 18th century are really a constellation of very different things under one label. And I think that's what is turning out to be true of the DSM labels.

Reliability vs. Validity

But that approach was really all that psychiatry could come up with if it wanted to make sure whether you were in Walla Walla or New York or San Francisco or Atlanta, you reached the same conclusion faced by the same patient — that you had a reliable diagnostic system.

That didn't mean necessarily it was a valid diagnostic system, if you understand the distinction between validity and reliability. Reliability means you and I faced with the same sets of facts reach the same conclusion, but that conclusion may or may not reflect the underlying reality of things, right?

So you had this diagnostic system, and it went through various iterations. Each time it went through an iteration, the number of possible psychiatric disorders you could get grew and grew and grew. And it became difficult to believe in some of those categories, shall we say — that they were really illnesses rather than some sort of social construct.

The Search for Underlying Pathology

But beyond that, psychiatrists wanted to be more like other medical doctors — to root their diagnoses in an understanding of the underlying pathology of the disorder. What was it that caused people to become schizophrenic? The sense was: if we could grasp that, we'd have a better handle on how to attack it, how to treat it.

And when DSM-5 was mooted — the fifth edition, in the early 2000s — NIMH, then under the leadership of Steven Hyman, who's at Harvard now, and succeeded by Thomas Insel, who ruled NIMH for about 13 years, the two of them had pushed psychiatry and psychiatric research in a very particular direction. On the one hand, towards understanding the genetics of mental illness, and on the other, to looking at what the new discipline of neuroscience could contribute to understanding things.

Both of them were heavily invested in the idea that mental illness was brain disease. And if it was brain disease, then the question was: what was making the mechanism here go awry? What was causing people's emotions, or their cognitive skills, or their sense of the world, to become so disordered? And they invested a lot of money in that approach.

Insel's Confession: $20 Billion and No Improvement

When Insel stepped down, he gave an interview actually to somebody at MIT — and he's repeated it since in a book he wrote about his experiences — where he said:

"Well, you know, as I look back on my 13 years, I funded an enormous amount of really cool scientific research. I funded geneticists, and I funded neuroscientists, and they did a lot of really interesting science. And after spending 20 billion dollars, the lot of the mentally ill has improved not one bit."

Lex: Wow.

Scull: Which was a pretty devastating statement, I thought.

Lex: And NIMH is National Institute of Mental Health?

Scull: National Institute of Mental Health. Yes, I shouldn't resort to jargon. [laughter]
