这段访谈埋着一个精妙的递归悖论：Rosenhan 的实验本身是一场学术欺诈，但正是它推动了 DSM-III 的诞生——而 DSM-III 的核心缺陷（可靠性有余、有效性不足），恰恰又是**如果 Rosenhan 实验是真的**，它本会揭露的问题。换句话说，精神医学被一个假证据推着走上了改革之路，而这条路最终产生的系统，正是那个假证据本该批判的对象。**制度性变革不需要真相，只需要一个可信的故事**——这一点在科学史、法律史、金融史里反复出现，但很少有案例像这样自我指涉。
## 可靠性 vs. 有效性：一个被严重低估的跨领域裂缝
Scull 提到的 reliability/validity 之分，看似是精神病学的内部术语，但它其实是**现代文明所有分类系统的通病**。想一想： - LLM 基准测试（MMLU、HumanEval）高度可靠——同一模型每次得分接近——但它们衡量的是"智能"吗？ - FICO 信用分具备极高的银行间一致性，但它究竟测的是"还款能力"，还是"过去被信贷系统接纳的程度"？ - 大学 GPA 在不同评分者之间

item.title: [Latent Space] A Worm With 302 Neurons Inspired Their Architecture — Ramin Hasani, Liquid AI
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"偏置反转定律"：小模型要更"生物"，大模型要更"愚钝"

Hasani 抛出了一个反直觉的架构学：模型越小，越需要加入结构性偏置（反馈回路、门控、递归）；模型越大，反而必须"去偏置化"，让架构回归到最朴素的 1D 卷积与注意力堆叠。

这颠覆了大多数人对"复杂问题需要复杂结构"的默认假设。它揭示了一个隐藏的真相：规模本身就是一种通用先验。当参数足够多、数据足够多，任何精巧的归纳偏置都会变成天花板；而在小模型的贫瘠世界里，架构必须"聪明地偷懒"，用生物学式的递归结构来弥补参数量的匮乏。

这与生物演化诡异地对称——线虫用 302 个神经元的高度专业化结构击败了任何工业机器人，而人类大脑的规模让它可以承担"通用"的奢侈。规模决定了智能可以有多"不加设计"。

二、跨领域连接：期货交易者的随机微积分 × 蠕虫神经元 × 视网膜的"差分感知"

播客中隐藏着一个几乎无人察觉的三角连接：

  • 主持人自曝曾是期权交易员，用随机微积分求解连续时间的 SDE；
  • Liquid AI 的核心数学是连续时间一阶微分方程建模的神经元；
  • Hasani 顺口提到了一个惊人的神经生理学事实：人眼看到的不是"帧"，而是两帧之间的差分（differential）——你的大脑处理的是变化量，而不是状态量。

三者共享同一个数学骨架：导数即真理。Black-Scholes 模型的核心是价格变化率，视网膜的核心是亮度梯度，而 Liquid 神经网络的核心是 dh/dt。这暗示了一个更深的猜想——当代 Transformer 处理的是"状态序列"（离散 token），而下一代真正接近生物的智能，可能是处理"变化率序列"的架构。SSM 之所以在音频上碾压 Transformer，正是因为音频本质上是连续变化率而非离散状态。

这也解释了为什么 Hasani 敢押注 photonics（光子计算）：当序列计算以光速进行，"非线性递归"就不再是硬件彩票的输家，而是可以直接读取物理世界的"微分感受器"。

三、意外观察：真正的商业奇迹发生在"车里的 100 美金芯片上"，而不是万卡集群里

行业注意力集中在数据中心的 GPU 战争，但 Hasani 揭示了一个几乎被主流叙事屏蔽的真相：

  • 每年 3-4 亿台 AI PC 出货，其中 1 亿颗 AMD 芯片；
  • 奔驰将在今年把 Liquid 模型部署到全北美 Gen3 车型上，运行在约 100 美金的芯片上；
  • Apple/Galaxy AI 目前 90% 的调用仍然打到云端——不是因为不想本地跑，而是没人有能力做到生产级的端侧可靠性。

这里藏着一个更深的洞见："云 vs 端"不是技术之争，而是毛利率之争。当你有 40 亿终端用户，云端推理成本就是财务黑洞——本地化不是为了隐私（那是话术），而是为了保住毛利。这解释了为什么 Liquid 的商业护城河不是"更聪明的模型"，而是"更能装进 600MB 里且不会热失控的模型"。

四、隐藏的下一代金矿：不是推理 token，是"定制化 token"

Frontier Labs 靠推理 token 赚钱的时代正在到达平台期。Hasani 精准命名了下一个战场：customization tokens——从预训练、中训练、后训练到 RL、数据生成的整条链路，都可以被 token 化定价。

有趣的是，这与"主权 AI"叙事形成了神秘共振：每一次企业定制化，本质上都是在把通用智能"局域化"成企业自己的知识生态。这与生物学惊人相似——通用基因组通过表观遗传的定制化，产生了肝细胞、神经元、免疫细胞。未来的 AI 经济，可能不是模型工厂，而是"表观遗传"工厂。

📝 转录文本

Intro

[music] Okay, we're in a remote studio with our new head of editorial, Richard. Say hi. [laughter]

Hi, everyone. Dialing in from the UK. And Raine, uh, CEO of Liquid. Welcome. Thanks for having me.

Most people when they've heard about Liquid, they know about LFM or they've heard of LFS. They maybe haven't personally tried it. The other interesting, I guess, public data point is that it is very inspired by worm DNA or something. I never really pay much attention to that because obviously I think that that's an analogy — but you can tell us how seriously to take it.

From Vienna to the C. elegans Worm

Yeah, absolutely. Well, you know, when we started our kind of research about 12 years ago, we wanted to see if we can bring inspirations from brains back to machine learning. So that's where everything got started.

And then when we started looking into human brain, we realized — when I say we, my current CTO and myself — we started back in Vienna University of Technology. It's called TUNI. So I started my PhD. My co-founder was a master student there. And what we wanted to do, we wanted to understand how we can bring in like continuous-time math inside machine learning kind of systems. And that's what we did.

So we basically look into neurons, how neurons exchange information with each other. And this was governed by very simplistic first-order differential equations, and that's kind of how the nervous system dynamics are actually working at the level of neurons and synapses.

And then our first focus — we wanted to start with human brain, but human brain has spiking neurons and it's very difficult to actually learn. We still don't know anything about human brain, how computation actually happens. We know a lot more now about a fruit fly's brain, but we don't know that much about human brain.

But I can tell you that we got to this animal because we wanted to do it first principles. We got to this animal, C. elegans worm, which has only 302 nerve cells in its body, and it's 2 mm long. And one of the nice things about the worm was the fact that its neurons behave very similar to artificial neurons — they don't spike. That graded behavior in these neurons, in neuroscience they call it electrotonic behavior of a neuron.

And that behavior was very interesting for us because if you build systems inspired by the brain of this worm, you would be able to build very continuous-time kind of systems, and they're differentiable. So you can do backprop and all sorts of other things on top of these things. This was the model organism that we were looking at at that time.

Why the Worm Matters

The most fascinating thing for us was that with 302 neurons it could control 95 muscle cells better than any robotic systems that we had on the planet — and this is 2016 and 2017.

Another interesting thing about the worm is the fact that 600 million years ago, humans actually got split from this worm in the tree of evolution. So whatever neuroscientists are discovering about the brain of this worm or the cell structure of this worm is actually transferable to humans as well to some extent — 78% similarity to human genome. So it is actually a very very important worm for us, and so far it has won four Nobel prizes for humanity.

So it's a very popular animal. And that's why our research — we started even working with neuroscientists themselves that are working on the brain of these neurons.

Building Liquid Neural Networks

So long story short, we mathematically modeled how two neurons exchange information based on the inspirations that we know about the brain of the worm. And we got those mathematics and we built something called liquid neural networks — liquid time-constant neural networks. Liquid was basically for flexibility, because one of the things that we realized is that these are highly nonlinear systems governed by differential equations in a forward pass, and they are differentiable. So you can actually run them backward pass and you can learn them really nicely because of the multiple feedback structures that they had. They are really representation learners — they learn representation from data really well.

One of the things that we realized is that with a small subset of these neural networks, you can control robots very similar to how the worm itself was doing it. And when I say small subset, we were talking about tens to hundreds of neurons. We're talking about very very small subsets of neurons.

We got very excited, so we started applying these things to controlling robots. On the robot you don't have that much compute, so the fact that you can actually pack that much intelligence to control autonomously a kind behavior inside a robot — that was a very attractive feature for us. So efficiency of this computation and bringing intelligence into the smallest unit of compute became a research topic for us.

The MIT Chapter and Daniela Rus

And then in 2017, Professor Daniela Rus of MIT — she's one of my co-founders as well. She's the mother of robotics arguably. She has done tremendous contribution to the field of robotics and distributed robots and soft robots as a whole. She started learning about our research and she was blown away, and she said, "Okay, you guys, would you consider coming to MIT and continue this research in real world, really applying this technology into let's say cars and drones and many different kinds of vehicles?"

And we were like — both Matias and I — we joined MIT. So since 2017 I've been working with Daniela. I met my fourth co-founder Alexander Amini. Alexander was a PhD student at that time at MIT. So Matias and I were both there, and the four of us since 2017 started working on these topics of continuous-time dynamical systems and continuous-time learning systems, and the scaling of all of these things, applying them into many different domains.

Predictive sequence models — sequence modeling became kind of our thing. We started doing contributions, and in this field of continuous time it became a little bit better because a lot of other researchers from different places — like from Yoshua Bengio's lab, David Duvenaud's lab from University of Toronto, and some people from Stanford — everybody was contributing to this field of continuous-time dynamical systems.

This was like imagine recurrent neural networks that are discretized dynamical systems, that are basically computing one step at a time, but the time difference between one step to the other step doesn't change that much. This continuous-time type of dynamical systems allows you to have a little bit of control over when events are happening. In a discrete way, you also account for the time between the events that are happening. So sequences that are continuously evolving — you have a lot more adaptability in the time dimension as well. That kind of aspect of recurrence and feedback calculation — this was the intuition that we brought to machine learning.

Scaling Meets Reality

Again, not only us from the MIT side, but also a lot of other people were simultaneously working on this with topics such as neural ODEs, state space models — you can think about all these other names that people started putting on top of these dynamical systems.

Then it was time around 2020, everybody was talking about scalability. From the MIT side, we were competing with the OpenAIs of the world and the Googles of the world, from a research point of view. We were putting algorithms that are efficient and perform really well in new learning scenarios in the robotics environments. Because if you remember between 2017 and 2020, OpenAI was very active in reinforcement learning and also doing a lot of robotics — OpenAI Gym, for example.

So we were trying to get creative around controlling robots with these type of continuous-time algorithms and showcase how you can take learning to out-of-distribution — how can we have learning systems that are small but at the same time they can do a lot better in out-of-distribution generalization. That was the whole thesis.

But then we started thinking about scale, because everybody had started thinking about scale as well. We wanted to evolve from this worm-inspired intelligence to something that is more complex and get into human-understandable signals — with audio, vision, and text being a corpus of data that we cared about.

The Nonlinearity Problem

As soon as we start scaling continuous-time and recurrent highly nonlinear loops, you realize how difficult it is to perform computation. It becomes really computationally not tractable. You need to get creative around how to scale these systems.

Recurrent neural networks — their major blocker has been sequential computation. Parallelizing recurrent operators when they are nonlinear is really difficult, especially on GPUs. This is one of the beauties of transformer architecture: they're unbiased, they are basically matrix multiplications, and you can actually scale them. It's the hardware lottery. That's the beauty of the transformer architecture — for scale, for unlocking general-purpose behavior.

But the recurrence itself is so attractive because the computation doesn't explode. If you think about attention, when you consume more and more data, exponentially — the quadratic cost of attention is something that people have paid attention to. So we've always realized that recurrence is actually bringing this computation lower and making it sub-quadratic or linear, closer to linear computation as you consume more data. So these algorithms are more efficient — but this is only theoretical. If you cannot really scale and do the operations in parallel, you cannot scale these systems.

Linearization and Its Discontents

So one of the things that we tried was: one way to solve for these nonlinear systems to become linear is to linearize them. When I say linear, you dynamically reduce all the nonlinearities of the system so you can apply linear algebra tricks on the system so that the system actually becomes computable — you can perform linear algebraic operations in parallel.

That's something that, for example, state space models are: linear versions of recurrent neural networks, and they lost that nonlinearity, that nonlinear relationship between the parameters. The reason is that you want to make a scalable computation. So SSMs became a very popular version of a dynamical system, because you can now parallelize other forms of operations as well — not just attention, but you can have parallel scan and you can apply linear algebra tricks to scale another format of operations.

So linearizing this dynamical system allowed us to scale. But the problem again — there's no free lunch in computer science, right? When you linearize a complicated dynamics, you're losing expressivity. The system is not going to be as expressive as this nonlinear form. Then we realized when we apply state space models to solving language problems, they have troubles learning dependencies at long context. They can compute really efficiently, but they cannot express very efficiently. So the expressive power of these neural networks always falls short of transformers.

STAR: The Meta Architecture Search

So with all the nonlinear mathematics that we learned from liquid neural networks, from dynamical systems, from SSMs, from convolutional neural networks — there's many different variations of operators that you can bring together to build a general-purpose computer. With everything that we learned, we thought: okay, let's not put ourselves into a biased way and say, "All right, so our architecture is the holy grail and everybody has to start building an alternative architecture, and put a bet on a single architecture."

What we thought day one at Liquid — this is about 3 years ago — we started bringing "Avengers" of alternative architectures all in one place. We had people from Yoshua Bengio's lab, from Stanford, from MIT — they're all inventors of various types of technology. There was Hyena Hierarchy, there was state space models, Jimmy Smith of Stanford, and ourselves on liquid neural networks. So we brought all of these teams into one place, and we said: let's build an unbiased way, let's build a meta AI system that searches through the operation space.

So we built a meta system that searches through operators of interest given the deployment environment. Imagine you want to deploy these solutions on a GPU or NPU. So we applied basically this massive search algorithm on top of building hybrid architectures that allowed you to optimize for things.

Number one, no sacrifice on quality — there are a bunch of quality metrics like reasoning capability, language understanding, knowledge. There are 100 different criteria. We thought that no sacrificing quality against the pure transformer model. Two, minimizing memory consumption. Three, minimizing latency. Four, maximizing the speed of computation.

These are the four criteria that we optimize a search-based algorithm on. There's a paper we published on the science of this thing — it's called STAR, Synthetic Tailored Architecture — synthetic design of tailored hybrid architectures. If you look up "STAR Liquid AI" you can find it.

From LFM1 to LFM3

That framework, that meta algorithm, is a recursive self-improving system. Three and a half years ago, we applied it to have a search algorithm to go through various hybrid architectures for a given chip. This system became the computational graph of different generations of liquid foundation models.

  • LFM1 was the first instance that came out of this architectural search. It had some elements of convolution, some elements of attention, some elements of original liquid. It was a mess of everything.
  • LFM2 — we optimized it specifically for running really well on CPUs. If you look at LFM2, they have a very elegant and simple architecture: basically 80% double-gated 1D convolutions plus some group query attention (20% of query). Very simplified, very fast, high quality — you can run them on a CPU really well.

Now the beauty of this architecture search is that imagine a new innovation or new invention in the architecture space happens — we add them to this massive meta AI search. So every generation of liquid foundation model that we put out would definitely have an improvement over the previous version. But the operators are from operators that we choose, and the target device implies what should be that hybrid architecture. That's how we started designing these liquid foundation models.

What you see today: we are at the LFM 2.5 instances of the models. We are a foundation model lab. We're building everything from scratch ourselves. We pre-train these models. We run the scaling laws. We scale these models from tens of millions of parameters now to 70 billion parameters. So far we've released the smaller instances of LFM2 and LFM 2.5. The next generation would be LFM3 — a slightly modified version with added quality, stability, better latency control on the deployment frameworks we care about.

Business: Beyond a Research Project

You just gave us a PhD abstract of what Liquid has. Okay, I have so much to dive into — neural architecture search, gradient-free evolution, all these things — but just for the people also listening on the business side, let's also give an update. The last time we covered Liquid on the podcast was with Mikhail from Shopify, who's a big fan of you guys. Only you would know, but bring people up to speed on — this is not just a research project, right? People are actually effectively using this. The benchmarks are not just goal-seeked; they actually reflect the world.

Absolutely. Mikhail is one of my mentors now. He's like one of those no-BS type of people. I really like how he gives his advice very directly. One thing he told us: "You guys, we have a very competent team at Shopify and we're building models. If your model — if you're telling me you have models, I have to see, our team..."

He's a mercenary. He just cares about the input.

That's it. You bring in the technology, we will test it and we will tell you: is it good or bad? Then they tested it the first time and they were positively surprised, of the quality and the efficiencies of our models. In the space of alternative architectures, we have really really good models.

Intelligence Outside the Data Center

Back to the business side: this range of models we are operating — we're optimizing for CPUs, we are looking into bringing intelligence outside of data centers. We started working with enterprises that care about data that goes to deployments outside data centers: car manufacturers, robot manufacturers, laptop producers, mobile companies. They have deployments of compute somewhere outside data centers. So we go in there and our foundation models are really good — you can bring the best of intelligence on top of these devices for various type of applications.

Examples of partners: AMD on the AI PC side. 300 million AI PCs are getting generated on the planet every year — 300 to 400 million laptops — and about 100 million of it could be AMD-powered. So we're working towards bringing our liquid foundation models directly running on the laptop, enabling local deployment of intelligence.

This can solve multiple problems: - Privacy filters — smart guardrails on what wants to get out of your computer. Imagine you want to send something to a ChatGPT terminal or Claude Code agent — that bulk of sensitive data that you want to send, you can pass first through a liquid foundation model that shields out sensitive information in a smart way, then share those. - Proactive agents directly on your device — an agent that has access to all sorts of information right now on your laptop, performs analysis and gives that to yourself. Everything you can achieve in the cloud, you'd want to bring it as an experience directly running on a laptop. That gives you offline capabilities, air-gapped capabilities.

Why On-Device Matters

Today when you think about device intelligence, there is a hybrid: one model in the cloud, models running on the device. There's always a collaboration. If you think about the most-used phones — Apple Intelligence, Galaxy AI — 90% of the calls are going to the cloud, 10% on the device. The reason is because the device models are not powerful enough or reliable enough to really take more off of those cloud use cases.

Why do companies want to run these AIs on the device? The first reason is sheer cost. If you have 400 million phones or billions of clients that you have to support and give them free intelligence access while you serve that intelligence in the cloud, that's going to become really prohibitive cost. So companies are trying really hard to bring the AI workload directly on the device — that way you're creating margins for yourself. That's the first and simplest solution.

Apart from that, you have offline features, privacy-sensitive topics, and many advantages on-device.

But it is very difficult building a model for the device and getting it to production quality. It's extremely difficult. It's not like downloading a model from open source and putting it on the device — now you're successful. It goes a lot more than that. You have to do thermal control. The behavior of a model in long context actually changes. You really have to have degree of reliability. Over the last two and a half years, we've gone through many cycles of production. Production-grade AI is way more than just benchmarking some quality benchmarks on the device.

Mercedes-Benz: AI Inside the Car

Another example: car manufacturers like Mercedes-Benz is one of our clients. We bring in-car intelligence. We announced a partnership last April — it actually happened really fast; in the space of automotive it is a significant partnership.

Imagine you're sitting in your car — you can talk to your car, all sorts of "Hey Mercedes" features, you're communicating with your car. Those are all happening with the foundation model that goes directly inside the car. The model we are powering is a multimodal solution that can get connected to the cameras and can do voice interchange, and has reasoning through the text-based models.

This model itself is about 600 megabytes. Imagine if you have a 600-megabyte intelligence that goes inside every car, you can do an over-the-air update (OTA) of every car on the planet.

The first deployments on Mercedes will happen this year — on all North America Mercedes-Benz Generation 3 cars. We're going to have the first deployment at scale of AI actually inside the cars. And this is running on a chip that is probably $100 in cost. It's absolutely insane to think about bringing really high-quality production-grade AI. It feels really good to work towards this efficiency at the levels we talk about, and taking these things into production in the car space.

Shopify: A Billion Requests a Month

I can tell you about millions of things we've done with Shopify. Shopify has been an unbelievable partner. They are not doing on-device AI, but they care about latency. They have private deployments they have to serve through the Shop app, merchant-facing and client-facing products of Shopify across many things. We have a lot of liquid foundation models deployed in production.

One example: if you go to the Shop app today and type in something, you would actually send the signal to a liquid foundation model. There is actually a liquid foundation model serving across the stack. We are passing through exponential statistics in terms of use. It seems like clients are really enjoying those features. Now we are exponentially at over a billion requests per month — just through Shopify's Shop app.

Open Source and Popularity

In terms of popularity of the models themselves — we deliver liquid foundation models to the community. We open source them. Models are very popular right now: over 40 million downloads overall, about 1.5 million downloads per week. A lot of developers are taking these things and putting them in production.

The range of parameters of liquid foundation models we've released so far: between 100 million parameters to 24 billion parameters. The bigger ones are mixture-of-expert architectures. This range of models is adding multimodal capabilities — processing audio, vision, and text at the same time as input, and generating audio and text as output. That's the portfolio.

Back to Robotics

Was wondering about robotics, since that was one of your inspirations when you started. You've got multimodal models — vision language model, audio models. Are those being used for robotics purposes, and can you talk about some experiments?

Absolutely. When you have vision language models, you can solve vision-action problems — robots seeing the world and taking an action based on what the robot sees. You can also use them as monitors. Imagine in factories there are cameras monitoring entire operations of a factory. We usually think about industrial operations of robots — not mostly humanoids, but industrial robots.

We worked with a company called RootTech — if you search "RootTech AMD Liquid AI" you'd find a demo of what we've done. There's another company called G-Bionics in Italy — they have modular robots and use our vision language model for some action space for the body of their robot. There's a camera on the body and they use these things for instruction-following capabilities — vision-action models. Use cases mostly go inside factories.

The smaller instances of the models — for low-latency applications in robotics — they're really popular. There's a lot of new engagements coming our way.

But robotics has been something that we deliberately put on pause day one. The reason: because the go-to-market motion around robotics and building a business around robotics is very difficult and delayed. If you think about production-grade robotics, you need to go down the rabbit hole of verification and validation of the technology, and then you get into regulatory aspects for deployment. Because we come from a robotics background ourselves, we know how hard it is to productize some robotics vertical. That's why we wanted to build a horizontal layer of intelligence on top of places where we can have OEMs first, and then enter into the action world where V&V becomes much more sensitive as a later step of the company.

But now it is a good time. A lot of our models are matured a little bit better now. We have a lot more control over data and post-training and customization process. I think it's a very good time for us to also start the robotic vertical much more seriously than before.

Same Family, Different Vertical?

Just on this — since you mentioned it and said it's a good time — do you basically use the same LFM family? A lot of people make a big deal about how different action models or world models are for robotics. I don't know how much of that is marketing versus fundamentally the same thing.

That's a great point. I'll tell you: innovations in the space of foundation models used in any vertical — I would categorize them in three different classes: 1. Model architecture of intelligence 2. Algorithmic aspect of intelligence — algorithms that are innovative 3. Data processing mechanisms — what kind of data work do you want to do

Innovation across this tree — what we've been focusing on from our research point of view is model architecture innovation. That's the model perspective. Then there are algorithms. You can train a model with an autoregressive loss. You can train a model as a diffusion process. You can train a model in a world modeling context.

World modeling — it's like an unsupervised way of learning systems, building a representation so that from that representation you have a world view. Of course, I would attribute world modeling on the algorithmic side of intelligence, rather than architectural change.

You could technically take some of these LFM architectures and use them in a world modeling pipeline and train them to have a better understanding of the physics of the world. Various algorithms allow you to learn some physical structure of the world with different ways. World modeling allows you to extract a different set of primitives from the physical world compared to next-token prediction. You wouldn't say next-token prediction wouldn't have a physical understanding — but it's very different than the humans' way of understanding the physical world.

There is still a debate between what learning algorithms are going to unlock what type of capability is needed for having the ChatGPT moment for robots. That's a big question mark on the algorithmic side. On the architecture side, you could use any general-purpose algorithm to be used in those frameworks.

Business Model: Design Partners and Licensing

Just so I understand the business model side before we go back to research — I assume these are all licensing agreements, because it's air-gapped, on-device. How much time do you have to spend to customize a model? Let's say I come to you with a very special set of compute constraints. Is it your guys doing it? Is it a collaboration?

Fantastic question. Our early engagements are usually with design partners. These design partners are the ones with whom we associate an applied ML team to work with, and we charge also for that duration of engagement. Then once the solution is built, we deploy the solution and charge licenses on a yearly basis, on a device basis, depending on where this thing is getting deployed. We charge for models as a recurrent cost.

Then after we build a solution in a vertical, the time of service reduces for the next customer in that vertical. Imagine if Mercedes-Benz is our design partner and we build a solution around our products — then the next customers coming in the automotive vertical, the amount of service that we provide reduces from our side; it becomes just the solution deployment. So we make solutions in every vertical, and those solutions are what allow us to sell faster.

The Self-Serve Platform

That being said, because as a foundation model company we've gone through the process of building a model from scratch and deploying these models in production many many times, we're building now a platform for model development — a self-serve platform. You can get access to this platform and using this platform you'd be able to automatically do that job. This is something we are building.

Wow.

It's a very difficult problem. You can close the loop also with recursive loops and everything, but we want to give these capabilities of model building — the quality that Liquid builds models — to the client space, to the enterprises themselves.

Is this platform fully rolled out? Is it in beta? This is my first time hearing about this.

It's in beta right now. We're still testing it out. Very excited about it. Very interesting problem.

Customization Tokens: The Next Wave

This customization and continual learning is a very important next step for the deployment of AI. Right now, 90% of the market is around inference tokens. Frontier Labs, inference providers like Fireworks — they host the models and they charge the inference. Inference tokens are the ones making money.

But I think the next wave of companies — I can name a couple: REI, Coreweave/Core Automation, Thinking Machines, Trajectory — many different companies in this category of customization. A lot of people are turning into customization tokens because now there are a lot of good base open-source models. Enterprises could actually — we are talking about enterprise AI — monetization of customization tokens is something people are going to capitalize on. It's going to be the next wave of decacorns emerging from this category — some are already decacorns. Jeff Dean just started a lab on similar type of topics.

Customization is going to become very important. And when I say customization, don't only think about post-training a model. Think about the depths of customization — from pre-training to inference. You can do pre-training, mid-training, post-training, data gen, RL — all fall into this category of customization of a model. And then allowing agents to do that, and looping the whole thing so you can have a recursive loop that allows the customers to own their own intelligence. That's what we are planning to do — providing this platform to customers so they can build liquid foundation models at the quality that we can build. Once they put them in production, they can keep them always up to date, always at the level they want.

Leap: The Developer Cookbook

Just before we head to the research — can I ask about your developer platform, Leap? How are developers using this platform, and what process do they use to deploy?

Leap is a library. We have a cookbook — at Liquid AI, this is like an open source place. You can go to our cookbook.

Got a lot of attention. There is so much going on in there.

We literally provide a lot of insights. This is manual, built for humans. Leap is built for humans. You're a developer, you want to use liquid foundation model, you want to fine-tune them — you go there. Leap Fine-tune is one place where you can fine-tune one of our models. Then there are deployments — Leap allows you to extract a bundle that you can deploy: an inference-ready GGUF format, a llama.cpp-ready system that can go directly on the device.

Think about our current platform we're building right now — it's literally the automated version of what we've been doing with Leap. There are functionalities Leap has and some it doesn't. We want to complete the Leap platform as tools, and be able to provide enterprises with the capability to do that in a way that we use those tools. Those are individual segmented tools you can use, or give your cloud agent to take them and use them to fine-tune an LFM.

That being said, there are also support of liquid foundation models in the very popular places — Unsloth, Hugging Face's TRL for fine-tuning. You can use any of those open-source packages. We try to be really connected to the open source community. We love the Hugging Face guys, the SGLang guys — we work very closely with them. The llama.cpp project itself is an amazing effort to really deploy intelligence outside of data centers.

Self-Serve vs Forward-Deployed

Yeah, I haven't heard TRL in a while. Every year or two there's a new hotness — right now it's Unsloth, we've also covered Axolotl. One thing — my eyebrows went up when you said self-serve. I had expected you would do a lot of services — maybe these days it's called forward-deployed. Is there a maturity hierarchy? Everyone's talking about continual learning, but probably most people aren't ready. You release, for example, quantization-aware distillation — that seems easy, that seems self-serve. Is there a stage of "you start here and work your way up"?

Absolutely. You touched on a very important problem. We've worked probably with 200 of the Fortune 500 companies so far. We're really in touch with all the enterprises. What enterprises are exhausted — they went through the process of building their own intelligence for a long time. They tried to have applied ML teams themselves. These mature enterprises tried out intelligence, downloading models from open source, building their own models from scratch — this did not result in actual production lines. They always defaulted back to cloud solutions. Some products are out there, but the ratio: 80% of the PoCs do not hit production level. That's one exhaustive thing I see.

Second: there is massive demand for developers right now that want access to the highest form of intelligence for development. They want to vibe-code stuff. Everybody wants to token-max. It's such a virus in the head of developers. When you actually attribute value — how much value was generated off of vibe-coded repositories happening at mature organizations — you again end up with 90% of these tokens being useless tokens.

So when enterprises see this and want to control the cost, there is massive demand for a self-serve platform that allows them to really get to the point they want to get as soon as possible to a value they want to receive, while satisfying the demand of their own developers.

Human-in-the-Loop Platform Design

What we try to do — we try to build the platform not as another UI or another new type of set. Our platform is literally going to sit inside a client, very similar to how you interface with Claude Code. You take your agentic harness and you just give it the tools of Liquid AI. Your own favorite agentic harness would be able, in a step-by-step manner, to walk you through developing and building and deploying a liquid foundation model, production-quality level, the way we would do.

This process is an interactive process with the developer at the moment. Human-in-the-loop aspect of it is very important to the point you mentioned — are they ready to do this? You've got to guide the customers, the developers, to really get to that point. That is the automated stuff. You can also put it on steroids — you can put it on auto mode, one click, deliver this, no intermediary. But obviously the quality of the resulting model is not going to be as good as when you're having an interactive developer actually interactively build something with it.

Let me push back on you. If I have good evals, why do I care what the process is? It should just auto-research itself.

I fully agree with you for the first deployment. Imagine you put the model in production based on the evals you had. Now new data is going to come in. Actual production environment — new requests, all of a sudden there's a massive distribution shift of the community wanting different things from your models. How do you handle that?

Your evals are going to become obsolete. Static evals are going to become obsolete. So you need to have some sort of dynamism, and this would only happen if you have a continuously evolving system. Evals cannot stay static. For the first iteration I fully agree — but if you go to production, the evals are not going to stay the same. You always have to change the criteria.

Trends in Post-Training and Environments

I think that's why we're moving towards environments and Harbor-style tasks. What other trends are you seeing in post-training? Are customers doing more and more of the post-training, and you are doing the architectural work — is that the division of labor?

Yes. I would say not just post-training. Don't forget: I talked about the whole model development from scratch. If you're as sophisticated as, let's say, Qualcomm — they want to design their own dedicated computation graph that works the best on Qualcomm chips on an NPU they're designing. There are also companies that are etching weights of a neural network directly inside the chips.

I covered Tenstorrent — yeah, Tenstorrent and etched before.

As you know, there's so much in the silicon world. Those guys would be interested in our architecture search more than anybody. Staying close with silicon partners is very important for us because our architecture search is hardware-aware. They want to put their hardware — or maybe next generation of the hardware — in the loop of finding out what is the best architecture for the criteria I care about. Silicon companies really like this automated foundation design platform we are putting in front of them.

As you mentioned, customization wants to get more and more to enterprises. Enterprises would be able to own their own model development and deployment. These are the two things. This is the true meaning of sovereign AI. Everybody would be able to own their own intelligence. Hopefully one step further — every single person on the planet would be able to own their own intelligence. That's the next level: personal intelligence. Hopefully we can unlock that.

Lessons from Architecture Search

Just wanted to touch on things quickly because you left so much in there. In terms of neural architecture search — you're the first, maybe second or third company. We recently covered Poolside where they talked about their model factory. I was also very excited by the tooling for search — Apple had this paper on Taria, their sort of LLM-ops layer-by-layer inspection and ablation tool. What have you found in your architecture search or model factory that thought would work doesn't work, or is surprisingly effective?

When we do architecture search in the space of foundation models, we run a scaling law. For every architecture candidate, we try to run up to a certain number of tokens — we run a scaling law. Throwing more data at a certain fixed size of the model or increasing the size of the model, and see how well it can actually train given that candidate architecture.

The things we learned:

Insight 1: The larger the neural network, the more unbiased the architecture should be. For example, if you look at LFM2 architecture — this doesn't have any gated delta nets and all these things. It's like a very unstructured 1D convolutions. Literally 1D convolutions — the simplest thing you can actually do. Attention itself is very unstructured. When architectures are not biased (like attention, like transformers) — you would be able to scale them. At scale, a lot less bias is needed inside the architecture. You've got to simplify the architecture the larger you make them.

On the other side of the spectrum: if you want to solve problems at a very small scale and cannot afford — you have a memory limit, let's say 8GB — you can get more creative on the architecture side. You can make the models to have multiple feedback loops, add a lot more complexity to the system. In the small-model regime, the more biases you add, the more expressive dynamics you get. In the larger scale, you remove those biases.

Insight 2: Data modality matters. There are some data modalities like audio — you could use continuous-time dynamical systems or SSMs, they're very effective in audio. But on text, they suck. SSMs don't work really well on text. When you think about — if you just want an audio model, throwing in a recurrent neural network at the scale needed for humanly like really good quality audio output — this is where recurrent networks would be very much shining. Again at small scale, when we talk about this category of models we search — below 20 billion parameters — recurrence can be really effective there. I would call them more biased architectures — they have more feedback, structural gates, certain architecture archetypes on top of them. You remove those things as you scale. That's the general understanding we have.

No surprise. Jason had a post where at small scale you add in biases and eventually you have to take them out. Also — I think it's called layer looping — that one is a bit unintuitive why it works at small scale but not at larger scale. It seems like it would work. It's mostly an efficiency thing, I guess.

Still, looping is again a bias. Any format of looping is a bias you're adding to your system. You make it complicated and you've got to find an infrastructure for by the way. We don't have the correct infra — the current GPU infrastructure we have is optimized for parallel matrix multiplication.

Photonics and Substrates of Intelligence

Imagine if you have photonics. This race of photonics would be amazing. If you can actually communicate with the speed of light, now compute in a serial way — what is the speed of serial computation when you're moving with the speed of light? It's humanly not perceivable. Photonics could be an unbelievable way for us — if you think about medium change — to move. That could unlock nonlinear operators. I know companies working on photonics and quantum computers. Everybody's working in this space of alternative mediums for intelligence or compute in general. I'm really excited about photonics because sequential computation — this is something we learned from a linear algebra point of view for nonlinear systems, because we cannot really parallelize nonlinear systems. But imagine if you have speed-of-light computational speed for nonlinear operators — then you can build the next generation of architectures, because then you're not limited by the substrate you're hosting intelligence on.

I'll give you one quote — I think it was from Christoph Koch, writing some book on neuroscience. I read it about 14 years ago. He was at a conference and he was saying: "Intelligence is a property of carbon." Because the substrate of humans is carbon. Natural life is happening on a different substrate, and we're building intelligence right now on silicon. So the base of intelligence is very different. I think substrate is going to play a role in the next generation of architectures. It would unlock various formats of computation apart from just parallel computation through GPUs. That's another space I would bring in.

The Quantum Debate

Okay, we don't have a ton of time to mention this, but you brought this up so I have to ask. A surprising number of people in my circles in SF are not that excited by quantum computing. If we did have at scale a bunch of qubits, do you actually think that it would change anything? Some people disagree.

I think the only thing that changes massively — search. Search is one of those algorithms that matters so much. Imagine if you can have parallel search.

And what is optimization at the end of it? We are submitting ourselves to gradient descent right now because we don't know any better way to perform massive search at scale. If you think about quantum computers, search is going to evolve massively.

That one hopefully is not controversial. But there are many other bottlenecks that matter to us that are not solved by quantum.

Absolutely. But I don't think we are close. In 2017 I was at one of these NeurIPS conferences and I was talking to — I think it was Microsoft or IBM. It was IBM — they were bringing, showing off their quantum bits, the thing hanging from the ceiling. I said, "Okay, when can everybody actually use something like this?" At that time, 2017, he told me 2035. So it's still too early to say anything.

Why SSMs Work for Voice

Okay, coming back closer actually for listeners. We've done a bunch of related podcasts. RWKV is another widely adopted non-transformers architecture, loosely inspired by RNNs. We've done a couple episodes on those. We've had Tri Dao on. We haven't had Cartesia on yet — but when you mentioned how SSMs are very attuned to voice: at first when Tri talked about it to me, and Karan talked about it to me, I didn't understand why voice. To me actually the simple explanation is there's just not that much state — voice is continuously inferencing anyway. So this actually pretty ideal.

Yeah. It's a continuous-on sequence, and sequences that are time series — if you throw a dynamical system that is designed to handle time-series data, that's the best version of things that you can actually model time series. That's why SSMs are pretty effective. SSMs and RNNs and continuous-time systems — very effective in sequential kind of data.

You brought out time series. The other thing about my background that I bring into this: I used to be an options trader, where we actually had to do stochastic calculus and solve those kinds of ODEs — which is another kind of continuous-time finance. I just think it's weird this hasn't been a priority till now. Once you explain it, it's relatively obvious that this is a thing we should exploit — a dimension we should exploit. Are there any others in your mind? Obviously you're 10 years into this journey — okay, if we're wrong about continuous time, what else?

Adaptability as the Next Frontier

That's a good question. When we started Liquid as an idea, we were thinking about efficiency of intelligence and adaptability of intelligence. I think we haven't explored too much on the adaptability of intelligence. Forward pass for us is basically forward pass to a model. A lot of forward-looking computation is literally just a forward pass computation.

What if — adaptability on the go? A lot of people would tell you: "In-context learning is solving that problem, because in-context systems, when you bring more data at test time, they would somehow kind of solve for some pseudo-backprop situation." It's like a least-squares algorithm as in-context learning happening on test-time compute.

But in general — approaches where we can combine forward pass and backward pass at the same time — this would be a new generation of architectures. I think there will be an evolution of this thing. I know that SSI is also working on very similar architectures to the original ideas of liquid neural networks. That's what I heard.

They have not reached out?

Come on, what's going on! But in general, you should also assume that all the foundation model labs — Anthropics, OpenAIs, everybody else — are massively invested. They have teams working on alternative architectures.

Why an Alternative Architecture?

Another thing I want to say: why do you want an alternative architecture? The first thing for us: efficiency. Everybody else is now focusing on post-hoc optimizations — really like speculative decoding, quantization, quantization of training. These are the places where people try to pack information. You can do a lot in there because these are kernel science.

With better AIs, I'm hoping for the next generation of AIs to get a lot better at what they do today. People can really optimize the current architectures to get efficiency out of the models. Now, if you want to unlock the next generation of capabilities, that's a different story. That could be a meta algorithm.

Cognitive Architectures

Think about it: how does our workflow of coding today look like? There's an orchestrator and a lot of agents. In the future, multi-agentic architectures — that's another thing I can think about. We can think at the atom level or at the system level. You can build new systems composed of smaller units of compute. A unit of compute could be neurons and synapses, or it could be an LFM, or a small model itself. You bundle them and build systems of systems. I would call them cognitive architectures — multiple agents that you bundle together to build a whole full-blown system as a whole.

A bunch of directions I pointed out that could be an exciting future step.

If I were to paraphrase — agents should be able to train models casually as part of their job, and obviously LFM would be quite adaptable. And it's not actually the LFM, it would be Leap, because you need the full platform as well to adapt to whatever situation you're deploying in.

Definitely.

Current Research Agenda

All these named directions — you probably also have more near-term research directions. What would you say is the current research agenda for Liquid?

We are very much focused on massively multimodal systems — training all the data modalities at the same time. At the same time, longer-horizon reasoning is one of the directions we want to do. Imagine if you want to do reliable on-device intelligence services like an assistant — all of those things require higher degrees of reliability for the models. So we work a lot on that direction.

We work a lot — we have a department for efficiency. We work on massive layers of efficiency: kernel design, inference, infrastructure, RL infrastructure that is much faster. Making all our processes from pre-training to delivering a model to production — how to make all the infrastructure more efficient.

From a research point of view we're looking also non-human understandable data. For example, think about signals — biology as well. We have some biomodels. We're building DNA foundation models. Your DNA — with your eyes you can't really read it. They're long-context data — not dense as let's say vocabulary. They're like four vocabs — letters you're dealing with. But from the sequence-length point of view, they're very large. A lot of applications we are excited about in that realm. Our type of technology naturally pushed us into looking into this alternative type of data as well. Our architectures — dynamical systems and longer sequences of data. DNA data could be one of those places where we can bring value. And as I mentioned, multimodal research is extremely hot right now at Liquid.

Multimodal Out — Video and Audio

You said video-audio in and video-audio out. Video, audio, text in — audio and audio and —

Text is assumed.

Text is assumed, exactly. The in is fine. The out is new.

Right, correct.

Typically I would never expect someone like you to care. Is it realistic to have image out, audio out, video out from a 7B model that is usable?

I don't think it's feasible to get a video out of a 7B — that's like a proper, very very high-quality, high-fidelity kind of video. But directionally, if you want to solve physical problems and have a vague understanding of the world — imagine you're training these LFMs, let's say in the range of 7B and below, with a world-modeling context. You would be able to encode some physical knowledge inside the model. But the model would not be able to output something very high-fidelity. It would add to its own understanding, but not be able to output that. It can have a little bit of a better representation internally. If you retrain them with world modeling, especially for video applications where video generation matters — not just for entertainment, we are talking about grounded industrial work of a robot operating in a factory.

Video understanding is actually so underrated. There's still not enough — mostly it's just interleaved images. We want more.

In the space of multimodal intelligence, there's really a lot to be learned so far. There are not that many highly multimodal systems. This is a very open research topic for foundation models as a whole. It's going to enable something completely different.

Modular, Mojo, and Ecosystem Lock-in

One thing I wanted to double-check is something adjacent to your space, which is Modular. They just got bought — went to Qualcomm. They just released their 1.0 open source. You guys famously switched from Jax to PyTorch. Did you explore Mojo? It's supposed to be for you guys — you're doing custom kernel work, you are Python-centric. If it didn't work, why?

Modular is basically operating on a space of kernels. They're one layer below the foundation models. They try to be also like us — Switzerland, working with all the hardware providers — but they now got locked in into Qualcomm.

I was on a panel with Chris actually some weeks ago on an AMD panel. He's one of my heroes. Chris Lattner — he's unbelievable.

Yeah, he's probably listening.

[laughter] What I can tell you is that one thing from first principles we try to do at Liquid: we don't want to reinvent the wheel. I'll tell you: there's a lot of inference companies trying to replace llama.cpp or building wrappers around llama.cpp for on-device AI. Almost every single one of these things that are not locked into one ecosystem, that try to be a general-purpose language for all hardware — all of them are worse. If you dig in, they're worse than the original llama.cpp. So we don't want to change base. There are some successful ones that lock into one ecosystem. I feel Mojo is going to go into a similar direction. Now that they're getting locked into the Qualcomm ecosystem, there's going to be a lot more success. The platform itself makes things easier to bring intelligence at that layer — for hosting intelligence — so what they provide is actually useful, but we haven't been using those for our own deployments yet.

Llama.cpp is better as a baseline, but is it just production hardening, or something fundamental about the approach?

It's a compiler. Very optimized C++ kernels.

Yes, but Chris Lattner knows C++ — this is not an issue.

As I said — it's extremely difficult to unify it. I don't believe in the uniformity of the Mojo platform. You need to do custom work — this is the work the modular team actually put into. The version of Mojo that runs on AMD — you have to design certain kernels for Mojo so they're AMD-specific, or Qualcomm-specific. All that underlying work is very solid work, and if anyone can pull it off, it's Chris's team.

Like what Chris does, what Jonathan Ross did with TPUs — these are very fundamental works. We would stick to the most native language, the most native platform that allows us to touch the computer as close as possible.

Ecosystem always wins. It's just really brutal. It's not fair to new entrants. It's a hard problem.

I would encourage entrepreneurs these days — a lot of my friends and people are coming and asking, "How's the journey?" I'm four years into our entrepreneurial journey. I would just say: if a problem is hard to solve, it's actually worth it. It makes it more attractive. Easy problems — everybody else is going to go solve it.

Closing: Is Attention All You Need?

Maybe the question I was going to end the episode with: it's going to be the 10-year anniversary of the transformer next year. Is attention all you need?

Attention is definitely one element that you need. I think it will be a long time that we will be living with attention-based systems. Attention is definitely going to be inside any of them.

You know how your eyes are working? Your body is — I randomly noticed, actually you're not seeing the whole view. Your eyes are just bouncing around all the time and your brain is compositing.

Yes.

You see the difference between two frames. By the way, this is what you see. So basically you see the differential.

Oh, left and right eye?

No — you're basically, the way humans see, you don't see one frame. You see the difference of two frames.

I need to go look this one up. Look this one up.

Beyond Attention: Embodiment and Adaptivity

So attention is one component. But then again — hardware awareness, customization. Embodiment — there's another aspect. Intelligence that wants to get deployed in the society outside of data centers — you've got to have some sort of embodiment. Agents that are actually inside the virtual world — they have also an understanding of their virtual physical environments they are operating in. So embodiment is also true for virtual agents by the way. Embodied intelligence and embodied reasoning is very important.

And then adaptive intelligence is another level we really want to add.

Is that routing related, or what do you mean by adaptive?

Adaptive — I mean systems that can always evolve. Continual learning, continuously improving systems.

Okay. Well, that was a really good deep dive. Is there anything that we should have asked you that we didn't cover?

No, I think that was a great session. Thank you so much.

[music]

item.description:
## 一、被忽视的"偏置反转定律"：小模型要更"生物"，大模型要更"愚钝"
Hasani 抛出了一个反直觉的架构学：**模型越小，越需要加入结构性偏置（反馈回路、门控、递归）；模型越大，反而必须"去偏置化"，让架构回归到最朴素的 1D 卷积与注意力堆叠。**
这颠覆了大多数人对"复杂问题需要复杂结构"的默认假设。它揭示了一个隐藏的真相：**规模本身就是一种通用先验**。当参数足够多、数据足够多，任何精巧的归纳偏置都会变成天花板；而在小模型的贫瘠世界里，架构必须"聪明地偷懒"，用生物学式的递归结构来弥补参数量的匮乏。
这与生物演化诡异地对称——线虫用 302 个神经元的高度专业化结构击败了任何工业机器人，而人类大脑的规模让它可以承担"通用"的奢侈。**规模决定了智能可以有多"不加设计"。**
## 二、跨领域连接：期货交易者的随机微积分 × 蠕虫神经元 × 视网膜的"差分感知"
播客中隐藏着一个几乎无人察觉的三角连接：
- 主持人自曝曾是**期权交易员，用随机微积分求解连续时间的 SDE**； - Liquid AI 的核心数学是**连续时间一阶微分方程建模的神经元**； -

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] What Happens When Every Employee Thinks Like a Founder? - Noam Brown
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个被忽略的反直觉：越会"深度思考"的 AI，越不会协作

Brown 说漏了一个真正惊人的事实——推理模型（reasoning models）陷入了"深思陷阱"：它们越擅长长链条思考，就越无法承受被打断去和其他 agent 通信。这几乎是一种数字版的"学者综合征"：博士越读越深，跨学科对话就越困难。你会发现这里存在一个隐藏的代价函数曲线——单体智能与群体协作之间并非线性叠加，而是存在负向的相互挤压。这意味着 AGI 的路径可能不是"单个模型变强"，而是需要专门为"被打断"训练的模型——一种反 Chain-of-Thought 的、面向社交带宽的架构。这跟人类进化里"社会脑假说"（Robin Dunbar）惊人地一致：灵长类大脑之所以变大，不是为了解题，是为了处理社群关系。

对齐问题的隐藏产业后果：AI 可能杀死"初创公司"这个物种本身

表面看 AI 帮助个体创业者，实则可能是大公司的救命稻草。这里 Brown 触碰到一个几乎没人明说的推论："创业公司凭什么打败大厂"这一整套硅谷神话，本质上依赖于大公司内部的错位（misalignment）——山头林立、KPI 冲突、政治博弈。一旦 AI 把 10,000 个员工变成 10,000 个"持股 20% 的共同创始人式对齐副本"，Coase 的企业理论就要被重写：交易成本坍塌，企业规模的上限被解除封印。这不是渐进式变革，而是对"创业公司"这一经济物种的存在合法性发起的挑战。历史上类似的时刻只有一次：福特流水线让作坊消失。下一个可能消失的，是"车库创业"这一神话本身。

跨领域连接：AI 的 fork 不像"招聘"，更像细菌分裂

我们习惯用"招聘更多人"的框架来理解 AI 扩容，这是错误的类比。生物学里，多细胞生物通过分化（differentiation）扩展能力，代价是细胞失去克隆自由；而细菌通过裂殖（fission）扩展，代价是缺乏专业化。AI 的 forking 兼具两者——既能瞬间克隆，又能保留完整上下文——这在自然界从未存在过。这产生一个奇特的推论：AI 组织学的最佳类比不是公司，也不是蚁群，而是"黏菌"（slime mold）——一种能在需要时聚合成整体、在完成任务后又分散为单体的中间态生物。而 Brown 承认"没测过 10,000 agents 是不是真的比 2,000 agents 快 2 倍"——这恰恰是Brooks 定律（"人月神话"）在 AI 时代的复活：加人不一定加速，甚至可能减速。软件工程 50 年前发现的教训，AI 行业正在重新交学费。

最出人意料的观察：Brown 的"保守"态度暴露了行业最深的秘密

注意听他两次强调"we haven't measured"、"I want to be conservative"——这是整段访谈里信号最强的地方。它揭露了一个几乎被市场营销掩盖的事实：前沿实验室并不真的知道 multi-agent 系统的规模化收益曲线长什么样。所有关于"AI 组织"、"agent swarm"的宏大叙事，都建立在未经验证的规模假设之上。这跟 1990 年代早期互联网泡沫惊人相似——那时也没人真的测过"网络效应"的定量收益。下一个五年真正的 alpha，可能不属于训练更大模型的团队，而属于第一个建立起"AI 组织学"实证测量科学的团队——就像 F. W. Taylor 用秒表和笔记本发明"科学管理"，把作坊改造成现代工厂那样。

📝 转录文本

缘起：一篇关于"自动化公司"的旧文

I wrote this essay a couple years ago called um something something AI, "what automated firms will look like," and I was thinking about: well, if you had fully automated firms of let's say human-level intelligences, what is different about the nature of AI minds that would make the organization's AI form different?

And there are a couple very important differences. For example, that AIs can share context much more seamlessly than humans can; they can merge their knowledge much more seamlessly. And also, you can spin up or spin down an arbitrary number of instances which have the right knowledge.

So if you want to hire more people, it's not like just all the schlep of finding the right talent or whatever. It's like your best talent, you can just make an infinite copy of them, or if you don't need them for the task anymore, you like spin them down. And you can just replicate the most effective parts of your organization, or replicate whole organizations together which are effective.

Um, I don't know—where do you see these multi-agent systems going a year from now or two years from now?

Fork 与合并：AI 同事和人类同事的根本差异

I think it's a great question of like: how do these things actually differ from working with a human coworker?

And I think there—I think you highlighted one really interesting thing—that I mean, if somebody's, if you have a person and you want just like two copies of them, you can't just like clone the person.

Um, but with AI, you—it's actually really easy to just say like, "okay, well just fork yourself" and then have both copies work on this thing and then like merge back together. I mean, we already have this I think in multi-agent for um, for Astra and and and 5.6 soul, that uh, when they spin up sub-agents, like the context is just forked so it has all the context that's relevant.

对齐问题：为什么创业公司能颠覆大公司？

Um, there are other interesting ways where the agents will differ from people. So I actually—I think a big one, and again this is kind of going back to the alignment stuff—but from a company perspective, like, what are some reasons why startups disrupt incumbents?

There, there's a few factors. Uh, one is that they're willing to take more risks. Um, but another major factor is: as companies grow in size, as organizations grow in size, you see increasing misalignment between the individuals in the organization.

Yeah.

Right. Like, if you have a startup with five people and each person has 20% share in the company, they're all highly aligned to the company succeeding. If you have like a massive company with 10,000 people, you see a lot more instances where people are territorial, or like just care about getting a lot of headcount for their project or their team, um, or like, you know, building their fiefdoms, getting a lot of resources so that they can publish cool work or whatever and get promoted—and this is actually a real detriment. I think this explains a lot of why startups are able to disrupt incumbents.

AI 的双刃剑：帮初创，也可能救大厂

And it's interesting that—I mean, it's true that AI does help startups in a way. Like, it's much easier than ever before for one person to step in and be like, "I'm going to make a multi-million dollar company." Like, it's just the AI amplifies an individual so much.

But there's also an argument that they could benefit incumbents, because if the alignment problem is solved, then you don't have the issue of misalignment between individuals in the company. Like, at least that's mitigated. Like, the AIs, if they're fully—if they're aligned well, they could just be aligned to the interest of the company, and you can have 10,000 of them and they're all going to be working as hard as if they were like a 20% share co-founder.

共享上下文 vs. 10,000 个数学家的思想实验

Yeah. And it's not only that, but it's also that they are much better able to like manage shared memory and context than different humans can. If you have—if like tomorrow you hire 10,000 mathematicians and you're like "solve this uh, solve Navier–Stokes," they're not going to be able to like cooperate effectively. Um, at least not off the bat. Uh, but you can have apparently 10,000 AIs.

Well, again, I want to be—I want to be conservative here, because we haven't measured how effective the 10,000 agents are at coordinating.

Uh, we think it helped. We don't actually have good measurements of saying like, "oh yeah, this 10,000 agents led to like a 2x speed up over 2,000 agents" or something like that.

Um, and it is actually—I would argue likely, maybe I don't know about likely, but I think it is very possible that 10,000 humans are better at coordinating than 10,000 agents right now.

I think that is a very—like, I think is entirely possible.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

Multi-Agent 的历史难题：让 Agent 学会互相说话

I think also one trend we've been seeing is like—look, we've been working on multi-agent for a while, and the early versions of this, it's very difficult to get right. It's very hard. It was very hard to get the agents to even talk to each other.

Yeah.

And it's because, like, look—when we first developed reasoning models, they weren't talking to other agents. And if now you put a bunch of agents together and say like, "oh, solve this problem together," they're in this local minimum where they're really good at thinking deeply about a problem, and um, it just like kind of interrupts their chain of thought—it interrupts their flow—to constantly be like checking in with other agents or like receiving messages from them. And the authorization is actually very hard to get right in that situation.

泛化能力是关键：模型越强，越会协作

Interesting. Is it getting the cold start of like getting the first collaboration, or like, what's the issue?

I mean, I think it's that they're not as general. Like, the earlier models were just not as um, generalizable, and were just more narrow.

Interesting.

As the models have become more capable, it's been easier for them to develop this capability. And I do think that as they become stronger and stronger just across the board, that they will become better at organizing themselves in large organizations.

And—like—I don't know, maybe they are better than people at organizing in 10,000 person groups. Um, but even if they're not, you know, a year from now, two years from now, like, yeah, it's quite possible that they'll do that even if we don't end-to-end optimize them for that.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

item.title: [Lex Clips] Does electroshock therapy (ECT) actually work? | Andrew Scull and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"解释饥渴"的隐秘专制：为什么有效不够、还要"可讲述"？

Scull 无意中戳中了现代医学一个近乎宗教性的执念——治疗必须附带一个可叙述的机制。他用癌症手术打比方："她切掉了，就是切掉了。" 潜台词是：ECT 之所以让公众不安，并非因为它无效，而是因为它拒绝被讲成故事。

但这里有个被系统性忽略的事实——全身麻醉的作用机制至今仍未被完整解释。每天全球数十万台手术依赖它，麻醉学教科书里那句"精确机制尚不明确"却从未引发任何伦理恐慌。阿司匹林在被广泛使用近 70 年之后（1897 年上市，1971 年 John Vane 才揭示前列腺素通路），才有了"为什么止痛"的答案。

同样是"知其然不知其所以然"，为什么麻醉与阿司匹林享有豁免，而 ECT 却被永久钉在耻辱柱上？ 答案可能残酷：因为它作用于"我之所以为我"的器官。人们能接受一把手术刀切开躯体的黑箱，却不能接受一股电流穿过意识的黑箱——这是笛卡尔身心二元论在当代医学直觉里未被清算的残余。

二、40 年"慢炖"作为方法论：与达尔文的隐秘同构

Scull 提到他 1981 年就构思了《绝望的疗法》，2022 年才成书——41 年。他自述秘诀是"永远同时进行两个项目"，让一个课题在潜意识里"渗滤"（percolating）。

这不是懒惰或拖延，而是一种被现代学术体制系统性摧毁的认知模式。达尔文 1838 年读到马尔萨斯即形成自然选择雏形，1859 年才出版《物种起源》——21 年。庞加莱在《科学与方法》里描述数学发现常出现在"停止思考"之后。创造性的深度理解需要一种"生物钟式的成熟"，而不是线性的努力叠加。

跨领域的意外连接在这里出现：Scull 的方法，本质上和红酒陈酿、发酵酱油、堆肥制作是同一类过程——都是让时间参与化学反应的工艺。当代 KPI 驱动的知识生产鼓励"一年一书"，恰恰扼杀了这种时间敏感的成熟机制。真正深刻的著作，大概率不是被"写出来"的，而是被"熬出来"的。

三、疯癫的"人类学恒常性"：一个反乌托邦的暗示

Scull 提到，从古希腊、古中国到现代，每一个他研究过的文明都必须处理"疯癫"这件事——形式各异，但存在恒常。

这里藏着一个令人不安的推论：如果疯癫是跨越所有文化制度的人类学不变量，那么它就不太可能仅仅是"社会病"或"资本主义的产物"（尽管流行的批判理论爱这么说）。它更像是智慧本身的税——语言、自我意识、复杂社会性给我们带来抽象能力的同时，也在神经系统里刻下了必然的裂痕。

更进一步的意外洞察：AI 系统的"幻觉"（hallucination）与人类的精神症状可能不是巧合的语言重合。任何足够复杂的、需要在噪声中构建连贯世界模型的系统，都会遭遇"符号与现实脱钩"的失败模式。这暗示了一种可能——精神疾病不是人类的 bug，而是任何高维认知系统的 feature。如果这个推测成立，那么未来我们不仅要为人类研发精神药理学，还要为 AI 研发某种意义上的"数字精神病学"。而 ECT 这种"重启式"疗法的存在本身，或许在暗示：对复杂认知系统而言，"关机再开机"有时比精细调参更有效——这个古老到近乎粗野的直觉，可能在下一个技术时代重新变得前沿。

📝 转录文本

一次意外的转变：从《飞越疯人院》到亲历者的证词

Lex： I think the surprising thing is I recently learned a friend of mine tried everything about 20 years ago, tried everything to with depression, and ECT is the last thing he tried — and it changed his life.

Scull: Yeah.

Lex: For the better.

Scull: That's not an uncommon story.

Lex: Yeah. And then I looked online and there's a lot of stories like this. And before learning of that, my — I'm embarrassed to say — knowledge of ECT was just One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest.

ECT 的黑暗历史与被迫的诚实

Scull: It has a terrible history in the 40s, 50s, and 60s. There are lots of — the CIA funded Ewen Cameron up in Canada. And he was giving multiple ECTs a day and reducing people to — well, they couldn't walk, they couldn't talk, they couldn't feed themselves, they were incontinent. And then he built them back up, or so he claimed, but in many cases they were left permanently damaged.

So I could recite lots of real horror stories about ECT. But it's also — if you're honest about the thing — what you just described, that is, patients who were on the brink of suicide, who had long-running depressions, some of them had ECT and they describe it as life-saving.

And as I say, when more controlled trials have been done recently, there's enough evidence now that it's hard to say this never works, this is just one of these desperate remedies we should consign to the dark ages.

关键困境：一种纯经验性的疗法

The complicating thing is: we do have no clue why it works. It's a purely empirical treatment.

Lex: Right.

Scull: And that itself, I think, tends to put people off. If you have a curable form of cancer and the surgeon says, "Well, I'm going to remove it," and she does — that's that. Because we understand, even a little bit, even if our knowledge of human biology is pretty primitive, we do understand a little bit that cancer is cells dividing uncontrollably and taking over and doing damage to the body and eventually killing you. And the fact that we can surgically remove it is a big deal.

There are lots of disorders. I have high blood pressure. If untreated, my blood pressure is like a 20-year-old's, thanks to treatment. It's an ongoing thing. I take the damn pill every day and it has a few minor side effects, but for me very minor ones. And it turns what could have killed me — either a stroke or a heart attack — into a condition that's very well controlled.

哪些疗法应被抛弃，哪些不应

So, you know, all of these things — they're complicated. It's easy with some of these things. With lobotomy, with insulin comas, deep sleep treatments, Henry Cotton's endeavors — those you can just say, "Well, we'll throw them away." And for a long time, I think ECT would have formed part of that cast of characters.

一本书的 40 年孕育：从 1981 到 2022

So when I first conceived the idea of writing Desperate Remedies, the book, it was back in 1981, and I was in London on a Guggenheim fellowship at the Wellcome Institute. And I hadn't done research in detail, but I was aware there were all these things looking about that had happened in the 1920s and '30s, and I thought that would be a very interesting thing to study.

And luckily, I didn't do it right away — or I did it piecemeal over the years. And I ended up writing a much more comprehensive look at psychiatry, really from its origins to now. I couldn't have written that book back then, and I would have missed all the developments from 1980 onwards, which are very, very important to the overall picture.

Lex: So, 40 years later, 2022.

Scull: Yes.

Lex: [laughter]

Scull: Yes, exactly.

Lex: Desperate Remedies: Psychiatry's Turbulent Quest to Cure Mental Illness.

双线并行的写作方法论

Scull: I've written a lot of books, and along the way — part of the way I think I've been productive and kept interested — I always had at least two projects on the go at once. You can't simultaneously write two things, but I'd have one and I'd work on it, and if I got tired of it, I'd pick up the other one for a bit and then go back.

And it also meant when I was working on one main project, I had other things percolating in my head. And I would come across things that were relevant to them and I'd make a note, and then I'd go back.

So when I finally did Desperate Remedies, I'd been thinking about those issues for 40 years. And that made a big difference, I think, to the way I approached things and to what I thought. Because — you either, like Thomas says, you say the same thing over and over and over again for 40 years, or you learn new things and you broaden what you know and you think about things in a different way, because you realize you haven't grasped the full complexity of what you're looking at.

为什么精神病学吸引了一生：苦难、跨文化恒常、与智识谜题

And so, look, what I found with psychiatry is: there are really a couple of fundamental things that have kept me engaged with the field.

One, it's an arena where there's tremendous human suffering, and it spreads out. As far as I know — and I wrote a big book called Madness and Civilization about from the ancient Greeks and ancient China to now — in every society I've studied, they have to cope with this. It takes different forms, it's regarded in different ways, it's treated differently, but there are people that deviate so far from the norm of what we regard as culturally appropriate. They exist everywhere.

So, the suffering, the difficulty of studying it, and then the fact that it is such a complex and difficult subject to understand. The very fact that we have such limits to our knowledge means there's space there to examine things in a very — in what needs to be a very — complicated way. And so it's an intellectual puzzle that's attracted some very, very smart people, but there's a long way to go.

Lex: Yeah, we have glimmers of insights about how the mind works, but if you look at the span of human history, we're probably in the very early days of understanding this particular one.
